not for one who is harsh toward sentient beings, and not for one who is hostile toward sentient beings.
Neither of the exhaustion of beings, nor of the destruction of beings,
nor of liberation from the non-exhaustion of beings.
not of the creeper Sattva,
not of the climbing plant Sattva,
nor of the vine Sattva;
Neither from the inequality of beings,
nor from the equality of beings, nor from the limitlessness of beings.
neither for the destruction of beings, nor for the incantation of beings,
nor for the food of beings;
It is not for the purpose of summoning beings,
nor for the purpose of dispersing beings, nor for the purpose of elevating beings, nor for the purpose of surpassing beings,
nor for the purpose of bringing peace to beings.
Neither of the *sattvailā*, nor of the *sattvavelā*,
nor of the *sattvatelā*.
not of Sattvaśailā, not of Sattvakelā,
nor of Sattvaśilā;
Neither from the *sattva-śvelā*, nor from the *sattva-nelā*,
nor from the *sattva-bhelā*.
Not of Sattvaselā, not of Sattvapelā, nor of Sattvahelā.
Not of the gathering of beings,
not of the swarm of beings, not of the wind of beings.
Neither of Sattvameruta, nor of Sattvakheluta, nor of Sattvamāluta.
Neither of one whose root is sentient beings,
nor of one whose source is sentient beings,
nor of one whose lotus is sentient beings.
Not for the sake of a beloved being, not for the sake of another being, nor for the sake of a dear being.
Not of one who is like a bamboo,
not of one who is like a reed,
not of one who is like grass.
Neither of the strength of a being,
nor of the form of a being,
nor of the broadness of the form of a being.
neither of the movement of a being, nor of the course of a being,
nor of the subjection of a being;
Neither of the excellence of beings, nor of the negligence of beings,
nor of the departure of beings.
Neither of the elevation of beings, nor of the designation of beings,
nor of the exhaustion of beings.
Not for the sake of one born as a sentient being, nor for the sake of one equal to a sentient being, nor for the sake of one possessing the nature of a sentient being.
Not of the blue-lotus-like being, not of the lotus-like being,
nor of the number of beings.
Neither of the approach to sentient beings, nor of the destiny of sentient beings, nor of the incalculability of sentient beings, nor of the revolution of the incalculability of sentient beings.
It is not for the sake of the immeasurability of beings, nor for the sake of the revolution of the immeasurable beings, nor for the sake of the boundlessness of beings.
not of the limitlessness of sentient beings, not of the boundlessness of sentient beings, not of the limitlessness of the cycle of sentient beings;
Not of a countable number of beings,
not of an incalculable cycle of beings, not of an incomparable number of beings.
not of a being equal to the unequalled, not of an inconceivable being, nor of an inconceivable transformation of a being;
Neither of the limitlessness of sentient beings,
nor of the revolution of the limitlessness of sentient beings, nor of the immeasurability of sentient beings.
neither of an expressible number of beings, nor of an inexpressible number of beings,
nor of an inexpressible multiple of beings;
It is not for the sake of inexpressibly inexpressible numbers of beings,
nor for the sake of inexpressibly inexpressible cycles of beings;
it is not for the sake of beings contained within a single world-system.
Not for the sake of beings included within inexpressibly inexpressible world-systems;
not for the sake of beings included within world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a four-continent world-system;
nor for the sake of beings included within world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a thousandfold world-system.
It is not for the sake of beings included within world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a two-thousandfold world-system;
nor for the sake of beings included within world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system;

nor even for the sake of beings included within world-systems as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-systems, that the bodhisattvas [strive] for enlightenment.

The mind is generated for the sake of bringing [beings] to maturity and discipline; moreover, the mind of the bodhisattvas is generated for the sake of awakening for the benefit of all sentient beings— without exception, without remainder, and without any left over— who are included within all world-systems, that is, for their maturation and discipline,
and not merely for the sake of attending upon a single Buddha.
The mind of the bodhisattvas arises for the sake of awakening—that is, for the purpose of pleasing, satisfying, honoring, and attending upon [the Buddhas].
It is not for the sake of pleasing, satisfying, honoring, and attending upon ten Buddhas;

nor does the mind of the bodhisattvas arise for the sake of awakening merely for the purpose of pleasing, satisfying, honoring, and attending upon as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable world-systems.

Bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for enlightenment merely for the sake of pleasing, honoring, and serving the lineage of Buddhas contained within a single world-system; nor even for the sake of pleasing, honoring, and serving the lineage of Tathāgatas contained within as many world-systems as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
It is for these purposes that the bodhisattvas generate the mind for enlightenment.

The bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for enlightenment merely for the sake of purifying a single buddha-field, nor even for the sake of purifying as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of world-systems;
nor do they do so merely for the sake of upholding the teaching of a single Tathāgata.
The bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for awakening until they have resolved to uphold the teachings of as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;

nor do they generate the mind for awakening until they have entered into the diversity of the vows and practices of a single Buddha, nor until they have mastered the diversity of the vows and practices of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

The bodhicitta of bodhisattvas does not arise for the sake of entering the array of a single Tathāgata’s buddha-field, nor even for the sake of entering arrays of Tathāgata buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields; rather, it arises for the sake of enlightenment itself.

Bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for enlightenment merely to enter into the differentiation of the assemblies and maṇḍalas of a single Buddha, nor even to enter into the differentiation of the assemblies and maṇḍalas of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
nor do they do so merely to uphold the wheel of Dharma of a single Tathāgata.
The bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for enlightenment until they have resolved to uphold the wheels of Dharma of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields;

nor do they generate the mind for enlightenment until they have resolved to enter the ocean of the minds of a single sentient being, nor until they have resolved to enter the ocean of the minds of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.

The bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for enlightenment for the sake of fully knowing the wheel of the faculties of a single sentient being, nor even for the sake of fully knowing the faculties of as many sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields;
nor for the sake of entering the ocean of the faculties of a single sentient being.

The bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for awakening merely to enter into the oceans of the faculties of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields;

nor do they generate the mind for awakening merely to enter into the succession of eons in a single world-system, up to entering into the succession of eons in world-systems as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.

The mind of enlightenment is generated for the sake of the awakening of bodhisattvas in order to enter into the continuity of the habitual tendencies of the conduct of all sentient beings included within a single world-system, and so on, up to entering into the continuity of the habitual tendencies of the conduct of all sentient beings included within as many world-systems as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
It is not for the sake of entering the ocean of all afflictions of the sentient beings contained within a single world-system,

nor even for the sake of entering the ocean of all afflictions of all sentient beings contained within as many world-systems as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, for the awakening of Bodhisattvas;
nor for the sake of entering the ocean of all karma of the sentient beings contained within a single world-system.

The bodhisattvas do not generate the mind for enlightenment until they have resolved to enter into the oceans of all the karmas of all sentient beings included within world-systems as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably, unspeakably many buddha-fields;
nor [do they do so] merely to enter into the oceans of all the conduct of all sentient beings included within a single world-system.

The mind of bodhisattvas for the sake of awakening does not arise merely to enter into the ocean of all the conduct of all sentient beings contained within world-systems as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields;

rather, the mind of bodhisattvas for the sake of awakening arises for the purpose of ripening and disciplining the realm of all sentient beings without exception, remainder, or residue. The mind of bodhisattvas for the sake of awakening arises for the purpose of pleasing, honoring, and attending upon all Buddhas without exception, remainder, or residue.
Bodhisattvas develop a yearning aspiration to please, honor, and attend upon all the lineages of Buddhas included within all world-systems without exception;
the resolve of bodhisattvas becomes firm for the sake of purifying all buddha-fields without exception.

The application of bodhisattvas arises for the sake of upholding the entire teaching of all Buddhas without exception; the mental impulses of bodhisattvas manifest for the sake of following the various distinctions of the practices and vows of all Tathāgatas without exception;
and the resolve of bodhisattvas is generated for the sake of entering into the arrays of qualities of all Buddha-fields of all Tathāgatas without exception.
The aspiration of bodhisattvas arises for entering the oceans of the circles of assemblies of all Tathāgatas without exception;

the prayer of bodhisattvas is born for plunging into the oceans of the minds of all living beings without exception; the longing of bodhisattvas is produced for the thorough knowledge of the wheel of the faculties of all sentient beings without exception.
The endurance of bodhisattvas arises for the sake of entering the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings without exception;

the aspiration of bodhisattvas is born for the sake of entering the succession of eons in all world-systems without exception; and the prowess of bodhisattvas arises for the sake of severing the continuity of the latencies of affliction of all sentient beings without exception.
The great sun of wisdom of the bodhisattvas rises to dry up the ocean of the karma and afflictions of all sentient beings without exception;
the light of insight of the bodhisattvas appears to fully comprehend the conduct of all sentient beings without exception;
the cloud of great compassion of the bodhisattvas arises to pacify the mass of the fires of suffering of all sentient beings without exception.
In brief, noble son, there are these ten foremost gateways to the methods of bodhisattva conduct, numbering hundreds of thousands of incalculables,
which are to be fully accomplished by a bodhisattva. Furthermore, noble son, the conduct of bodhisattvas is the convergence of all dharmas, namely, for the sake of following after primordial wisdom.

The conduct of bodhisattvas consists in the convergence of all buddha-fields, that is to say, for the sake of their purification. Noble son, for me who has such a vow, the ultimate limit of my vows is the purification of the realm of desire.
May they be so! May my vows reach that same consummation as the purification of the world-system;
may they reach that same consummation as the end of the latencies, connections, and underlying tendencies of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
May my vows be dedicated to that.
He asked, "Noble lady, what is the name of this liberation?

Noble son, regarding this..."
I know but a single liberation of a bodhisattva.

What could I possibly understand of those bodhisattvas whose minds are like the ocean because they receive all the qualities of a Buddha, and who are like Mount Meru because of the firmness of their resolute intention?

They are like the Sudarśana and Bhaiṣajyarāja medicinal herbs, in that they liberate all sentient beings from the diseases of the afflictions; they are like the sun, in that they dispel the darkness of ignorance for all sentient beings;
and their minds are like the earth, in that they serve as the foundation and support for all sentient beings.
They are like the wind, by virtue of accomplishing the welfare of the entire world;
they are like lamps, by virtue of providing the light of knowledge for all sentient beings;
they are like clouds, by virtue of raining down the Dharma correctly with a peaceful resonance.

To know the conduct or to speak of the qualities of those who are like the moon by virtue of emitting a network of light-rays of merit; or of those who are like Śakra by virtue of being committed to the protection of the entire world;
or to manifest the inconceivable trainings of the bodhisattvas—[this is impossible].
Or rather, it is impossible to fully demonstrate the conceptualizations of the bodhisattva’s vows, which are without end or middle.
Go, son of good family! Right here in the southern region, on the shore of the ocean, there is a country named Nalayu.

go to him and inquire.

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the laywoman Āśā; he circumambulated the laywoman Āśā hundreds of thousands of times, looking back at her again and again, prostrating himself, his face bathed in tears as he wept while reflecting upon the supreme difficulty of attaining awakening.
Reflecting upon the difficulty of pleasing a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), reflecting upon the extreme rarity of encountering a true person (satpuruṣa),

Reflecting on the rarity of the purity of a bodhisattva’s intention; reflecting on the rarity of encountering a compatible spiritual friend; and reflecting on the rarity of the mental realization that is directed toward awakening as it truly is.
Reflecting upon the rarity of the application of instruction in the method of the non-unequal Dharma; reflecting upon the rarity of generating the yoga of an unshakeable mental goodness;

(Gv 87) 11 Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, his mind following the instructions of the Bodhisattvas and his mind following the purification of the Bodhisattva conduct, [proceeded].

With a mind increasing the power of the merit of a bodhisattva; with a mind illuminated by the force of beholding the Buddhas; with a mental force born from the attainment of the treasury of the Dharma; with a mental force increased by the accomplishment of great vows; with a mind directed toward all directions of all phenomena; with a mind illuminated by the intrinsic nature of phenomena; with a mind that scatters all obscurations; with a mind that contemplates the realm of phenomena free from darkness; and with a mind of stainless intention, as indestructible as the vajra-jewel of Nārāyaṇa.
With a mind invincible and unassailable by the entire power of Māra, he proceeded by stages toward the region of Nālayu.
Having arrived there, he searched for the ṛṣi Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa.
At that time, the ṛṣi Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa was dwelling in a certain hermitage, which was delightful with its countless and diverse trees, creepers, and groves.

It was covered with various kinds of tree leaves; it possessed trees of diverse flowers that were always in full bloom and trees laden with fruit that were always abundant in produce; its ground was adorned with magnificent gem-stones from various jewel-trees; it featured well-distributed great sandalwood trees; it was graced by the constant emission of fragrance from delightful agalloch trees;

it was beautified by fragrances distributed in the four directions; it was decorated with *pāṭalī* trees arranged in the four directions; and it had a lovely configuration of banyan trees at its base.
In a place where trees bearing ever-ripening jambu fruits rained down [their bounty], and which was adorned with fresh lotus ponds and blue, red, and white water lilies,
the merchant’s son Sudhana beheld the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa, surrounded by ten thousand seers.
He was seated upon a grass mat within a hut whose floor was bound with sandalwood, wearing a crown of matted hair, and clothed in deerskins, darbha grass, robes, and bark garments.
Having seen him, he approached the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa.
Having approached, he beheld omniscience as the gateway to the spiritual friend— the intention of attaining a true spiritual friend—
and he beheld omniscience as dependent upon the instruction of the spiritual friend for the sake of leading one onto the true path.

Perceiving omniscience as dependent upon the service of spiritual friends through their leading one to the stage of omniscience; perceiving omniscience as illuminated by the torches of spiritual friends through their leading one to the jewel-island of the knowledge of the ten powers;
and perceiving omniscience as the path of spiritual friends through their generating the light of the knowledge of the ten powers.
Beholding omniscience as the lamp of the spiritual friend by virtue of its leading one to the unimpaired city of omniscience;
beholding the spiritual friend as the bridge to omniscience by virtue of his showing what is even and uneven;
and beholding omniscience as the parasol of the spiritual friend by virtue of its removing the fear of all precipices.

Perceiving omniscience as the impetus for spiritual friends through the production of the joy of the power of great loving-kindness; perceiving the nourishment of the vision of omniscience as dependent upon spiritual friends through the production of great compassion;
and perceiving the illumination of the method of the intrinsic nature of phenomena, he prostrated with his entire body, rose up, and [addressed] the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa.

Having circumambulated him many hundreds of thousands of times and standing before him with palms joined, he addressed him with pleasing words and gracious conduct, saying: "Noble One, I have set my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva."

How should I practice? I have heard, Noble One, that you give instruction and advice to the bodhisattvas; therefore, may the Noble One tell me: how should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct?
How should one practice?

Then the ṛṣi Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa, having looked upon those ten thousand youths, spoke thus: "O youths, by this son of good family, the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment has been generated, and all sentient beings have been invited with the gift of fearlessness.
O sons of good family, he stands ready for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, facing toward the ocean of gnosis."

Desiring to uphold the clouds of Dharma of all Tathāgatas, desiring to plunge into the oceans of the methods of all phenomena, desiring to abide in the light of great wisdom, desiring to bring forth the cloud of great compassion, desiring to pour down the rain of the great Dharma, having risen like the moon in the light of great wisdom, desiring to pacify the scorching heat of all afflictions, and desiring to increase the roots of virtue of all sentient beings.

Then indeed, those ten thousand young men, having scattered and strewn over the merchant’s son Sudhana flowers of various colors, beautiful and fragrant, and having saluted, paid homage, prostrated, and circumambulated him, uttered these words: "He shall be our savior."
It will pacify all the sufferings of the hells for all sentient beings; it will cut off the destiny of the animal realm; and it will turn back the destiny of the world of Yama.
He will bolt the door-leaves of all the gates to the inopportune states; he will dry up the ocean of craving;
he will sever the bond of craving.
He will turn back the mass of suffering;
he will dispel the darkness of ignorance;
and he will establish the protective circle of merit in the world.
He will reveal the ocean of the jewels of knowledge; he will cause the sun of knowledge to rise;
he will purify the eye of Dharma.
He will reveal what is even and uneven in the world.

Then the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa spoke thus to those young brahmins: "Young brahmins, he who has generated the thought of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, produces happiness for all sentient beings."
And in due course, he shall attain omniscience.
Young men, this son of good family has resolved his mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
he will fulfill the ground of all the qualities of a Buddha.
Then the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa said this to the merchant’s son Sudhana: "Noble son, I am a possessor of the liberation of the bodhisattva Aparājitadhvaja.

Thereupon, the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa extended his right hand, stroked the merchant’s son Sudhana on the head, and took hold of him with his right hand.
As soon as the merchant’s son Sudhana was grasped by the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa with his right hand,
at that very moment Sudhana saw buddha-fields in the ten directions equal in number to the atoms within a hundred thousand buddha-fields;
and he perceived himself at the feet of Tathāgatas equal in number to the atoms within those hundred thousand buddha-fields.
And he saw those buddha-fields, adorned with arrays of countless forms of purity;
and within them, he saw oceans of circles of assemblies of Tathāgatas, variegated with diverse colors and arrangements;
and within those oceans of circles of assemblies, he saw the bodies of the Tathāgatas, radiant and perfected with the primary and secondary marks.
And from them he hears the teaching of the Dharma, never turning away from even a single word or syllable; he maintains those wheels of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, which are mutually unconfused,
and he receives those clouds of Dharma as they rain down upon the various dispositions of sentient beings.
And he enters into the oceans of the former vows of those Tathāgatas, purified by the power of various inclinations;
and he enters into the oceans of the attainment of Buddhahood, purified by those oceans of various vows.
And he beheld those praises of the Buddhas, which communicate the satisfaction of thousands of sentient beings according to their respective inclinations;
he saw those networks of Buddha-rays, which were mandalas of various pure and stainless arrays;
and he entered into those powers of the Buddhas by following the light of unobstructed knowledge.
In some places he perceives a day and night at the feet of the Tathāgata; in some places seven days and nights;
in some places half a month.
In some cases he perceives a month, in some a year, in some a hundred years, in some a thousand years, in some a hundred thousand years,

in some ten million years, in some a billion years, in some ten billion years, in some a hundred billion years, in some a trillion years, in some ten trillion years, in some a hundred trillion years, and in some half an eon.
In some cases he perceives an eon; in some cases a hundred eons; in some cases a thousand eons; in some cases a hundred thousand eons; in some cases ten million eons;
in some cases a hundred ten-million eons; in some cases a thousand ten-million eons; in some cases a hundred thousand ten-million eons; in some cases a hundred thousand nayutas of ten-million eons;
and in some cases, at the feet of the Tathāgata, he perceives as many as ineffably ineffable eons.
In some places, he perceives eons equal in number to the atoms within Jambudvīpa at the feet of the Tathāgatas;

in other places, he perceives eons equal in number to the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Illuminated by the wisdom of the Bodhisattva Aparājitadhvaja’s liberation, having attained the illumination of the Vairocanagarbha samādhi, following the liberations and samādhis of inexhaustible wisdom, and having attained the gateway of the Samantadikpañjara dhāraṇī.
His mind was illuminated by the entrance to the *Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī*; he had attained the dwelling of the meditative absorption on the sphere of the well-distinguished peak of knowledge;

his range was the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) on the path of universal arrays; he was pervaded by the light of the meditative absorption of the *Buddhagaganagarbha-maṇḍala*;

his mind was illumined by the meditative absorption of the rim of the wheel of all the Buddhas' Dharma; and he had attained the light of the meditative absorption of the inexhaustible jewel-maṇḍala of the knowledge of the three times.
Then the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa released the merchant’s son Sudhana.
He perceived himself once again standing before the seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa.
The seer Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa said to him, "Do you remember, noble son?"
He said, "I remember it, Noble One, through the empowerment of my spiritual friend.
He replied, "Noble son, I know only this Bodhisattva liberation called 'Invincible Banner.
What can I possibly say of the Bodhisattvas who have attained the samādhi that enters into the superknowledges of the distinguished wisdom of all worlds?"

They have mastery over all wheels of time; they are skilled in bringing forth the knowledge of the characteristics of a Buddha; they possess arrays of communication that enter the days of the Tathāgatas; they have converged into the single-characteristic knowledge whose domain is the three times; their bodies are well-distributed throughout all world-systems; their bodies of knowledge illuminate the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
they arise facing toward the inclinations of all sentient beings; and their conduct and movements accord with the appropriate behavior suited to the inclinations of sentient beings.

To know the conduct of those who delight in universal radiance and whose maṇḍalas of stainless, vast, and beautiful gnosis are purified; or to speak of their qualities; or to indicate their particular vows; or to know their formation of buddha-fields; or to fathom the range of their gnosis; or to follow the domain of their meditative concentrations; or to enter into their miraculous transformations; or to [comprehend] their playful mastery in the power of liberation—[this is impossible].
or to follow after [them], or to grasp the cause for the differentiation of bodies, or to manifest the purity of the circle of sounds, or to display the radiance of primordial wisdom.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region there is a country named Īṣāṇa.
There dwells a brahmin named Jayoṣmāyatana.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then, indeed, the merchant's son Sudhana was illuminated by the wisdom of the bodhisattva liberation called "Invincible Banner."

He dwelt in the direct perception of the miraculous transformations within the inconceivable domain of the Buddhas; he possessed the supernormal knowledge of the direct realization of the inconceivable liberations of the Bodhisattvas;

his mind was illuminated by the wisdom of the inconceivable samādhis of the Bodhisattvas; he had attained the illumination of the wisdom of the samādhi that converges upon all times; he was illumined by the objective range of the samādhi that converges upon the attachment to all conceptualizations; and he had attained the light of wisdom that distinguishes the particularities of the entire world.

Facing toward the dwelling in the sphere that follows all three times; supreme in the knowledge that teaches the equality of non-dual conceptualization; possessing the light of knowledge extended toward all objects of perception; skilled in the treasury of pure resolve and patience directed toward the faith of sentient beings; having attained the light of the knowledge of certainty regarding the patience for the nature of phenomena;

with a mind never devoid of the cultivation of the intrinsic nature of the bodhisattva’s conduct and the superknowledges that follow everywhere; and with a mind irreversible due to the momentum toward omniscience.

He had attained the illumination of the lightning-flash of the knowledge of the ten powers; his mind was insatiable in its longing for the resonance of the Dharma-realm; his mind was intent on the practice of entering the sphere of the dwelling of omniscience;

his mind was dedicated to accomplishing the infinite arrays of the bodhisattva’s conduct; his mind was focused on purifying the mandala of the infinite great vows of the bodhisattvas; his mind was oriented toward the wisdom that follows the inexhaustible net of world-systems without center or end; and his mind was undaunted in maturing and disciplining the ocean of infinite sentient beings.

Beholding the infinite sphere of the bodhisattva’s conduct; beholding the infinite variety of destinies in world-systems; beholding the infinite diversity of the classifications of world-systems; beholding the inclusion within them of infinite subtle and vast objects of focus; beholding the infinite variety of the networks of perceptions and designations for the foundations of world-systems; beholding the infinite variety of worldly conventions, designations, and relative truths; [and beholding] the infinite variety of the inclinations of sentient beings.
Beholding the infinite diversity of the manifestations of sentient beings, beholding the infinite sequence of the ripening and disciplining of sentient beings,

and beholding the infinite variety of the perceptions of direction and time regarding sentient beings, he proceeded in due order toward the brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana in the region of Īṣāṇa, bringing the spiritual friends before him.
He approached him.
At that time, the brahmin Jayoṣmāyana was performing fierce austerities, having made omniscience his objective;
around him on all four sides, a great mass of fire, as large as a mountain, blazed forth.

"How should one proceed?
He said, "Go, son of good family;
having ascended this mountain with its path of razor edges, throw yourself here into the pit of fire."
In this way, your conduct as a bodhisattva will reach complete purity.
Then, this thought occurred to the merchant’s son Sudhana: "The turning away from the eight unfavorable conditions is difficult to obtain;
the acquisition of human birth is difficult to obtain;
the purity of the perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to obtain."
The arising of a Buddha is difficult to encounter;
the possession of unimpaired faculties is difficult to obtain;
hearing the Buddha’s Dharma is difficult to find.

genuine spiritual friends are difficult to find;
the bestowal of instruction in the true method is difficult to find.

the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma is difficult to find.
Let this not be Māra, or one possessed by Māra, or a member of Māra’s host, or a counterfeit spiritual friend, or a destroyer of Bodhisattvas.
He who has set out to create an obstacle to my roots of merit,
he who has risen up to bring about the end of my life.
May he not wish to create an obstacle for me regarding omniscience;
may he not wish to lead me along a perilous path;
may he not wish to create an obstacle for me regarding the entrance to the Dharma for the sake of attaining the Buddha-dharmas.
As he was thus engaged in such reflection and mental attention, ten thousand Brahmās, stationed in the sky above, spoke as follows: "O son of good family, do not fortify your intention in this way.

O son of good family, this noble one has attained the illumination of the *vajrārcis* (diamond-flame) samādhi; he possesses irreversible vigor and is committed to a great undertaking for the sake of crossing over [samsara]. He has risen up to exhaust all affection for the world."

He is engaged in tearing asunder the net of all views, he has set himself to burn away the thicket of all afflictions and karmas, and he is striving to illuminate the wilderness of all unfavorable conditions for knowledge.

He is established for the sake of turning back the fear of falling into the precipice of old age and death for all sentient beings; he is devoted to the destruction of the darkness of the three times; and he has set out for the sake of emitting the rays of light of all dharmas.

For, noble son, while he was practicing the fivefold heat, all those brahmins who— being attached to various types of views— imagined within themselves agency, lordship, and preeminence over the entire world, [were all overcome] by the power of his undertaking of such fierce ascetic vows.
They do not take delight in their own abodes;
not relishing the pleasure of meditative concentration, they approach him.

Upon their arrival, he overcomes them through the power of his supernatural faculties and by means of his fierce vows and asceticism, and for the sake of turning them away from all views and abandoning all pride and intoxication, he teaches them the Dharma.

He teaches the Dharma for the sake of pervading all worlds with great loving-kindness and great compassion, for strengthening the firm resolve for enlightenment, for making the production of the thought of enlightenment vast, for facing the manifestation of all Buddhas, for the attainment and fulfillment of the mandala of the Buddha’s voice, and for the non-obstruction and non-hindrance of the Buddha’s sound which resonates everywhere.

And ten thousand Māras, standing in the sky above, scattered divine jewels and gems and spoke thus: "O son of good family, as he performs the five-fold austerity, light rays have issued from this mass of flames and have eclipsed our palaces, our bodies, our dwellings, our ornaments, and our enjoyments.
Having become filled with spiritual urgency, we, together with our retinues, approach his presence."

And to us who have approached her, she teaches the Dharma in such a way that, having attained realization within our own minds and having generated the resolve for awakening, we become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And ten thousand kings of the gods who exercise power (vaśavartin), having scattered divine flowers, spoke thus: "O son of good family, while he was practicing the five-fold heat, we found no pleasure in our own abodes;
therefore, we, together with our respective kinsmen and retinues, have approached his presence."
To us who have approached him, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining mastery over one's own mind;

for the sake of attaining mastery over all afflictions; for the sake of attaining mastery over rebirth according to one's intention; for the sake of attaining mastery over the purification of all karmic obstructions;
for the sake of attaining mastery over all meditative attainments; for the sake of the array and purity of the mastery of requisites; and for the sake of mastery according to one's intention.
And he teaches the Dharma.

And ten thousand Sunirmita kings of the gods, standing in the sky above, having performed worship with the sweet resonance of the sounds produced by celestial musical performances, spoke thus: "O son of good family, as you practice the five-fold heat, such radiance issues forth from these mountain peaks of fire that our celestial palaces are being scorched by it."
They become purified and even more radiant;
and these ornaments—
And these apsarases,
as well as we ourselves, now accompanied by our retinues of sons of gods and hosts of apsarases, find no delight in sensual pleasures;
we do not rejoice in the happiness of desire.
With our bodies and minds thus gladdened, we approached him; and as we drew near,
he taught us the Dharma for the purification of the mind—

for the luminosity of the mind, for the wholesomeness of the mind, for the adaptability of the mind, for the generation of joy in the mind, and for the attainment and purification of the knowledge of the ten powers.

He teaches the Dharma for the sake of increasing the great momentum of the Dharma, for the purification of the body, for the manifestation of the immeasurable bodies of the Buddhas; for the purification of speech, for the attainment of the voice of the Tathāgata; and for the purification of the mind, for the attainment of omniscience.
And ten thousand Tuṣita kings of gods, together with their retinues of sons of gods and hosts of apsarases, standing in the sky above, rained down a cloud of all kinds of fragrant powders;
having thus honored and paid homage, they spoke as follows: "O noble son, while you were practicing the fivefold heat-penance, we found no pleasure in our own abodes."
Being dissatisfied with those things, we approach him.
Then, for us who have approached him, he teaches the Dharma so that we may disregard all sense objects;

he teaches the Dharma for the sake of a mind of contentment, for the sake of mental satisfaction, for the sake of generating roots of virtue, for the sake of attaining the arousal of the thought of awakening, and so on, up to the complete fulfillment of all the qualities of a Buddha.

And ten thousand Suyāma deva kings, together with their retinues of devaputras and hosts of apsarases, having rained down divine showers of māndārava flowers, spoke thus: "O son of good family, while you are practicing the five-fold austerity, we find no delight in our divine music. Being thus disenchanted, we have come into your presence."
Then, for us who have approached him, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of turning away from all delight in sensual pleasures, up to the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha.
And one hundred thousand Śakra-devendras, each accompanied by thirty-two Upendras and surrounded by hosts of devaputras and apsarases,

having rained down clouds of divine garments, jewels, ornaments, and flowers, spoke thus: "O son of good family, as you practice the fivefold austerity, we find no delight in all our Śakra-heavens, gardens, pleasure groves, divine musical instruments, cymbals, services, songs, and enjoyments."
Being dissatisfied with that, we approach him;

then, for us who have approached him, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all delight in sensual pleasures, uttering these words: "All this is impermanent, unstable, and subject to decay."
He teaches the Dharma for the sake of utterly severing all pride and negligence, and for the purpose of increasing the aspiration for unsurpassed enlightenment.
Furthermore, noble son, by his very glance these peaks of Mount Meru have been shaken.
We, with hearts agitated and stirred, through the firmness of our resolve to generate the mind set on omniscience, bring forth our vow toward the wisdom of omniscience.
And ten thousand nāgas, headed by the nāga kings Airāvaṇa, Nanda, and Upananda, moving through the sky above,
rained down clouds of divine kālānusāri sandalwood, accompanied by the sweet sounds of the singing of nāga maidens and the discharge of streams of divine fragrant water,
and spoke thus: "O son of good family, while you were practicing the five-fold heat, light was emitted from these great masses of fire."
Having illuminated all the abodes of the nāgas, they dispel the fear of the suparṇins by raining down sand;
having pacified their outbursts of anger and gladdened their dispositions, they cause their minds to become serene. Then, for us whose minds are thus serene, he teaches the Dharma.
That is to say, for the sake of loathing the state of an inferior elephant and for the abandonment of all obstructive karma,
he causes them to confess their transgressions, to generate the resolve for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and to establish themselves in omniscience.

Then ten thousand lords of the yakṣas, standing in the expanse of the sky, having honored them with various kinds of worship, spoke thus to the brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana and the merchant’s son Sudhana: “Noble son, as this one performs the five-fold austerity, a mind of loving-kindness toward human beings arises within our retinue.”
All the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*).
With these minds of loving-kindness, intent on non-harming, they approach us, saying: "We too are now overcome by the sovereign power of loving-kindness; we find no delight in our respective abodes."
Therefore, we, together with our kinsmen and retinues, approach his presence.
When we have approached him, the radiance issuing from his body illuminates us, and with its bliss it pervades our entire bodies.
To us, whose bodies and minds are thus gladdened, he teaches the Dharma in such a way.
That many yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, kaṭapūtanas, and others generate the aspiration for awakening.

And ten thousand lords of the Gandharvas, standing in the sky above, spoke thus: "Noble son, even while we dwell in our own palaces, the light issuing from these mounds of fire as he performs this five-fold austerity illuminates our abodes.
Touched by that radiance and endowed with inconceivable bliss, we have come into his presence."
To us who have approached him, he teaches the Dharma in such a way that we become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And ten thousand lords of the asuras, having emerged from the great ocean, bowed their right knees upon the ground in the sky, joined their palms in reverence, and paid homage, saying: "O son of good family, while you were practicing the five-fold heat, all our asura worlds, along with the oceans, mountains, and the great terrestrial circles, trembled.
Consequently, we, with all our pride, intoxication, and arrogance destroyed, overcome by your vows and asceticism, have approached your presence."

To us who have approached him, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all deceit and guile, for entering into the patience regarding the profound Dharma, for being established in the immovable nature of phenomena, and for the perfect accomplishment of the knowledge of the ten powers.

And ten thousand lords of the *garuḍas*, headed by the lord of the *garuḍas* Mahāvegadhārī, having manifested a magnificent form as young brahmins, spoke thus: "O son of good family, as you perform the five-fold austerity, light radiates from these masses of fire, illuminating our abodes and causing them to tremble.
We, being afraid, terrified, and with agitated minds, have approached your presence."
This very person, noble son,
through his teaching of the Dharma, establishes us in great loving-kindness and encourages us to undertake great compassion.
He establishes them in plunging into the ocean of saṃsāra; he establishes them in uplifting sentient beings submerged in the mire of desire;
and he applies them to the purification of the gateway of the resolve for awakening.
He establishes them in the sharpness of wisdom and skillful means;
he incites them to the discipline of sentient beings who have not yet reached maturity.
And ten thousand lords of the *kiṃnaras*, standing in the sky above, spoke thus: "O son of good family, as he performs the five-fold austerity,
from the rows of palm trees in our palaces stirred by the wind— from the *kiṃkiṇī* nets, jeweled thread garlands, musical trees,
all kinds of musical instruments, precious ornaments, and household articles— the sound of the Buddha issues forth."
The sound of the word "Dharma," the sound of the irreversible Bodhisattva Saṅgha, and the sound of the resolve for the Bodhisattva's setting forth resounded:
"In such-and-such a world-system, a Bodhisattva named so-and-so is making a vow for enlightenment;
in such-and-such a world-system, a Bodhisattva named so-and-so is performing the renunciation of difficult deeds."
In such-and-such a world-system, a bodhisattva named so-and-so purifies the mandala of the knowledge of omniscience;
in such-and-such a world-system, a bodhisattva named so-and-so approaches the seat of awakening;
in such-and-such a world-system, a bodhisattva named so-and-so, having defeated Māra along with his retinue, awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"In such a number of world-systems, a Tathāgata named so-and-so turns the wheel of Dharma; in such a number of world-systems, a Tathāgata named so-and-so, having completed all the works of a Buddha without exception, passes into final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder."

"Noble son, the number of all the grasses, woods, branches, leaves, and petals in Jambudvīpa, even when divided into their ultimate atomic particles, would be finite; but there is no end to those names of Tathāgatas, the vows of Bodhisattvas, and the specific distinctions of the Bodhisattvas' setting out in their conduct— from which,

as they are stirred by the wind from the rows of palm trees in our palace up to all the musical instruments, jeweled ornaments, and household enjoyments, the sounds of the Buddha-dharma and awakening issue forth and resound."
They come within the range of our auditory consciousness.

Noble son, having given rise to a great surge of joy and rapture through the sound of the names of the Buddha, the Saṅgha, the bodhisattvas’ setting forth, their vows, and their conduct, we have approached his presence.
When we approach him, he teaches the Dharma in such a way that many beings in our assembly become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

And immeasurable thousands of sons of the gods from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), possessing most sublime and magnificent complexions, stood in the sky and, having performed worship with mind-made offerings, spoke thus: "O son of good family, as this one performs the five-fold heat-penance, such radiance issues forth from these mounds of fire that, having illuminated all the hells down to the Avīci hell, has brought to rest all the sufferings of the beings in those hells."
By that very radiance, he has come into the range of our vision.
Having purified our minds toward him, we were reborn among the sublime classes of gods belonging to the desire realm.
Out of gratitude for him, never satiated by the sight of him, we have abandoned all delight in sensual pleasures and approach his presence.
Then, as we approached him, he taught us the Dharma in such a way that immeasurable beings resolved their minds toward awakening.

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness, having heard this Dharma-method, conceived the perception of the Brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana as a true spiritual friend.
He prostrated at the feet of the Brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana and said: "Noble one, I confess my transgression as a transgression."
"I am one who disregards the instructions of the spiritual friend.
Then the brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana addressed the merchant's son Sudhana in verse:
"The Bodhisattva who provides instruction by performing a circumambulation..."
Having fixed the mind single-pointedly upon the gurus, one should have no doubts;
then all his aims will be fulfilled, and those [teachings] will be auspicious.
Furthermore, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he awakens to the auspicious wisdom of a Buddha. // 1 //
Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, having ascended that mountain precipice-path strewn with razor edges, fell into a great mass of fire there.
As he was falling, he attained the bodhisattva samādhi called "Well-Established.
And by that touch of fire, he attained the bodhisattva samādhi called "Knowledge of the Bliss of Tranquility."

He spoke thus: "It is wonderful, Noble One, that this mass of fire is so pleasant to the touch, and yet this mountain path leading to the precipice is strewn with razor edges! He replied: "I am [the one], O son of good family."

I am a possessor of the bodhisattva liberation called "The Sphere that is Never Exhausted. Noble son, this is the extent of my knowledge regarding this bodhisattva liberation of the "Sphere that is Never Exhausted.

What could I possibly know of the bodhisattvas who are like rays of radiant light, whose vows never exhaust the afflictions and views of all living beings, whose banners are irreversible, whose hearts are never exhausted, whose minds are not dejected, and whose mentalities do not shrink back?

To know the conduct or to speak of the virtues of those who are like Vajragarbha-Nārāyaṇas in their great undertakings, who do not despond in crossing over [the ocean of existence], whose application is never slack, who are like whirlwinds, who are dedicated to the welfare of the entire world, whose vigor is irreversible, and whose armor is never turned back? Go, son of good family!
Right here in this very southern region is a city named Siṃhavijṛmbhita;
there dwells a maiden named Maitrāyaṇī,
the daughter of King Siṃhaketu.
She is accompanied by a retinue of five hundred maidens; go to her and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana, circumambulated the brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana hundreds of thousands of times, and departed from the presence of the brahmin Jayoṣmāyatana. 10.
(Gv 96) 13. Maitrāyaṇī.
Then indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, having emerged from the inconceivable range of spiritual friends and being purified by his noble resolve, [proceeded].

Facing toward the Mahāyāna, desiring the wisdom of a Buddha, converging upon the qualities of a Buddha, longing for the company of spiritual friends, investigating the range of the Dharma, facing toward unimpeded knowledge, well-settled in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), having as his domain the station of the pinnacle of knowledge,

following the pinnacle of moments in the three times, facing toward the non-duality of the limit of space, having attained certainty regarding the limit of non-duality, he dwells without conceptualization in the limit of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

He has entered the cessation of discipline at the limit of non-obstruction; he is supreme in the non-contradiction of the limits of karma; he dwells in the non-conceptualization of the limits of the Tathāgatas;

he is supreme in the wisdom that scatters the net of conceptualizations regarding all sentient beings; he is free from attachment to all fields; his mind is harmonized within the circles of the assemblies of all Buddhas; he dwells without a home within the purities of all Buddhas; he perceives all sentient beings as being without self and without a sentient-being-nature; and [he is so] regarding all sounds.
Having transcended the path of speech and being supremely skilled in the cognition of reflections within all forms, he proceeded by stages toward the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhita.
Searching for and seeking out the maiden Maitrāyaṇī, he heard it said:
"This maiden Maitrāyaṇī, the daughter of King Siṃhaketu, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred maidens, has ascended to the terrace of the Vairocanagarbha palace."

Seated upon a magnificent throne covered with divine robes, draped with a network of golden threads, and supported by legs of uragasāra sandalwood, he was teaching the Dharma. Having heard this, Siṃhavijṛmbhita entered the city, approached the palace of King Siṃhaketu, and stood at the outer gatehouse, desiring to see the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
There he saw many hundreds of living beings,
many thousands of living beings, and many hundreds of thousands of living beings entering [the city].
Having seen them, he asked: "Where are you going, noble sons, or from where have you come? They replied: "To the presence of Maitrāyaṇī, in order to hear the Dharma."
The thought occurred to him: "No one here is prevented from entering.
Thus he entered.
Having entered, he beheld that Vairocanagarbha palace upon a ground established of crystal.

It was adorned with pillars made of lapis lazuli and walls made of diamond; it was embellished by hundreds of thousands of turrets and pinnacles of Jāmbūnada gold; it was fashioned with circular jewel-mirrors containing thousands of various kinds of innumerable mani-gems;

it was an array of world-illuminating mani-jewels, surrounded by an incalculable net of jewels, and graced with the inconceivable adornment of the sweet resonance of hundreds of thousands of golden bells being stirred.
And he saw that daughter of Maitrāyaṇī, with her deep-blue eyes, deep-blue hair, and golden-colored skin.

Having bowed his head at her feet and circumambulated her hundreds of thousands of times, he stood with palms joined and said this: "Noble Lady, I have set my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva."

"How should I practice? I have heard, Noble Lady, that you give instruction and advice to the bodhisattvas; therefore, may the Noble Lady tell me how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct."
"How should one practice?
He replied, "Look, noble son, at the arrays of my palace.
As he looked all around, he saw that from each wall, each pillar, each mirror-disk, each form, each configuration, and each jewel-gem, [there appeared...]

From each single golden bell, from each single jewel tree, from each single pore, and from each single jewel necklace, there appeared through the power of manifestation Tathāgatas whose essence is the *dharmadhātu*, together with their initial generation of the mind of awakening, their spheres of conduct and vows, their arrays of departure, their miraculous displays of perfect enlightenment, their turnings of the wheel of Dharma, and their demonstrations of final nirvana.
And just as it is from one object of focus, so it is from all objects of focus.
It is just as, for example, in a lake of water that is clear, untroubled, and serene, the sky— adorned with the moon, the sun, and the host of stars— is seen through the occurrence of a reflection.
In this very way, from each and every object within the Vairocanagarbha palace, Tathāgatas pervading the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) are seen through the power of reflection;
that is to say, by virtue of the outflow of the girl Maitrāyaṇī’s former roots of merit.
Having observed that, and maintaining the sign of that array of visions of the Buddhas, he stood with palms joined and gazed upon the words of the girl Maitrāyaṇī.
She said, "Noble son, I am a recipient of this chapter on the entrance to the perfection of wisdom called the Universal Array (*Samantavyūha*).

This chapter on the entrance to the perfection of wisdom, the Universal Array, has been sought out by me from the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in thirty-six Ganges rivers.
And those Tathāgatas caused me to enter this chapter on the entrance to the perfection of wisdom, the Universal Array, through various modes of entry."
And that which was taught by one is not [the same as] that taught by a second.
He asked: "Noble Lady, what is the domain of this chapter on the entrance to the perfection of wisdom called 'The Universal Array'?"
He said: "Noble son, for me— who was bringing this chapter on the entrance to the perfection of wisdom called the Universal Array (*samantavyūha*) face-to-face,
who was contemplating it, following it, investigating it, reflecting upon it, forming its mental images, retaining it, arranging it,
accomplishing it, adorning it, and discerning it— the dhāraṇī named 'Universal Gate' (*samantamukhā*) arose."
In that dhāraṇī-maṇḍala, ten hundreds of thousands of incalculable gateways of the Dharma revolve,

converge, become manifest, descend upon, and circulate— namely: the gateway of the buddha-field, the gateway of the Buddha, the gateway of the Dharma, the gateway of all sentient beings, the gateway of the past, the gateway of the future, the gateway of the present, and the gateway of the limit of existence.

The gateway of merit, the gateway of the accumulation of merit, the gateway of knowledge, the gateway of the accumulation of knowledge, the gateway of aspiration, the gateway of the differentiation of aspirations, the gateway of conduct, the gateway of the purity of conduct, the gateway of the arising of conduct, the gateway of the fulfillment of conduct, the gateway of action, the gateway of the illumination of action, the gateway of the stream of action, the gateway of the formation of action, and the gateway of the sphere of action.

The gateway of avoiding unwholesome actions, the gateway of practicing right action, the gateway of mastery over karma, the gateway of good conduct, the gateway of encouraging others in good conduct, the gateway of meditative concentration, the gateway of following after concentration, the gateway of investigating concentration, the gateway of the domain of concentration, the gateway of emerging from concentration, and the gateway of supernormal knowledge.

The gateway of the ocean of mind; the gateway of the enumeration of mind; the gateway of the purification of the creeper of mind; the gateway of the illumination of the thicket of mind; the gateway of the clarification of the lake of mind; the gateway of the arising of mind; the gateway of the investigation of mind; the gateway of the activity of the afflictions of sentient beings; the gateway of the latencies of affliction; the gateway of the application of affliction; the gateway of resolute belief; the gateway of the conduct of sentient beings; and the gateway of the diversity of the conduct of sentient beings.

The gateway of the world’s arising; the gateway of the inclinations of sentient beings; the gateway of the sphere of perception of sentient beings; the gateway of the directions; the gateway of the directions of the Dharma;
the gateway of great compassion; the gateway of great loving-kindness; the gateway of peace; the gateway of the path of speech; the gateway of method; the gateway of following;
the gateway of differentiation; the gateway of convergence; the gateway of the limit of non-attachment; the universal gateway; and the gateway of the Buddha-dharmas.

The gateway of the bodhisattva-dharma, the gateway of the śrāvaka-dharma, the gateway of the pratyekabuddha-dharma, the gateway of worldly dharmas, the gateway of the arising of the world, the gateway of the dissolution of the world, the gateway of the structure of the world, the gateway of the purification of world-systems, the gateway of the defilement of world-systems,

the gateway of world-systems that are both defiled and purified, the gateway of world-systems that are both purified and defiled, the gateway of exclusively defiled world-systems, and the gateway of exclusively purified world-systems.

The gateway of following the level surface of world-systems; the gateway of inverted world-systems; the gateway of hanging head-downward; the gateway of entering the net of Indra; the gateway of the revolution of world-systems; the gateway of the sphere of perception regarding foundations; the gateway of following the subtle and the vast; the gateway of entering the vast and the subtle; the gateway of beholding the Buddhas; the gateway of the diversity of the bodies of the Buddhas; the gateway of the manifold variety of the nets of light-rays of the Buddhas; the gateway of the differentiation of the mandala of the voices of the Buddhas.

The gateway of the accomplishment of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma; the gateway of the indivisibility of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma; the gateway of the etymological explanation of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma;
the gateway of the turning and revolving of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma; the gateway of the Buddha’s body; the gateway of the Buddha’s assembly circle;
the gateway of the differentiation of the Buddha’s assembly circle; the gateway of entering the oceans of the Buddha’s assembly circles; the gateway of the illumination of the Buddha’s powers.

The gateway of the samādhis of the Buddhas; the gateway of the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas' samādhis; the gateway of the abodes of the Buddhas; the gateway of the empowerments of the Buddhas;

the gateway of the emanations of the Buddhas; the gateway of the communication of the minds of other beings by the Buddhas; the gateway of the miraculous displays of the Buddhas; the gateway of dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven up to the manifestation of final parinirvāṇa; the gateway of performing the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings; and the gateway of the profound method of the Dharma.

The gateway of the manifold methods of the Dharma; the gateway of the form of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma; the gateway of the Dharma whose nature is the arising of the thought of awakening; the gateway of the nature of the provisions for the thought of awakening; the gateway of the nature of the vow; the gateway of the nature of conduct; the gateway of the nature of the superknowledges; the gateway of the nature of the departure [from saṃsāra]; the gateway of the nature of the purification of the dhāraṇīs; the gateway of the nature of the purification of the mandala of gnosis; the gateway of the nature of the complete purity of wisdom.
The gateway of the form of the immeasurables of awakening; the gateway of the purity of mindfulness.
Noble son, I know only this chapter on the gateway of the perfection of wisdom called the Array of Universal Mindfulness.
What could I possibly know of those whose minds are equal to the realm of space?

Of the Bodhisattvas, whose intellects are vast as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), whose mental continuums are sustained by the accumulation of merit, who have entered upon the supramundane path, for whom worldly conditions no longer manifest, who have obtained the eye of the light of knowledge free from darkness, who have penetrated the entire realm of phenomena without obscurity, whose intellects are immeasurable like space, whose eyes are the recollection of all objects of focus, who contain within them the light of the unattached stage, and who are skilled in the distinctions of the words and meanings of all phenomena.

To know the conduct or to speak of the virtues of those who have overcome all worlds; who investigate the methods of worldly behavior; who possess blameless courses of action throughout all worlds; who are supreme in performing beneficial deeds for all worlds; who are the refuge for the entire world; who understand the rules for the conventional usage of speech in all worlds; who dwell within the intentions of all worlds; who manifest their communications according to those very intentions; and who exercise mastery over the wheel of time in all its aspects.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region there is a country called Trinayana.
There dwells a monk named Sudarśana.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the maiden Maitrāyaṇī, circumambulated her hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at her again and again, departed from the presence of the maiden Maitrāyaṇī. 11.
(Gv 99) 14. Sudarśana.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, reflecting deeply upon the investigation of the bodhisattva’s wisdom, [proceeded].
Contemplating the profound penetration into the depths of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
contemplating the profound all-pervasive subtle knowledge, and contemplating the profundity inherent in the conceptual categories of the world;
Reflecting upon the profundity of the ground of non-conditioning,
reflecting upon the profundity of the ground of the stream of consciousness,
and reflecting upon the profundity of the ground of dependent origination.
Contemplating the profundity of the ground of the truth of intrinsic nature; contemplating the profundity of the ground of the truth of the conventional transactions of all worlds;
contemplating the profundity of the ground of the array adorned by the realm of phenomena.
Reflecting on the depth of the surface of the body-mechanism,
and reflecting on the depth of the surface of the world of karma and mind,
he proceeded by stages toward the region of Trinayana, seeking out the monk Sudarśana.

In the course of his travels through districts, cities, towns, market towns, villages, cowherd settlements, hermitages of seers, various regions and localities, waterways, mountain ranges, and great forest groves, he saw the monk Sudarśana in a certain place.

And in a forest grove, he saw a young man, youthful, handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold; one whose hair was deep blue and curled to the right, whose head was shaped like a parasol and crowned with a *uṣṇīṣa*, who had a broad forehead and large, deep-blue eyes with eyelashes like those of a cow; one whose nose-bridge was sweet, elevated, lovely, and high, whose lips were as well-knit as vermilion or gold, who possessed forty even, uniform, very white, complete teeth, and a jaw like that of a lion.

With full and well-developed cheeks, with eyebrows as beautiful as a curved bow, marked with a tilaka by a moon-like ūrṇā hair between the brows, with long, hanging ears, and a face as gentle as the rising moon; with a neck as beautiful and rounded as a conch shell, a heart adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, the upper body like that of a lion,
with broad shoulders and well-rounded muscles, with long arms, fingers joined by a web, and hands and feet marked with wheels.

With hands and feet soft, youthful, and well-fleshed; possessing the seven protuberances and a waist like a diamond; with large, straight limbs and well-rounded thighs; with the private organs withdrawn into a sheath; with shanks like those of the *aiṇeya* deer; with long fingers and broad heels; with a fathom-wide aura and skin the color of gold; with body hairs each growing singly and curling to the right;
with a body as perfectly proportioned as a royal *nyagrodha* tree; with a physical form adorned by the primary and secondary marks; and with an unblinking, steady gaze and established mindfulness.

Like the Himavat, the king of mountains, adorned with various grasses, forests, medicinal herbs, and creepers; possessing vast intelligence and a range of knowledge that cannot be diverted; having a majestic array of a voice and form like a rain-cloud; with a mind free from the conceptual proliferation of all worldly agitation, pride, and movement; whose sphere of knowledge is undifferentiated; who has attained the illumination of the vast domain of a Buddha’s wisdom; and whose resolve is uninterrupted in its maturation and discipline of all sentient beings.

He had generated the vast mandala of great compassion; for the sake of upholding the eye of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas and for the sake of generating the light of wisdom for all sentient beings, he was recollecting the way of the Tathāgatas. He was walking with a gait that served the welfare of the entire world—neither hurried nor slow, steady, well-composed, and graceful—dwelling like a resident of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, surrounded by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, humans, and non-humans.
surrounded.
Furthermore, as that monk Sudarśana was walking back and forth, the directional deities facing him caused the circles of the quarters to revolve.
Deities moving on foot received his lifting of each step with jeweled lotuses.
Deities whose spheres of light blazed forth inexhaustibly dispelled the thick darkness.
The forest deities of Jambudhvaja rained down a shower of masses of flowers;
the earth deities within the womb of the mountains revealed mines of jewels;
and the sky deities, possessing the glory of universal radiance, adorned the expanse of the firmament.
The ocean deities, Śrīsaṃbhavas, strew great maṇi-jewels;
the Sumeru deities, Vimalagarbhas,
pay homage with their palms joined in reverence.
The wind deities of unimpeded power release a breeze filled with perfumes, incense, and flowers;

the night deities of spring, their bodies beautifully adorned, bow with prostrate limbs in homage. The day deities of the ever-awakening mandala stand in the expanse of the sky, holding banners of directional-illuminating jewel-gems, for the purpose of producing light.

Then the merchant’s son Sudhana approached the monk Sudarśana; prostrating himself at the soles of the monk Sudarśana’s feet, kissing and stroking the soles of the monk Sudarśana’s feet, he stood before him with palms joined in reverence and said: "Noble one, I have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
I am thoroughly seeking the conduct of a bodhisattva,
and I have heard that the Noble One gives instruction and advice to bodhisattvas and bestows his guidance upon them.
"May the Noble One tell me this: how should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, and how should they practice?
He replied, "Noble son, I am young by birth,"
But [he was] junior by virtue of his ordination.
Therefore, noble son, in a single lifetime I have practiced the holy life in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in thirty-eight Ganges rivers;
in some cases, I have practiced the holy life day and night in such a manner.
In some cases for seven days and nights,
in some for half a month, and in some for a month.
In some places for a year,
in some places for a hundred years,
and in some places for a thousand years.
In some cases for a hundred thousand years, in some cases for ten million years,
and in some cases for a hundred billion years.
In some places for as many as inexpressibly inexpressible years,
in some places for an intermediate kalpa, and in some places for half a kalpa.
In some cases for an eon, and in others for as many as inexpressibly inexpressible eons, I have practiced the holy life under Tathāgatas according to this very calculation of eons;
from all those Tathāgatas, I have heard the teaching of the Dharma.
He has received instruction and admonition;
he has purified the arrays of his vows;
and he has purified the circle of conduct that has entered the sphere of full realization.
The oceans of perfections have been fulfilled;
the miraculous displays of perfect enlightenment have been understood;
and the turnings of the wheel of Dharma, which are mutually unconfused, have been maintained.
Their equality of power was entered into by me,
and their teaching was upheld until the ultimate limit of the True Dharma;
and for all those Tathāgatas, their former vows for the purification of their own Buddha-fields were brought to fulfillment by the power of the accomplishment of the samādhi of the circle of vows.

And for me, the former bodhisattva practices of all those [Tathāgatas] were brought forth for the sake of purifying my own practice, by the power of attaining the samādhi that enters into all practices.
And for me, the purification of the perfections of all those Tathāgatas was brought forth by the power of the departure through the Samantabhadra practice.
Furthermore, noble son, as I am walking in this manner, the streams of all directions revolve before me, because of the gateway of well-observed knowledge.

The streams of all world-systems are turned back by a single production of thought for the sake of transcending and purifying ineffably ineffable world-systems—namely, through the power of accomplishing the great vows.

In a single moment of thought, the gateways to the modes of conduct of ineffably ineffable sentient beings are turned toward them for the fulfillment of the knowledge of the ten powers, through the power of accomplishing the vows for the conduct of the Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. By a single production of thought, there is the purification of the vision of ineffably ineffable Buddha-fields.
They become oriented toward the service, attendance, and worship of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.

By the power of having previously accomplished the vows for worshipping past and future Tathāgatas, through a single thought-moment, clouds of the Dharma of unspeakably unspeakable Tathāgatas descend upon their resolve.

By the power of accomplishing the vows and dhāraṇīs for upholding the wheel of Dharma that follows the methods and courses of incalculable teachings, through a single thought-moment, oceans of the conduct of unspeakably unspeakable Bodhisattvas [arise].
They turn toward the purification of the entire mandala of conduct.

By the power of accomplishing the vows for the fulfillment of the bodhisattva conduct— which is like the strength of Indra— through a single production of the thought of awakening, oceans of inexpressibly inexpressible samādhis turn toward them for the sake of purifying the entire mandala of all samādhis.

By the power of the accomplishment of the vow for the convergence of all gateways of samādhi through the gateways of a single samādhi, in a single production of thought, oceans of faculties— unspeakably unspeakable in number— turn toward them for the sake of following the wheel of time of all the wheels of faculties.

By the power of the accomplishment of the vow for the attainment of the faculty of the limit of mindfulness, in a single production of thought, wheels of time— unspeakably unspeakable in number— turn toward them for the sake of turning the wheel of Dharma at all times.

By the power of the accomplishment of vows that reach the limit of all beings without exception, through a single thought-moment, oceans of all the three times— beyond expression and inexpressible— turn toward him in all world-systems by the power of the accomplishment of vows for the light of knowledge that follows after them.
Noble son, this is the bodhisattva liberation called "The Lamp of Unceasing Knowledge" that I know.

What is it possible for me to know of those Bodhisattvas whose resolve is like a diamond, who are nobly born into the lineage of all the Tathāgata families, whose life-faculty is unobstructed, who possess the lamp of unextinguished wisdom, whose bodies are indestructible and indivisible, who have manifested forms through illusion, whose bodies consist of limbs and members equal to conditioned phenomena, who manifest bodies that communicate with the world according to its inclinations,
who display bodies of form, color, shape, height, and girth that are comparable to the entire world, and whose bodies cannot be harmed by fire, poison, or weapons?

whose bodies are indestructible with a firm vajra-circumference; who render powerless all the forces of Māras and rival disputants; who resemble mountains of Jāmbūnada gold; whose bodies rise above the entire world; who are the basis for the perception of the entire world; who are heard through perceptions from every direction; whose faces are looked upon by the entire world; who have become like clouds of all dharmas; and who illuminate all directions.

To know the conduct or to speak of the virtues of those whose appearance is never disagreeable because they have shattered the mountain of all obscurations; those whose appearance is supremely heroic because they have utterly uprooted all unwholesome roots; those whose appearance is longed for because it arises as the natural outflow of vast roots of merit; and who are like the udumbara flower because their manifestation is so exceedingly rare.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region, in the country of Śramaṇamaṇḍala, there is a city named Sumukha.
There dwells a boy named Indriyeśvara.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, whose supreme purity was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s valorous stride, whose mind was illuminated by the light of the Bodhisattva’s powers, whose heart was pervaded by the invincible heroism of a Bodhisattva, whose mind did not shrink from the armor of the Bodhisattva’s firm vows,
who had reached the ultimate expansion and stability of the Bodhisattva’s resolute intention, and whose disposition was set upon maintaining the cloud of Bodhisattva conduct—
His mental continuum was never satiated by the Bodhisattva-cloud of Dharma; his vows were directed toward entering into all the qualities of a Bodhisattva;
he desired to present himself as a charioteer and gatherer for the entire world; he wished to lead the entire world across the wilderness and forest of the great saṃsāra;
and he remained insatiable in seeing, hearing, and attending upon spiritual friends, having conceived an immeasurable reverence for the Dharma.

Having bowed his head at the feet of the monk Sudarśana and circumambulated the monk Sudarśana hundreds of thousands of times, he looked back at him again and again and departed from the presence of the monk Sudarśana.
(Gv 102) 15 Indriyeśvara.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, reflecting upon that instruction of the monk Sudarśana, [proceeded].
Setting it forth, bestowing it, discerning it, proclaiming it, making it manifest, uttering it, demonstrating it, reflecting upon it, and practicing it.
Dispelling misconceptions, investigating and illuminating that method of the Dharma, entering into it, revolving it, breaking through [delusions], demonstrating it, making it manifest,
and surveying it, surrounded by a retinue of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, he proceeded in due order toward the circle of ascetics.
He approached the city of Sumukha in that country, searching for the boy Indriyeśvara.

While he was in the air above him, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas announced: "Noble son, this boy Indriyeśvara is near the confluence of rivers, surrounded by ten thousand boys, playing at playing with dust."
Then Sudhana, the merchant's son, approached the city of Sumukha near the confluence of rivers.
There he saw the boy Indriyeśvara playing with sand, surrounded by a retinue of ten thousand boys.
Having seen him, he went up to where the boy Indriyeśvara was and [touched] the feet of the boy Indriyeśvara.

Having prostrated with his head at the feet of Indriyeśvara and circumambulated the boy Indriyeśvara hundreds of thousands of times, he stood before the boy Indriyeśvara with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus: "Noble one, I have generated the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
