And he heard the terrible cries of distress of those condemned ones being slaughtered, as they were subjected to various tortures and wailed with a great, thundering roar, producing a sense of intense agitation and terror, just like in the Saṃghāta Great Hell.

Upon seeing that most cruel, terrifying, and supreme slaughter, this thought occurred to him: "I have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, and am intent on seeking the conduct of a bodhisattva; I am questioning my spiritual friends as to what is to be done by a bodhisattva for the sake of virtue."
"What unwholesome thing is to be avoided? [He replied:

"And this King Anala has fallen away from wholesome qualities; he is a perpetrator of highly blameworthy deeds, possessed of corrupt mental intentions, intent upon obstructing the lives of other beings, devoted to the oppression of other beings, and indifferent to the next world."
Faced with falling into the miserable destinies,
he thinks, "From this, there will arise for me the hearing of the bodhisattva conduct.
While he is thus engaged in such reflection and mental attention, being intent on protecting the realm of all sentient beings, (Gv 122)

To him, whose mind was born from vast compassion, the deities in the expanse of the sky above proclaimed: "Noble son, do you not remember the instruction of your spiritual friend, the seer Jayoṣmāyatana?
Looking upward at the expanse of the sky, he said: "I remember.
The deities said: "Do not [forget], noble son!"
Give rise to doubt regarding the instructions of spiritual friends;
for spiritual friends guide with perfect equanimity, not with partiality.
For, noble son, the knowledge of the conduct of skillful means of bodhisattvas is inconceivable.
Inconceivable is the wisdom that gathers all sentient beings;
inconceivable is the wisdom that benefits sentient beings;
inconceivable is the wisdom that restrains sentient beings.
Inconceivable is the knowledge of restraining sentient beings;
inconceivable is the knowledge of gathering sentient beings;
inconceivable is the knowledge of purifying sentient beings.
Inconceivable is the wisdom that protects sentient beings;
inconceivable is the wisdom that introduces sentient beings [to the Dharma];
inconceivable is the wisdom that brings sentient beings to maturity.
"Inconceivable is his knowledge of how to discipline sentient beings.
Go, noble son,
and ask him about the conduct of a bodhisattva."
Then, having heard the words of the deity, the merchant’s son Sudhana went to where King Anala was.

Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of King Anala, he circumambulated King Anala hundreds of thousands of times, stood before him with palms joined in reverence, and spoke thus: "I have resolved my mind upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor how one should practice it.
I have heard, however, that the Noble One gives instruction and advice to bodhisattvas.
May the Noble One tell me this: how should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, and how should he practice?
Then King Anala, having attended to his royal duties, rose from his lion throne, took the merchant’s son Sudhana by the right hand, and entered the capital city of Tāladhvaja.

Proceeding in due order, he entered his own palace, led the merchant’s son Sudhana into the inner apartments, sat upon a noble seat, and said this: "Noble son, look upon these enjoyments of my household."

Looking about, he saw that house— vast and expansive, surrounded by walls made of the seven precious gems, adorned with palaces of various jewels and gems, decorated with hundreds of thousands of multi-storied pavilions of many jewels, blazing with the radiant splendor of the light from inconceivable mani-jewels, featuring lofty pillars made of red pearls variegated and beautifully distinguished by various kinds of mani-jewels, and furnished with lion-thrones well-arranged and exquisitely adorned with hundreds of thousands of diverse gems and musāragalva.

He saw the city of Vairocana, with its lion-banners raised high bearing *jyotīrasa* jewel-gems; spread over by a canopy of precious gems; covered by a great net variegated with wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*); adorned with a magnificent arrangement of turrets decorated with countless diverse precious gems;
provided with lotus-pools made of cool water and emerald (*aśmagarbha*); and surrounded by rows of trees made of every kind of jewel.
And he saw his retinue of ten million women, who were handsome, gracious, and beautiful to behold, owing to the excellence of their most sublime and pure complexion.

They were endowed with proficiency in all arts and rituals; they rose before others and retired after them; they possessed hearts of loving-kindness; and they responded to the commands of their servants and attendants with respectful compliance.
Then King Anala said this to the merchant’s son Sudhana: "What do you think, noble son?
Can such a maturation of karma arise even for those who have committed evil deeds? Is there such perfection of physical form?"
What is this perfection of retinue, what is this perfection of great wealth, and what is this perfection of great sovereignty and power?
He said, "No indeed, Noble One.
He replied, "Noble son, I have attained the bodhisattva liberation called 'the illusory state' (māyāgata).
And these, noble son—"

The beings dwelling in my realm for the most part are killers, takers of what is not given, practitioners of sexual misconduct, speakers of falsehoods, slanderers, harsh-speakers, idle chatterers, covetous, malevolent in heart, and holders of wrong views; they are evildoers, cruel, fierce, reckless, and possessed of various unwholesome deeds.
They could not otherwise be restrained, turned back, or instructed from their evil conduct.

Therefore, noble son, for the sake of taming, ripening, and disciplining these beings, and for the purpose of establishing them in what is beneficial, I place great compassion at the forefront and have executioners created by magical transformation execute victims created by magical transformation.
By means of created executioners, I cause those who have committed unwholesome courses of action to undergo various forms of punishment.

I manifest them as experiencing intense painful sensations, consisting of the severing of hands, feet, ears, noses, limbs, minor members, and heads. Upon seeing this, these beings dwelling in my realm experience a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Fear arises, terror arises, and a state of paralysis comes upon them.
That is to say, for the purpose of turning them away from the engagement in evil deeds.

Having perceived, noble son, that these beings have minds and selves agitated by fear and weary in spirit, I turn them back from the ten unwholesome paths of action and establish them in possession of the ten wholesome paths of action.

Having established [them] in ultimate security and well-being, in the severance of all suffering, and in the bliss of omniscience, I do not, O son of good family, cause harm to any sentient being by body, speech, or mind,
nor would I cause them to wander in the endless, uninterrupted sufferings of the future limit.

Noble son, I would not wish to obstruct the suffering of even a single-minded thought of a bewildered being in the animal realm, down to a mere ant; how much less so for one who has become a human, who is like a field capable of growing the paths of wholesome action.
Noble son, even while in the midst of a dream, no engagement with unwholesome dharmas arises within me.
How much more so, then, for one who is fully endowed with it?
Noble son, I am a possessor of this bodhisattva liberation called "the illusory nature."

What is possible for me to know of those bodhisattvas who have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), who follow all states of existence as having the nature of an illusion, who have emerged from the conduct of bodhisattvas that is like a magical creation, who perceive all worlds as being like a reflection, who have penetrated the nature of reality (*dharmanaya*) as being like a dream, who follow the method of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through the gateway of non-attachment, who have entered the net of conduct that is like a magician’s trick, and whose sphere of activity is the domain of unobstructed gnosis?

To know the conduct or to speak of the virtues of those who have emerged from the path of the Samantasamavasaraṇa-samādhi, who possess mastery over the infinite-turning dhāraṇīs, and who are ever-attached to the sphere of the Buddha’s range of activity.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region there is a city named Suprabha. There dwells a king named Mahāprabha.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of King Anala, circumambulated King Anala hundreds of thousands of times, and, looking back at him again and again, departed from the presence of King Anala. 18.
Mahāprabha.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, recollecting that illusion of knowledge, [continued his journey].

Contemplating that bodhisattva liberation which has reached the state of illusion, examining that nature of phenomena which has reached the state of illusion, and penetrating that equality between karma and illusion, he—
Contemplating that equality of the illusory nature of phenomena, following that equality of the emanations for the ripening of beings,
and pursuing that inconceivable light arising from primordial wisdom, he proceeded.

He brought forth the accomplishment of that manifestation of the illusion of infinite vows; he purified that reality-nature of the emanation of unattached conduct; and he discerned that characteristic of the illusion-penetration of the three times.
Traveling by stages from country to country, inquiring, searching, and looking about,

with an untiring mind and an unwearied body, seeking everywhere through all directions and intermediate points, on paths low and high, level and uneven, by water and land, and across mountains, hills, caves, villages, towns, market towns, provinces, kingdoms, and royal capitals, he approached the vicinity of the great city of Suprabha.
He asked, "Where is that King Mahāprabha?
A great multitude of people pointed it out to him, saying, "Noble son, this is the great city of Suprabha, where King Mahāprabha dwells."
Then the merchant’s son Sudhana approached the great city of Suprabha and beheld the great city of Suprabha.
Having seen it, he was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; he reflected thus: "Where does my spiritual friend dwell?
Today I shall see that spiritual friend."
Thereafter, I shall hear of the conduct of a bodhisattva, the gateway to the bodhisattva’s departure, the inconceivable nature of a bodhisattva,
the inconceivable spheres of a bodhisattva’s qualities, the inconceivable preeminence of a bodhisattva, the inconceivable dwelling in the meditative absorptions of a bodhisattva,
the inconceivable sport of a bodhisattva’s liberations, and the inconceivable purity of a bodhisattva’s great undertakings and deliverances.

Thus engaged in such reflection and mental attention, he approached the great city of Suprabha. Having arrived, he gazed upon the great city of Suprabha, which was wonderful to behold and composed of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearl, emerald, and musāragalva.

It was completely encircled on all sides by seven moats filled with deep, noble water, their bottoms strewn with golden sand and covered with divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses;
their waters were turbid with the mud of black sandalwood paste;
and it was surrounded on all sides by rows of palm trees made of the seven precious gems.
It was completely encircled on all sides by seven walls of vajra-jewels,

namely: the wall of the lion-like beautiful vajra, the wall of the invincible vajra, the wall of the vajra of penetrating vigor, the wall of the vajra of irresistible vigor, the wall of the firm vajra of non-attachment, and the wall of the interior of a network of vajra rays.
It was surrounded by a perimeter wall of variegated arrays of stainless colors;
and all those great walls of vajra-jewels were inlaid with countless mani-gems, adorned with beautiful rows of teeth made of Jambūnada gold,
adorned with beautiful rows of teeth made of silver-mani, adorned with beautiful rows of teeth made of vaidūrya-mani, and adorned with beautiful rows of teeth made of crystal-mani.
They were adorned with rows of teeth made of beautiful coral gems, rows of teeth made of beautiful red pearls, and rows of teeth made of beautiful pearls from the depths of the ocean.
And that great city had eight gates, ten yojanas apart from one another, which were variegated and beautiful, composed of the seven precious jewels.
That great city was vast and extensive, well-divided into various sections of eight parts, and established upon a ground made of blue beryl.

And in that great city there were ten crores of streets; on both sides of each street were situated mansions made of various jewels, adorned with many diverse arrays of gems, with jeweled parasols, banners, flags, and victory-pennants raised aloft, abundant in all necessary articles, and inhabited by many millions of beings.
Hundreds of thousands of great mansions.

And that great city was adorned with innumerable palaces made of gold, jewels, and gems; it possessed innumerable gabled chambers of Jāmbūnada gold, arrayed with inconceivable jewels and covered by lattices of beryl-gems; it possessed innumerable gabled chambers of silver, arrayed with inconceivable jewels and covered by lattices of red pearls; and it possessed innumerable gabled chambers of beryl, arrayed with inconceivable jewels and covered by lattices of various precious gem-treasures.

There were countless crystal gabled palaces with inconceivable arrays of jewels covered by kings of *vipulagarbha* gems; countless gabled palaces of *jagadrocana* jewel-gems with inconceivable arrays of jewels covered by kings of *ādityagarbha* gems;

countless sapphire gabled palaces with inconceivable arrays of jewels covered by kings of *śrīraśmi* gems; and countless gabled palaces of kings of *jagatsāgara* jewel-gems with inconceivable arrays of jewels covered by kings of *jyotīraśmi* gems.

It contained innumerable vajra-pinnacled palaces with inconceivable arrays of jewels covered by nets of *aparājitadhvaja* jewel-kings; innumerable *kālānusāri-candana* pinnacled palaces with inconceivable arrays covered by nets of divine *māndārava* flowers;

and innumerable pinnacled palaces of incomparable king-of-fragrances with inconceivable arrays of jewels covered by nets of various divine flowers—adorned with many jeweled finials, surrounded by railings of the seven precious substances, and encircled by rows of jeweled *tāla* trees.
And all those jeweled arches and jeweled nets were bound together by mutual cords of jewels;
all those jeweled cords were adorned with garlands of golden bells;
and all those garlands of golden bells were further fastened with clusters of variegated jewel-strings.
And all those clusters of jewel-thread garlands were suspended from nets of jewel-bells;

and that entire great city was covered by an incalculable net of mani-jewels, covered by an incalculable net of jewel-bells, covered by an incalculable net of divine perfumes, covered by an incalculable net of various divine flowers, covered by an incalculable net of jewel-reflections, covered by an incalculable canopy of vajras, covered by an incalculable canopy of jewels, and covered by an incalculable canopy of jewel-parasols.

It was covered with canopies of countless jeweled gabled pavilions, covered with canopies of countless jeweled cloths, and covered with canopies of countless garlands of jeweled flowers; various jeweled banners and pennants were unfurled. And in the center of that great city, Suprabha, the palace of King Mahāprabha was constructed, measuring four *yojanas* in circumference and made of the seven precious gems, adorned with seven railings made of various kinds of jewels.

It was surrounded by seven nets of jeweled bells with delightful and sweet sounds, adorned on all sides by seven rows of palm trees made of the seven precious gems, and embellished by hundreds of thousands of arrays of inconceivable gabled pavilions made of various jewels;
its waters were covered with divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, water lilies, and white lotuses, filled with water possessing the eight qualities, and its bottom was strewn with golden sand.

It was adorned with lotus ponds made of various jewels, decorated on all four sides with trees bearing every kind of jewel, flower, and fruit, and featuring well-proportioned staircases constructed of piled jewel-bricks; it was graced by the warbling of flocks of various divine, sweet, and charming birds, rivaling the palace of the Lord of the Immortals.
And in its center stood a peaked pavilion made of the *jagadrocana* jewel.
The King Mahāprabha established a treasury of the True Dharma that was variegated, beautiful to behold, and resplendent with an inconceivable array of countless jewel-gems.

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, with a mind unattached to the jeweled moats, not marveling at the jeweled walls, not becoming impassioned by the rows of jeweled palm trees, not savoring the sound of the networks of jeweled bells and tinkling chimes, his mind unattached to the sweet resonance of the music of divine instruments,
paying no attention to the enjoyment of the various and diverse jeweled palaces and gabled chambers, [he passed through] the throngs of men and women who were greatly rejoicing.

Delighting in the joy of the garden of Dharma, with a mind detached from delight in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, and supremely intent on the contemplation of the Dharma, he approached the city crossroads by way of continuously questioning the beings and spiritual friends he had encountered along the way.
Having arrived and looking all around, he saw King Mahāprabha not far from a shrine-hall in the middle of the city crossroads.

Upon a magnificent throne of great array, with feet made of blue lapis lazuli gems and a body made of white lapis lazuli, supported by lions, draped with a white net of Jāmbūnada gold thread, provided with an exquisite arrangement of various divine and surpassing jewel-cloths, adorned with ornaments fashioned from countless jewel-images,
covered by a canopy of inconceivable arrays of precious gems, and spread over with a canopy of Jāmbūnada gold bands variegated by diverse patterns of divine jewels.
He was seated cross-legged upon a great Dharma-throne whose core was a lotus made of the wish-fulfilling king of jewels;
his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
and his limbs were beautified by the eighty various secondary characteristics.
It was resplendent with the arrangement of various jewels like a mountain of gold;
it possessed radiant splendor like the orb of the sun;
and its appearance was gentle like the orb of the full moon.
Shining like Brahmā in the assembly of Brahmā;
like the ocean, a vast accumulation of jewels that are the qualities of the profound Dharma;
like a great cloud, with a resonance whose very nature is rain.
Like the sky, adorned by a multitude of luminous stars that are the principles of the Dharma;
like Mount Sumeru, where the reflections of the minds of the ocean-like beings of the four castes appear;
and like an island of jewels, its surface strewn with the jewels of diverse wisdom.
And before him were many heaps of gold, gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, native gold, silver, and jewels;
heaps of various divine garments made of precious gems;
and heaps of diverse divine jeweled ornaments.
He saw heaps of various kinds of food and edibles, collections of diverse and exquisite delicacies, arranged in various displays throughout the area.
And there were many hundreds of thousands of millions of divine jewel-chariots, many hundreds of thousands of millions of divine musical instruments,
and many hundreds of thousands of millions of divine fragrant enclosures.
Many requisites for the sick and medicinal supplies, many heaps of various excellent articles of use,
all of which were permissible and blameless.

He saw that many hundreds of thousands of cows— with golden horns and hooves, and bronze milking vessels— had been set aside for the gathering-in of destitute beings so that they might enjoy them according to their wishes;
and he saw many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of maidens, beautiful, gracious, lovely to behold, and adorned with every kind of ornament.

He saw them stationed there, wearing celestial garments, their bodies anointed with divine uragasāra sandalwood paste, skilled in the sixty-four arts and proficient in the practice and service of all sensual pleasures.

Just as they were positioned before him, so too were twenty *koṭis* of celestial palaces—fully equipped with every necessity—stationed at all the streets, crossroads, junctions, gates, and street entrances; that is to say, twenty *koṭis* on both sides of each and every street.

For the sake of gathering beings, for the sake of embracing beings, for generating joy in beings, for producing delight in beings, for clarifying the minds of beings, for refreshing the hearts of beings, for the pacification of the afflictions of beings, for the application of beings to the meaning of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
for making beings share in the same goal as omniscience, for turning beings away from thoughts of malice toward others, and for turning beings away from all misconduct of body and speech.
For the purpose of extracting the thorn of the view of a self-entity and for the purification of the paths of action of sentient beings.

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, prostrated himself with his entire body before King Mahāprabha, circumambulated King Mahāprabha hundreds of thousands of times, and standing before him with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus: "Noble one, I have set my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how one should practice it.
I have heard, however, that the Noble One gives instruction and admonition to the bodhisattvas.
"May the Noble One tell me this: how should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, and how should they practice?
He replied, "Noble son, I purify the bodhisattva conduct known as the Banner of Great Loving-kindness."

I fulfill it. And this, noble son, is my bodhisattva practice of the Banner of Great Loving-kindness, [practiced] under many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, up to an inexpressible number of inexpressible Buddhas.

It has been questioned, interrogated, purified, arrayed, scrutinized, investigated, sought after, examined, diversified, and expanded by me in the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. O son of good family, abiding in this bodhisattva practice called the Banner of Great Loving-kindness, I govern the kingdom according to the Dharma and sustain the world according to the Dharma.
I traverse the world according to the Dharma; I lead sentient beings according to the Dharma;
I act toward sentient beings according to the Dharma.
I cause sentient beings to turn toward the mandala of Dharma; I bestow the method of Dharma upon sentient beings;
I cultivate sentient beings through the Dharma.

I engage sentient beings in the practice of the Dharma; I establish sentient beings in the realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena. I establish them in a mind of loving-kindness, under the sovereignty of great loving-kindness, in the power of loving-kindness, in a mind intent on benefit, in a mind of happiness, in a mind of compassion, and in a mind of assistance.

With a mind intent on favoring sentient beings, with a mind that neither grasps nor abandons sentient beings, and with a mind that never interrupts the vow to turn back all suffering, I establish sentient beings in the cessation of their habitual tendencies toward the practice of establishing them in ultimate happiness;
and I refresh their very basis.

By generating the bliss of pliancy, I turn back their creeper-like minds from attachment to the pleasures of saṃsāra; I transform the continuum of their minds toward delight in the garden of the Dharma, and I purify them therein.
I purify them from all unwholesome states;
I turn them away from all unwholesome states;
I cause them to turn back from the stream of saṃsāra.
In the oceans of the principles of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), I burn away their ignorance of mind in order to sever rebirth in all states of existence;
with the radiance of their minds, I generate in them the resolve for the sake of attaining the fruit of omniscience;
and I clarify the ocean of their minds in order to produce the power of faith that cannot be shaken.
Thus, noble son, abiding in the bodhisattva practice called the Banner of Loving-kindness (*maitrīdhvajā*), I govern the world through the Dharma.
Indeed, noble son, no fear, terror, paralysis, or horripilation arises from my presence for the beings dwelling in my realm.
And those beings who are poor, lacking various necessities, and who approach me seeking food, or seeking drink, or seeking clothing, up to seeking all things—whatever they require—[I provide].
"I permit you to take those very royal treasuries with which you were previously acquainted and which have now been opened—
even for the sake of which you would undertake evil deeds, such as killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander,
harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, malice, or wrong view."
Or whatever various other views you might adhere to—
therefore, from this great city of Suprabha, from its city gates, streets, road-mouths, crossroads, and junctions, let whoever needs anything take it;
it was already given by me as my own.
Furthermore, noble son, all those beings who dwell within the great city of Suprabhā are bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna;
it is through the purity of their respective inclinations that this great city of Suprabhā appears to them.
That is to say: for some it was small, for others vast; for some the ground was mere earth, for others the surface was strewn with lapis lazuli and precious gems;

for some there were earthen walls, for others they were surrounded by great walls made of the *aparājita* cloth, banners, and precious cloths; for some it was strewn with gravel and pebbles, uneven with highs and lows, and abounding in chasms and precipices.

For some, its surface was strewn with many great maṇi-jewels, made ready for use, and as level as the palm of a hand; for others, it appeared as an array of countless jewel-palaces, celestial mansions, towers, gabled halls, terraces, porticos, windows, lattices, crescent-shaped ornaments, and lion-cages, variegated with jewels and beautiful to behold—

even for those pure-intentioned inhabitants living outside the city who had planted roots of merit, who had attended upon the arising of many Buddhas, and who were oriented toward and took refuge in omniscience, there appeared this radiance consisting of jewels.
Those whom I previously gathered through the four means of attraction while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva appear to others as being made of clay.
And when, noble son, the beings dwelling in my realm, in various regions— whether in villages, towns, market towns, provinces, or royal capitals— [behold me...]
In this world of five corruptions, when people, agitated by the nature of the times, even desire to practice the ten unwholesome paths of action,

I then enter the bodhisattva samādhi called "Turning According to the Faculties of the World," preceded by great loving-kindness, for the sake of benefiting them. And as soon as I had entered this samādhi, noble son—

Then, those fears of those beings, those calamities, those enmities, those conflicts and disputes, those agitations of mind, and those thoughts of violence are pacified, stilled, turned back, and ceased,
precisely through the attainment of the nature of the Bodhisattva-samādhi called "The Turning of the World’s Faculties," which is preceded by great loving-kindness.
Moreover, noble son,
wait a moment until you shall see it for yourself.
Then, at that very moment, King Mahāprabha entered the bodhisattva-samādhi called "The Turning of the World’s Faculties," preceded by great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

As soon as King Mahāprabha had entered this bodhisattva-samādhi, "The Turning of the World’s Faculties," preceded by great loving-kindness, the great city of Suprabha— along with its regions and sub-regions, its villages, towns, market-towns, districts, kingdoms, royal capitals, and surrounding areas— trembled in six ways.
As he moved, those jeweled walls, jeweled palaces, jeweled inner chambers,
jeweled houses, jeweled mansions, jeweled celestial chariots, jeweled gabled towers,
jeweled turrets, jeweled terraces, jeweled windows, jeweled railings, jeweled archways, jeweled half-moons, jeweled lion-thrones, jeweled pedestals, and jeweled statues also moved.
The jeweled canopies, the networks of jeweled threads and bells, the jeweled bells, the jeweled banners, the jeweled flags,

and the jeweled palm-tree fans were all set in motion, resonated, and struck together; and as they clashed, they emitted a sound that was beautiful, charming, and pleasant to hear, which reached out toward King Mahāprabha.
They bowed down to him and prostrated themselves;
and those who were inhabitants within the great city of Suprabha, [did likewise].

With their minds entirely suffused with joy and gladness, they all bowed down with their whole bodies toward where King Mahāprabha was. And all those beings dwelling in his realm— those in every village, city, town, district, country, and capital—
who were likewise gladdened in body and mind and filled with joy and gladness, also bowed down toward where King Mahāprabha was.
And those beings who had been born in the animal realm—
all of them, with hearts of mutual loving-kindness and benevolence, bowed down toward King Mahāprabha.
And as for the mountain peaks and other elevated regions of the earth, they too [bowed].
They all bent toward King Mahāprabha;
and whatever flowering trees, fruiting trees, leafy trees, or seeds, living beings, crops, grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and forest giants there were, they too all bent toward King Mahāprabha.
And all the springs, lakes, ponds, pools, cascades, rivers, lotus-pools, and wells within his realm also directed their currents toward where King Mahāprabha was.

And ten thousand nāga kings rained down from the four directions fine streams of fragrant water, accompanied by clouds of fragrant water and masses of smoke from great kālāguru incense, illuminated by the blazing flashes of various streaks of lightning and emitting thunderous roars.
And ten thousand sons of gods, headed by the divine kings Śakra, Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, and Vaśavartin, having gone into the sky,
provided an adornment of magnificent sounds released from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of clouds of celestial musical instruments.
It was adorned with the delightful and sweet resonance of the divine music of countless hosts of apsarases, sounding like the rumbling of clouds;
it was adorned by the raining down of clouds of countless, diverse, divine jewel-flowers; and it was adorned by the raining down of countless divine fragrances of various colors.

An adornment consisting of a rain of clouds of various divine garlands made of incalculable celestial jewels; an adornment consisting of a rain of clouds of divine powders of various incalculable colors; and an adornment consisting of a rain of clouds of various divine jewel ornaments.
An adornment consisting of a rain of clouds of various colors of countless divine jewels, garments, variegated, stainless, and subtle fabrics;

an adornment consisting of a rain of clouds of countless divine jewels and various variegated parasols; and an adornment consisting of a rain of clouds of countless divine lion-beautiful jewel-banners.

He stood in the midst of the sky as an adornment raining down clouds of jeweled banners blazing with the radiance of incalculable divine jewels, for the purpose of making offerings to King Mahāprabha.

And the great nāga king Airāvaṇa stood in the entire expanse of the sky, covering it with clouds of incalculable divine lotuses made of various jewels, draped with countless divine necklaces of mani-gems,
and hung with clusters of countless divine silk ribbons and cords.
It was adorned with countless hanging garlands of various divine jewels, adorned with countless hanging garlands of various divine jewel ornaments,
and adorned with countless hanging wreaths of various divine jewel flowers.
An adornment covered by clouds of fragrance that pervade all directions, consisting of divine fragrances of various colors and incalculable varieties;
an adornment characterized by the raining down of clouds of divine jewel-garments of various colors in incalculable numbers;
and an adornment characterized by the raining down of clouds of layers of divine incense-powder in incalculable numbers.
It stood pervading the entire expanse of space, adorned by a subtle, excellent rain from clouds of countless divine powders of various colors,

and adorned by a continuous downpour covered by clouds of hymns accompanied by the sweet, charming, and resonant sounds of celestial music and songs from countless hosts of apsarases— through the power of inconceivable miraculous transformations like the prowess of a lordly elephant or a bull.
And hundreds of thousands of incalculable lords of rākṣasas— those dwelling in the clouds, those inhabiting the ground that supports the world-system of the four continents,

those who feed on flesh and blood, those who steal the vital energy (*ojas*) from water-dwellers, wild animals, cattle, birds, oxen, horses, elephants, donkeys, men, and women, those with corrupt mental intentions, and all those who were constantly intent upon harassing and harming the world— all of them came to possess hearts of supreme loving-kindness and benevolence.

With countenances of extreme serenity, devoted above all to non-violence and non-harming toward the entire world, mindful of the next world, with palms joined in reverence and hearts filled with supreme joy, they bowed down toward where King Mahāprabha was;
and they experienced an incomparable, noble physical and mental bliss.

And many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and lords of bhūtas— possessing hearts of supreme loving-kindness and benevolence, with most serene facial expressions, intent on non-violence and non-harming toward the entire world, mindful of the next world, with palms joined in reverence and minds of supreme joy— approached where King Mahāprabha was.
Because of that, they bowed down in reverence and experienced incomparable, sublime physical and mental bliss. Likewise,

throughout the entire world-system of four continents, all the fears, calamities, misfortunes, hostilities, conflicts, disputes, mental agitations, and harmful intentions of all sentient beings [ceased].
They become tranquil, they become thoroughly pacified, they turn back, they cease, and they recede;
just as it is in a world-system of four continents,
so it is in the entire triple-thousand great-thousandfold world-system, and even throughout ten hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of world-systems in the ten directions.
For all sentient beings, all fears, calamities, misfortunes, enmities, conflicts, and disputes, as well as mental agitations, sinful thoughts of violence, and malicious intentions, became pacified;
they were thoroughly calmed, ceased, suppressed, and turned back— namely,
through the attainment of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the Bodhisattva samādhi called "The Turning of the World’s Faculties," which is preceded by great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

Then, King Mahāprabha, having emerged from that samādhi, said this to the merchant’s son Sudhana: "Noble son, I know only this entrance to the light of knowledge of the bodhisattva practice called 'The Banner of Great Loving-kindness.
What could I possibly say of the bodhisattvas who possess the immeasurable parasols of great loving-kindness, by means of which they pervade all world-systems with the intention for their happiness?"

Because they possess an inseparable retinue with all the retinues of the entire world; because they apply themselves equally toward the low, the high, and the middling among those set forth to protect the entire world;
and because they have resolved to sustain the entire world with a mind of loving-kindness equal to the earth.

They are like the orb of the full moon, for they emit rays of merit and wisdom that extend equally throughout the entire world; they are like the orb of the sun, for they illuminate all objects of knowledge with the light of wisdom;

they are like great lamps, for they dispel the darkness in the dense thickets of the minds of all sentient beings; and they are like water-clearing jewels, for they remove the turbidity of deceit and hypocrisy from the hearts of all sentient beings.

To know their conduct or to speak of their virtues— to weigh their mountain of merit— is as difficult as it would be for those who are like the wish-fulfilling king of jewels (*cintārājamaṇiratna*) because they fulfill the intentions and vows of the entire world, or for those who are like the great wind because they establish the great city of omniscience within the dwellings of the meditative concentrations and attainments of the entire world.
To behold the sky of the multitude of the lights of qualities,
or to delimit the circle of the wind of great vows,
or to measure the power of the equality of phenomena—

or to illuminate the praises of the array of the Mahāyāna, or to speak of the specific methods of the conduct of Samantabhadra, or to open the gateway to the cultivation of the meditative absorptions of the great bodhisattvas;
or to fully describe the clouds of great compassion.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region is a royal capital named Sthirā.
There dwells a female lay disciple named Acalā.
Go to her and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of King Mahāprabha, circumambulated King Mahāprabha hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at him again and again, departed from the presence of King Mahāprabha. 19.
(Gv 131) 22. Acalā.
Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, departed from the great city of Suprabha; having followed the road for a short while, he reflected upon the instructions of King Mahāprabha.

Recalling that method of the bodhisattva practice, the banner of great loving-kindness; cultivating that illumination of the entrance into the great samādhi called "The Revolution of the World's Faculties";
and actualizing that inconceivable variety of the lion-throne arrays and ornaments for the purification of the bodhisattva body;
Increasing that inconceivable sovereign power of the merit of the bodhisattva’s vows; strengthening that inconceivable method of knowledge for maturing sentient beings belonging to the bodhisattvas;
and reflecting upon that inconceivable and uncommon majesty of the bodhisattva’s enjoyments.
Taking as his object that inconceivable excellence of the bodhisattvas, recollecting that inconceivable purification of the maturation of sentient beings by the bodhisattvas,
and conceiving that inconceivable perfection of the purity of the bodhisattva’s retinue;
As he gained conviction in that inconceivable method of observing and contemplating the welfare of sentient beings belonging to the bodhisattvas,

he obtained a surge of joy and serene clarity of mind, a rapture of mind, an elation of mind, a delight of mind, an uncloudedness of mind, a luminosity of mind, a firmness of mind, a vastness of mind, and an inexhaustibility of mind.
Thus engaged in the mental attention of recollecting the spiritual friend, he shed tears and reflected:
"Oh, how wonderful is this vision of the spiritual friend! It is a mine of all the jewels of virtue; it purifies and fulfills all the conduct of a bodhisattva;

it brings about the purification of the mindfulness of all bodhisattvas; it cleanses the entire mandala of the dhāraṇīs of all bodhisattvas; and it generates the light of all the samādhis of all bodhisattvas."

They bring about the attainment of the vision of all Buddhas, cause the rain from the clouds of all Buddha-dharmas to fall, indicate the methods of the vows of all Bodhisattvas, generate the light of inconceivable wisdom and knowledge, and increase the sprouts of the firm faculties of Bodhisattvas.
My spiritual friends are my protectors from the precipitous paths leading to all miserable rebirths.
My spiritual friends are my guides by following the method of the equality of all phenomena; my spiritual friends are my revealers of the evenness and unevenness of the path;
my spiritual friends are the illuminators of the Mahāyāna.
My spiritual friends are instructors in the conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
my spiritual friends are teachers of the path to the city of omniscience; they are those who cause me to enter it.

My spiritual friends are those who cause me to enter the city of omniscience; my spiritual friends are those who provide illumination within the ocean of the principles of the realm of phenomena; my spiritual friends are those who illuminate the ocean-like principles of what is to be known throughout the three times.
My spiritual friends are the revealers of the entire assembly of all meaningful mandalas;
my spiritual friends are the increasers of all pure, wholesome dharmas.
As he was thus weeping, crying out, and lamenting, the hosts of gods situated in the vault of the sky—

the ever-attendant exhorters and messengers of the Buddhas, who are deities of the Bodhisattvas— spoke as follows: "Noble son, when a Bodhisattva practices according to the instructions of a spiritual friend, the Buddha Bhagavats become delighted in their hearts."
For a bodhisattva who abides without contradicting the words of a spiritual friend, omniscience draws near.

For a bodhisattva who has no doubt regarding the words of a spiritual friend, spiritual friends draw near. For a bodhisattva who is never separated from the mental attention directed toward a spiritual friend, all goals become manifest.
Go, noble son,
to where the laywoman Acalā resides in the royal capital of Sthirā;
there you will hear about the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, having emerged from that light of meditative concentration and knowledge, proceeded by stages toward the royal capital of Sthirā. Arriving there, he searched for and sought out the laywoman Acalā. A great multitude of people pointed her out to him, saying: "Noble son, this is the laywoman Acalā, residing in her own home with her parents, remaining in the state of maidenhood, surrounded by her circle of kinsmen, and [attended] by a great..."
He teaches the Dharma to the assembly of people.
Then, indeed, Sudhana the merchant’s son, his mind suffused with great joy, serene faith, and gladness, approached the residence of the laywoman Acalā.

Having arrived, he stood at the gate of the laywoman Acalā’s residence and saw that entire dwelling illuminated and pervaded by a golden-colored radiance that gladdened both body and mind. And as soon as Sudhana the merchant’s son was touched by that light,

He entered and attained five hundred gateways of concentration— subtle and gentle— headed by the concentration called the Banner of Sovereignty over All Feelings, headed by the concentration on the regions of peace, headed by the concentration for the welfare of the entire world, headed by the concentration possessing universal vision and equanimity, and headed by the concentration that is the treasury of the Tathāgata.
Just as the consciousness of an embryo that has entered the womb for half a day,
so too were those gateways of concentration subtle and tender in their arising;
and they smelled such a fragrance as had never been smelled by gods or goddesses, nor by nāgas or nāga maidens.

Neither of the yakṣas nor of the yakṣa maidens, neither of the gandharvas nor of the gandharva maidens, neither of the asuras nor of the asura maidens, neither of the garuḍas nor of the garuḍa maidens, neither of the kinnaras nor of the kinnara maidens, neither of the mahoragas nor of the mahoraga maidens, nor of humans nor of human maidens.
No woman exists to be found in the world of the ten directions who is equal to her in beauty, much less superior.

There is no radiance of color to be found in the world in the ten directions— setting aside the radiance of the Tathāgata’s color and the radiance of the color of bodhisattvas who have attained consecration— that is equal to her radiance of color.

How much more so beyond that? There exists no bodily stature, circumference, or configuration in the worlds of the ten directions— excluding the bodily stature, circumference, and configuration of the Tathāgata’s own body,
and the bodily stature, circumference, and configuration of the bodies of Bodhisattvas who have attained consecration.

There was nothing equal to her in the height, girth, and shape of her physical form, let alone anything superior; indeed, there exists no such array of splendor in the worlds of the ten directions, with the exception of the Tathāgata’s own array of splendor.
And there was the array of light of the conduct of bodhisattvas who have attained consecration;
how could anything be equal to that array of light, let alone superior?

There is no such fragrance in the world of the ten directions, nor in the abodes of the gods, nor in the abodes of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans, that can compare to the fragrance emitted from the treasury of her mouth; how much less could there be anything superior?
There is no such array of celestial palaces or enjoyment in the world of the ten directions, setting aside the enjoyment of the Tathāgata.
And it was the enjoyment of Bodhisattvas who have attained consecration; it was equal to the enjoyment of the array of that palace, so how could there be anything superior?

There is no perfection of retinue in the worlds of the ten directions— setting aside the perfection of the Tathāgata’s retinue and the perfection of the retinue of bodhisattvas who have attained consecration— that is equal to her perfection of retinue.
How much less could there be anyone superior?
Among the classes of beings in the worlds of the ten directions, no such being exists who would be capable of looking upon the laywoman Acalā with a mind of lust.
There is no being to be found within the assembly of beings in the worlds of the ten directions who would not have their afflictions pacified by the mere sight of the female lay follower Acalā.

Just as, for example, the ten hundred thousand Great Brahmas who exercise mastery do not manifest the afflictions belonging to the realm of desire, even so, upon merely seeing Acalā, the afflictions of sentient beings do not manifest.

(Gv 133) No being is to be found within the realm of sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who, upon seeing the laywoman Acalā, would not attain satisfaction—except for those already satisfied by wisdom.
Then, Sudhana the merchant’s son, with palms joined in reverence, beheld the inconceivable sovereign power of the body of the laywoman Acalā;
her inconceivable excellence of form, color, shape, height, and circumference;
and her inconceivable array of networks of light-rays that were unimpeded by any ground, city, or great mountain on the surface of the earth. Having seen this inconceivable...

Having smelled the fragrance emanating from all his pores as he performed deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, having beheld his boundless excellence of retinue, having gazed upon his invincible array of palaces and celestial mansions, and having plunged into his immeasurable oceans of virtues,
he praised the laywoman Acalā with this verse:

Because you have always guarded your stainless morality, because your vast patience has been fully cultivated, and because you have maintained a vigor as firm as a diamond, you have risen above the world and shine like the immovable king of mountains. // 1 //
Then, having praised the laywoman Acalā with this verse, the merchant’s son Sudhana said to her: "Noble lady, I have set my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
however, I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct, nor how one should practice it."
"I have heard, Noble Lady, that you give instruction and admonition to the bodhisattvas;
therefore, may the Noble Lady tell me: how should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, and how should one practice?"
Then the laywoman Acalā, having greeted the merchant’s son Sudhana with affectionate, pleasing, and endearing words of a bodhisattva, spoke to him thus: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!
It is well that you have resolved your mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Noble son, I am one who has attained the bodhisattva liberation called 'The Womb of Knowledge Difficult to Conquer'."
I am training in the gateway of the bodhisattva practice of firm commitment,
and I have attained the gateway of the dhāraṇī of the stage of the equality of all phenomena;
I am training in the gateway of the bodhisattva practice of firm commitment.
I have attained the entrance to the dhāraṇī of the level of the equality of all phenomena;
the light of the wisdom of eloquence that illuminates the reality of all phenomena has entered my mind;
and I have acquired the entrance to the samādhi called the array of tirelessness in the quest for the Dharma.

She asked: "Noble Lady, what is the domain of this bodhisattva liberation-gate called 'The Womb of Wisdom of Duryodhana,' and the domain of the bodhisattva practice-gate of 'Firmly Maintained Vows,' the dhāraṇī-gate of 'Sustaining the Level of Equality of All Phenomena,' the eloquence-light-gate of 'Illuminating the Reality of All Phenomena,' and the samādhi-gate of the 'Array of Unwearied Search for the Dharma'?"
She said: "Noble son, this matter is difficult to resolve with conviction.
He said: "Speak, Noble Lady!

Through the power of the Buddhas and by being sustained by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), I shall have conviction, I shall enter into it, I shall understand it, I shall investigate it, I shall follow it, I shall contemplate it, I shall focus my attention upon it, and I shall examine it."
I shall not contradict it, I shall not conceptualize it,
and I shall not superimpose upon it.
I shall equalize them.
Then the laywoman Acalā said this to the merchant’s son Sudhana: "Long ago, noble son, in the past, in the eon called Vimalaprabhā, a Tathāgata named Pralambabāhu appeared in the world.
And I was the sole daughter of King Vidyuddatta."
I was her daughter.
During that night, when it had grown quiet and the city gates were closed, while my mother and father were asleep, [she spoke].

While the multitudes of men and women were fast asleep, while the sounds of musical instruments, cymbals, and drums had subsided, and while the five hundred maidens of similar conduct were lying down;
As she lay upon her bed, beholding the night sky filled with hosts of stars, she saw in the space above the Blessed One,

the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Pralambabāhu— resembling Sumeru, the king of mountains, surrounded by a retinue of many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, and encircled by an inconceivable and innumerable host of bodhisattvas; his body was pervaded by a net of light rays that met no obstruction in any direction.
And from every pore of that Tathāgata’s body, such a fragrance wafts forth, by which my body and mind are refreshed and my heart is filled with joy.
Rising from my bed, I stand upon the surface of the earth with my palms joined in reverence with ten fingers extended, and [I gaze] toward that Blessed One.
Having paid homage with my head to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha Pralambabāhu, and gazing upon him,
I do not find his limit; I cannot perceive the extent of his left or right sides.
Reflecting upon the perfection of the primary marks and secondary characteristics, I could not attain satiety.
Then, noble son, this thought occurred to me: "By performing what kind of action is such a perfection of the body obtained?
By what is the perfection of the primary marks and secondary characteristics produced?"
How does the excellence of the array of radiance come into being?
How is the excellence of the retinue brought forth?
How does the excellence of the enjoyment of mind-made palaces manifest?
How is the perfection of merit produced?
How is the perfection of knowledge purified?
How does the perfection of the miraculous transformations of inconceivable samādhi arise?
"How is the perfection of dhāraṇīs accomplished? How does the perfection of eloquence come under one's mastery?
Then, noble son, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Pralambabāhu, knowing my inner intention, said this: "Daughter, you should generate an invincible mind for the sake of destroying all afflictions."
An unconquerable mind for the sake of weariness with all dogmatic attachments;
an unshrinking mind for the sake of following the profound methods of the Dharma;
and an unshakeable mind amidst the whirlpools and precipices of the ocean of sentient beings' sensory objects and inclinations.
A mind free from delusion regarding all states of existence, destinies, and places of rebirth; a mind never satiated for the sake of never ceasing its longing to behold all Buddhas;
and a mind of insatiability for the sake of receiving the clouds of Dharma from all Tathāgatas.
A mind of profound contemplation for the sake of following the light of the methods of all Buddha-dharmas;
a mind of preservation for the sake of all the wheels of Dharma of the Tathāgatas;
and a mind free from delusion, even regarding mere conventional designations.
How much more so, then, regarding the wisdom issuing from the mouth of the Tathāgata!
Daughter, you should give rise to a mind of distribution, for the purpose of sharing the jewel of the Dharma with all sentient beings according to their inclinations.
Noble son, it was from that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Pralambabāhu, that I received these...

Having heard such gateways to the instructions on the methods of the Dharma, they longed for the knowledge of the All-Knowing One, aspired to the state of the Ten Powers, desired the eloquence of a Buddha, wished to purify the array of a Buddha’s radiance, sought to bring to perfection the excellence of a Buddha’s body, yearned for the purity of a Buddha’s primary and secondary marks, and aspired to the excellence of a Buddha’s circle of the assembly.
Longing for the purification of a buddha-field, desiring the perfection of a Buddha’s deportment, and rejoicing in the perfection of a Buddha’s lifespan,
she gave rise to a mind that was indestructible by all afflictions, all śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas— like a diamond that cannot be shattered by the strength of all mountains or weapons.

Noble son, from that time onward, I do not recall ever having indulged in sensual desires even for as many eons as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa by virtue of this production of the thought of awakening,
let alone through the union of a couple.
Noble son, from that time onward, I do not recall ever having produced a single thought of resentment toward my own kinsmen.
How much less so toward other beings who have committed no offense!
Since that time, I do not recall giving rise to even a single thought associated with the view of a self,
let alone developing a sense of "mine" or attachment toward other possessions.

I do not recall ever experiencing mental confusion, a perception of otherness, or an indeterminate state of mind— even during death, rebirth, or dwelling in the womb— much less when I am consciously attending to it.
Furthermore, I do not recall having forgotten the sight of even a single Buddha throughout all those eons.
Even in a dream-vision,
let alone when they have attained the manifestation of the ten eyes of a bodhisattva,
I do not recall ever, from that time onward, having mentally forgotten even a single word or syllable of a dharma while receiving the clouds of dharma from all the Tathāgatas.
Not even that which is merely designated by a name,

let alone that which has issued from the treasury of the Tathāgata’s mouth; from that time forth, as I have been drinking these oceans of Dharma, I do not recall having failed to contemplate or examine even a single word.
Even regarding worldly phenomena,

from that time onward, I do not recall even a single door of a method among those oceans of methods of the Dharma in which I have not brought forth meditative concentration— even including the methods of knowledge for worldly crafts.

From that time forth, I do not recall having forgotten even a single word or syllable of the wheel of Dharma upheld by so many Tathāgatas as I have maintained it, except for what was done through the power of training sentient beings, even down to the pursuit of subsequent knowledge. From that time forth, I do not recall having failed to bring to fulfillment even a single vow among the oceans of visions of Buddhas seen by me, which were not undertaken for the purification of the ocean of all sentient beings.
Even regarding the contemplations on the vows of emanation-buddhas,

from that time onward, I do not recall even a single bodhisattva practice among those oceans of past bodhisattva practices of so many oceans of buddhas that was not undertaken by me for the sake of purifying my own conduct.
I have accomplished this.
Since that time, I do not recall ever having allowed even a single sentient being who came within the range of my vision to go without being established in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Since that time, I do not recall ever having produced even a single thought associated with the mental orientations of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.

Noble son, from that time forward, I do not recall having produced even a single doubt regarding a single word or syllable throughout as many eons as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa; nor have I ever produced the notion of duality, the notion of conceptualization, the notion of diversity, the notion of grasping,
the notion of inferiority or superiority, or the notion of attachment and aversion.
From that time on, noble son, I have never been separated from the arising of Buddhas;
I have never been separated from the Blessed Buddhas;
I have never been separated from the Bodhisattvas.
They were never separated from true spiritual friends;
they were never separated from hearing the vows of the Buddhas; they were never separated from hearing the conduct of Bodhisattvas.
They were never separated from hearing the method of the bodhisattva’s perfections; they were never separated from hearing the method of the light of knowledge regarding the bodhisattva stages;
and they were never separated from obtaining the hearing and acquisition of the inexhaustible treasury and storehouse of the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇīs and samādhis.

They were never separated from hearing the method for entering and descending into the net of world-systems that is without end or middle; they were never separated from obtaining the hearing of the causes for the arising of the realm of sentient beings that is without end or middle;
and they were never separated from the light of knowledge that completely exhausts the entire circle of the net of afflictions of all living beings.

They are never separated from the attainment of the knowledge that is the cause for the arising of the roots of goodness of all sentient beings; they are never separated from manifesting bodies according to the inclinations of all sentient beings;
they are never separated from the purity of the circle of sounds used to instruct all sentient beings.

And this, noble son, is the bodhisattva liberation of the blissful womb of knowledge of invincibility; and this is the gateway to the samādhi of the array of tireless pursuit of all dharmas, which I have entered,
and this is the gateway to the practice of awakening through firm commitment, which I am discerning.
And this is the gateway to the dhāraṇī of the level of the equality of all phenomena;
and for one who investigates this gateway of the light of knowledge consisting of eloquence that illuminates the fundamental nature of all phenomena, inconceivable miracles occur.
Do you wish, noble son, [to hear them]?
"Can he become visible?
She replied, "I wish so, Noble One."

Then, while remaining seated as she was, the laywoman Acalā [entered] the gateways to the samādhis preceded by the bodhisattva liberation-gate of the "Womb of Knowledge Difficult to Conquer," preceded by the array of the samādhi-gate of "Unwearied Search for All Dharmas," and preceded by the array of the samādhi-gate of the "Fruitful Mandala."

She beheld, investigated, followed, and contemplated one million gateways of meditative concentration— those preceded by the gateways of the *samādhi* that faces the mandala of the wisdom of the ten powers, and those preceded by the gateways of liberation and the *samādhi* of the inexhaustible treasury of the Buddha-lineage.
And immediately upon the laywoman Acālā entering [this state],...

The merchant’s son Sudhana saw, in the ten directions, world-systems as numerous as the atoms in ten inexpressible Buddha-fields, quaking in six ways and established as being composed of pure lapis lazuli.
And in each single world-system, he saw a hundred billion world-systems of four great continents and a hundred billion Tathāgatas.

He saw some [Tathāgatas] residing in the sublime abodes of the Tuṣita heaven, and others even up to the point of entering final nirvāṇa— this being because the world-systems were made of pure vaidūrya and free from all obscurations—
and he saw each individual Tathāgata as a circle of light consisting of a net of rays that pervades the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
And he saw each individual Tathāgata with an ocean of well-arranged circles of assemblies;
and from each Tathāgata, he heard the circle of sounds that illuminates the wheel of all dharmas and makes itself known to the ears of all sentient beings.
Then the laywoman Acalā, having emerged from that samādhi, said this to the merchant’s son Sudhana: "Noble son, have you seen, heard, and understood?
He replied, "I have seen it, Noble Lady."
"It has been heard and understood.
She said, "In this way, noble son, as I train myself in the bodhisattva practice of firm commitment, I have entered the samādhi called the 'Array of Unwearied Search for All Dharmas.'"
Established in the gate of liberation of the Bodhisattva Duryodhanajñānagarbha through the following of the dhāraṇī of the stage of the equality of all phenomena,
and through skill in the light of the knowledge of eloquence that illuminates the fundamental nature of all phenomena, I satisfy all sentient beings with well-spoken words.
How could I possibly know the conduct or describe the qualities of the Bodhisattvas who are endowed with inconceivable and immeasurable virtues?
Those who, like the best of the twice-born, wander without a fixed abode across the expanse of the sky;
those who, like the great lords of the Garuḍas, plunge into the ocean of beings for the sake of uplifting mature bodhisattvas;
and those who, like merchants, roam the island of jewels of omniscience, longing for the jewels of the wisdom of the Ten Powers.

Those who wander through the ocean of saṃsāra like powerful fishermen, holding in their hands the net of the beautiful wheel-mandala of the Dharma, for the sake of ripening and uplifting the beings born of craving;
those who roam pervading the city of the three worlds like lords of the asuras, for the sake of pacifying the agitation and upheaval caused by the asuras of the afflictions;
those who rise up in the sky of the realm of phenomena like the orb of the sun, for the sake of drying up the water of the thirst of beings and the mud of the afflictions.
Those who rise in the sky of wisdom like the orb of the full moon for the purpose of awakening the water-lilies of the minds of those to be trained;

those who abide in the world as level as the surface of the earth amidst the unevenness of attraction and aversion, rising and falling, for the purpose of causing the sprouts of the faculties of virtue in all living beings to grow and flourish;

those who move through all directions without attachment like the wind, for the purpose of uprooting the groves and thickets of the trees and creepers of the afflictions and views of all sentient beings.

Those who move about in the world like universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), for the sake of gathering the entire world through the equipment and requisites of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—
go, noble son,
right here in the southern region, to the country of Amitatosala, to the city named Tosala.
There dwells a wandering mendicant named Sarvagāmin;
go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva? How should one practice?"

Then the merchant’s son Sughana, having bowed his head at the feet of the laywoman Acalā and circumambulated the laywoman Acalā hundreds of thousands of times, looked back at her again and again, and departed from the presence of the laywoman Acalā. 20.
(23) Sarvagāmin.
Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, having brought the laywoman Acalā before his mind and recollecting the instructions of the laywoman Acalā, [proceeded].

Reflecting upon, following, contemplating, entering, cultivating, bringing to conclusion, meditating upon, illuminating, and harmonizing that which was shown, proclaimed, taught, praised, applied, analyzed, manifested, and disseminated by the laywoman Acalā, he proceeded in due order.
Wandering and traveling from region to region and from district to district, he arrived at the district of Amitatoṣala.
Having reached the city of Toṣala and searching and inquiring about it, he eventually reached the city of Toṣala.
At the time of sunset, having entered the city of Toṣala, he stood in the middle of the city crossroads.

Seeking and searching for a wandering mendicant who could go anywhere— going from street to street, from square to square, and from road to road— he saw, when the night had become tranquil, a mountain named Sulabha in the northern quarter of the city of Tosala.
On its peak, which was adorned with various grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, forests, and groves, he saw a great radiance like that of the risen sun.
Seeing that light, a surge of noble joy arose within him, and this thought occurred to him: "Without doubt, I shall see a spiritual friend here on the mountain peak.
He then departed from that city toward Mount Sulabha.

Having approached and ascended Mount Sulabha, he proceeded toward that mountain peak of great splendor; from afar, he beheld the wandering mendicant Sarvagāmin, whose complexion surpassed even that of Mahābrahmā, blazing with glory, surrounded by ten thousand Brahmās,
and walking back and forth upon the promenade.

Having bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and stood before him with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus: "Noble One, I have set my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva."
How should one practice?
I have heard, Noble One, that you give instruction and counsel to the bodhisattvas;
therefore, may the Noble One tell me: how should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva path?
"How should one practice?
He replied, "Excellent, excellent, noble son, you who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening!"

"Noble son, I am established in the bodhisattva practice that goes everywhere and follows after all things; I am endowed with the gateway of samādhi called the light of universal investigation, and with the gateway of the light of the wisdom of the perfection of wisdom, which is non-abiding, noble, unconditioned, and characterized by the differentiation of the entire foundation of the dharma-realm."

Thus, noble son, throughout the investigations of the receptacle world of all sentient beings, throughout the investigations of all the destinies of sentient beings, throughout the gateways of death for all sentient beings, throughout the gateways of rebirth for all sentient beings, throughout the various mixtures of the states of existence and destinies, and within the diverse arrangements of the world with its manifold bases of rebirth—
among sentient beings of various colors, shapes, heights, and circumferences, who possess various fetters of rebirth and various applications— I [have observed].

For those with diverse inclinations, namely those included within the realm of gods, those included within the realm of nāgas, those included within the realm of yakṣas, those included within the realm of gandharvas, those included within the realm of asuras, those included within the realm of garuḍas,

those included within the realm of kinnaras, those included within the realm of mahoragas, those included within the realm of hell-beings, those included within the realm of animals, and those included within the realm of the world of Yama.

I work for the benefit of beings— those included within the human realm and those not included within the human realm, those relying on various paths of views, and those resolved upon the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna— by means of diverse skillful methods and the application of various systems of knowledge.
That is to say, for some beings, I work for their benefit by teaching various worldly arts, through the light of the dhāraṇī that possesses the distinctions of all knowledge of arts.
For some beings, I act for their benefit by employing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), namely, to lead them toward the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
For some beings, I act for their benefit by praising the perfections (*pāramitā*), namely, by generating the light of the method of knowledge that transforms [merit] into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
For some beings, I act for their benefit by praising the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), namely, by generating the support for the non-wastage of the seed of awakening (*bodhibīja*).

For some beings, I act for their benefit by describing the conduct of bodhisattvas in all its aspects—that is, to generate the vow to purify all buddha-fields and to bring all beings to maturity; for other beings, I act for their benefit by generating a sense of spiritual urgency—that is, by demonstrating the experience of the suffering of the hells as the ripening and outflow of misconduct.

I benefit some beings by generating great joy in them—namely, by proclaiming that the offerings made to all Tathāgatas are certain to result in the fruit of omniscience; and I benefit some beings by manifesting the praise of the qualities of all Tathāgatas—namely, for the sake of generating the aspiration for omniscience and a longing for the body of the Buddha’s qualities.

For some beings, I act for their benefit by indicating the majesty of the Buddha, that is, to generate in them the aspiration for the attainment of a Buddha-body that is irreversible, effortless, never-ceasing in the performance of Buddha-activities, and free from attachment.

For some beings, I act for their benefit by demonstrating the sovereign power of the Buddha, that is, to generate in them the aspiration for the attainment of the perfection of a Buddha’s physical form which cannot be surpassed.
Furthermore, noble son, I—
In this city of Tośalī, among all the streets, all the squares, all the crossroads,

all the entrances to the alleys, all the houses, all the guilds, all the families, and all the family circles— among the men, women, boys, and girls who had gathered there according to their inclinations, their applications, their dominant influences, and their modes of conduct— he manifested bodies that were concordant with them in height, girth, and shape.
Having brought forth [this teaching], I teach the Dharma;
yet those beings do not realize by whom this was taught, or from where it has come.
Having heard it elsewhere, they practice for the sake of suchness.
Furthermore, noble son, as for these ninety-six heretical sects in Jambudvīpa who are attached to various types of views,
I follow them everywhere in order to bring to maturity those beings who are clinging to various types of views.
And just as I, noble son, work for the benefit of sentient beings here in the city of Tośalā,

so do I work for the benefit of sentient beings in all the villages, cities, towns, marketplaces, provinces, kingdoms, and royal capitals throughout Jambudvīpa; and just as in Jambudvīpa, [so do I do likewise elsewhere].
Likewise throughout every four-continent world system, and so on through the thousandfold, the two-thousandfold, the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system,
and likewise in the ten directions.

In immeasurable world-systems, throughout all paths of sentient beings, all abodes of sentient beings, all dwellings of sentient beings, all that which is designated as the resting places of sentient beings, all transformations of sentient beings, all convergences of sentient beings, all oceans of sentient beings, and all lineages of sentient beings.

In all directions and intermediate directions of all sentient beings, and in all the modes of existence of all sentient beings, I act for the benefit of those beings according to their inclinations and resolute convictions;

by means of various methods, various approaches, various gateways, various reasonings, various applications, various methods and approaches, various activities, and by manifesting various forms and colors to inspire faith.
I benefit sentient beings by articulating various paths of speech.
Noble son, this is the bodhisattva practice that goes everywhere and follows after all things, which I understand.
But what can I know of the bodhisattvas whose bodies consist of the entire world, who have attained the samādhi of the non-differentiation of their own body from all bodies?

They possess vast wheels of emanation that follow all states of existence; they traverse their own bodies through births in all worlds; they are supreme in the wheels of beautiful emanations that delight the eyes of the entire world; they manifest birth, lineage, and origin in every realm of beings; they possess wheels of vows that are unimpeded in dwelling throughout all eons; and they have attained the illumination of the array of conduct which is like the surface of Indra’s net.

To know the conduct or to speak of the virtues of those who are supremely consistent in their engagement in the welfare of all worlds, who have attained equality with the ground of the world throughout the three times, whose essence is infinite great compassion manifested from the realm of gnosis characterized by selflessness, and who are intent upon establishing the roots of virtue for all worlds.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region there is a district named Pṛthurāṣṭra.
There dwells a merchant-chief of perfumes named Utpalabhūti.
Go to him and ask: "How should bodhisattvas train in the conduct of a bodhisattva? How should they practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the wandering mendicant Sarvagāmin, circumambulated the wandering mendicant Sarvagāmin hundreds of thousands of times, and, looking back at him again and again,
departed from the presence of the wandering mendicant Sarvagāmin. 21.
(Gv 140) 24. Utpalabhūti.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, regardless of his body and life, [set out].
He is indifferent toward all states of existence, enjoyments, possessions, grasping, attachments, and transgressions;
he is indifferent toward the pleasures of all beings and places;
he is indifferent toward all forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
He is indifferent toward all retinues, enjoyments, and possessions; he is indifferent toward all the pleasures of sovereignty and dominion over a kingdom;
yet he is concerned with the ripening, disciplining, and purification of all sentient beings, by means of accomplishing the complete purification of an unsurpassed buddha-field.

He is full of longing because of his insatiable desire to perform worship, service, and attendance upon all Tathāgatas; he is full of longing for the thorough comprehension of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
and he is full of longing so as not to fall away from the practice of all the qualities of Bodhisattvas, which are oceans of all virtues.
He is intent upon all the great vows of the bodhisattvas, for the sake of dwelling together with the bodhisattva practices throughout all kalpas without exception;
he is intent upon entering the oceans of the circles of assemblies of all the Tathāgatas;

he is intent upon all the gateways of bodhisattva samādhis, for the sake of manifesting the miraculous power of entering into the incalculable number of all bodhisattva samādhis within each single gateway of samādhi.

With a longing gaze toward the wheels of light of knowledge regarding all phenomena, in order to remain insatiable in receiving the wheels of Dharma from all Tathāgatas, he beheld the sources of all spiritual friends and the arising of all spiritual friends,
as well as all other qualities of a bodhisattva. Gradually approaching the district of Pṛthurāṣṭra, he searched for and sought out the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti, and finally saw him.
Having seen him, he approached the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti;

having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti, circumambulated the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti hundreds of thousands of times, and standing before the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti with palms joined in reverence, he spoke as follows:
— “Noble one, I have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; desiring the equal gnosis of all Buddhas,
wishing to fulfill the entire circle of the fulfilled vows of all Buddhas, wishing to behold the form-body of all Buddhas,
wishing to bring to perfection the dharma-body of all Buddhas, and wishing to fully comprehend the gnosis-body of all Buddhas.”
