Desiring to purify the mandala of all bodhisattva conduct; desiring to illuminate the mandala of all bodhisattva samādhis; desiring to establish the mandala of all bodhisattva dhāraṇīs; desiring to dissolve the mandala of all obscurations;
and desiring to traverse the mandala of all buddha-fields.
And I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, how he should practice,
or how practicing, a bodhisattva goes forth to omniscience.
He said: "Excellent, excellent, noble son! It is well that you have resolved your mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Noble son, I know all fragrances."
I understand all mixtures of perfumes, all incenses, and all applications of incense;
I understand all ointments, all applications of ointments, all powders, all applications of powders, and all sources of perfumes, ointments, and powders.
I discern the scents of gods;
I also discern the scents of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
I discern all various kinds of scents as well.
scents that pacify diseases, scents that remove dejection,
and scents that produce worldly joy;
There are also fragrances that inflame the afflictions, fragrances that pacify the afflictions,
and fragrances that produce the pleasure and delight of various conditioned things.
They also possess the fragrances that produce a sense of revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena, the fragrances that remove intoxication and negligence,
and the fragrances that arise from the practice of mental attention directed toward the Buddha.
the fragrances that follow the methods of the Dharma,
the fragrances enjoyed by the noble ones,
and even the various degrees of fragrance of all bodhisattvas;
I also understand the fragrances that define all the stages of the bodhisattvas;
and I understand all those fragrances by way of their form, their origin, their production, their manifestation, their perfection, and their purity.
I understand it by way of avoidance, by way of application, by way of enjoyment, by way of object, by way of power, by way of dharma, and by way of root.
Noble son, in the human world there is a fragrance called Hastigarbha, which arises from the agitation of the *nāgas*.

A single pellet of this fragrance, the size of a sesame seed, covers the entire kingdom and countryside with a dense cloud-net of great fragrance and causes a rain of fine streams of fragrant water to fall for seven days.
Upon whichever sentient beings' bodies or robes those streams of fragrant water fall, [they are transformed].
They all become variegated with golden-colored flowers;
and those palaces, celestial mansions, and gabled halls upon which they fall, all become variegated with golden-colored flowers.

Furthermore, those beings who, while remaining within their inner dwellings, smell the fragrance of those networks of fragrant clouds wafted by the wind— all of them remain pervaded for seven days by sublime joy and gladness,
and they experience many kinds of physical and mental bliss and happiness.
No physical illness arises in their bodies, whether born from an imbalance of the elements or caused by external circumstances;
nor does mental suffering or dejection arise, nor do fear, terror, paralysis with fright, agitation of mind, or malice manifest.

And all those beings become mutually friendly in mind, filled with joy and gladness. Noble son, for those who have thus become filled with joy and gladness, I teach the Dharma starting from the purity of their intention,
such that they become destined for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Noble son, there is a sandalwood called *gośīrṣa* that originates from Mount Malaya;
one whose body is anointed with it is not burned even if they fall into a pit of fire.
Noble son, there is a fragrance called *aparājita* that originates from the coastal regions of the ocean.
By the sound of a drum or a conch shell anointed with it, every hostile army is defeated.
Noble son, there is a black aloe wood called Padmagarbha, which grows on the shore of Lake Anavatapta;
even a pellet of it the size of a sesame seed pervades the entire Jambudvīpa with its fragrance.
And whatever sentient beings smell that fragrance, they all attain a mind of restraint through revulsion toward evil.
Noble son, there is a species of fragrance called Aruṇavatī, which originates from Himavat, the king of mountains.
Upon smelling its fragrance, sentient beings become dispassionate in mind;
for them, I teach the Dharma in such a way that they attain the samādhi called Virajomaṇḍala.

Noble son, there is a species of incense born in the realm of the rākṣasas called Sāgaragarbha, which arises for the enjoyment of a universal monarch; by the mere scenting of it, the fourfold army of the universal monarch stands poised in the expanse of the sky.
Noble son, there is a species of incense called Śobhanavyūhā, produced in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods; by its mere fuming, the gods attain the recollection of the fragrance of the Buddha.

Noble son, in the abode of Suyāma, the king of the gods, there is a species of pure fragrance by which, when it is perfumed, all the sons of the gods of the Suyāma heaven approach the presence of Suyāma, the king of the gods. To them, having approached, Suyāma, the king of the gods, delivers a discourse on the Dharma.
Noble son, there is in the Tuṣita heaven a species of incense called Sindhuvāritā.

When this is burned before a Bodhisattva who is bound to only one more birth and is seated upon the Dharma-throne, it pervades the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) with a great cloud of fragrance and causes a great rain of clouds of Dharma, with manifold arrays of forms, to fall within all the circles of assemblies of the Tathāgatas.
"Noble son, in the palace of the god-king Sunirmita there is a species of incense called Manoharā;
when it is burned in the palace of the god-king Sunirmita, it rains down an inconceivable cloud of Dharma for seven days.
Noble son, I know this formulation of incense."

How could I possibly know the conduct or describe the virtues of the Bodhisattvas who are free from the scent of impurity, who have transcended all desires, who are liberated from the snares of the Māra of the afflictions, who have passed beyond all states of existence, who move within forms that have entered the illusion of primordial wisdom, who are unstained by any world, whose ethical discipline is unattached, whose mandala of knowledge is purified and unobstructed, whose sphere of activity is the range of unimpeded knowledge, who do not rely on any dwelling-place or abode, yet who traverse the dwellings and abodes of all states of existence?
Either to illuminate the gateway of the purity of conduct,
or to manifest blameless behavior.
Or, it is to teach the practice of non-malice through body, speech, and mind.
Go, son of good family,
right here in the southern region to a city named Kūṭāgāra;
there dwells a fisherman named Vaira.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti, circumambulated the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at him again and again,
departed from the presence of the perfumer-merchant Utpalabhūti. 22.
Vaira.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, setting out upon and traveling along the road leading toward the city of Kūṭāgāra, proceeded on his way.
Having observed the downward slope of the path, the upward rise of the path, the levelness of the path, the unevenness of the path, the dusty nature of the path, the dust-free nature of the path,

the security of the path, the thicketiness of the path, the unobstructed nature of the path, the crookedness of the path, and the straightness of the path, he formed this thought: "Truly, this approach of mine toward that spiritual friend is the cause for practicing the path of the bodhisattvas."
It will become the cause for practicing the path of knowledge that benefits sentient beings;
it will become the cause for practicing the path of the perfections, and the cause for practicing the path of knowledge that benefits all sentient beings.

It is for the sake of turning back the fall into the heights and depths of attachment and aversion toward all sentient beings, for the sake of warding off the uneven intellects of all sentient beings, and for the sake of pacifying the dust of the afflictions of all sentient beings.

It will serve as the cause for removing the stumps, thorns, pebbles, and potsherds of the various unwholesome views of all sentient beings; for the attainment of the supreme state of the unobstructed realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); and for leading [beings] to the gateway of unimpaired omniscience.
For what reason?
All wholesome qualities have spiritual friends as their source;
omniscience depends upon spiritual friends.

Engaged in such reflection and mental attention, his conduct difficult to fathom, he proceeded by stages toward the city of Kūṭāgāra; searching everywhere for Vaira the fisherman, he saw him at the entrance of the great city on the shore of the ocean’s descent,
surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and many hundreds of thousands of living beings who desired to hear his various discourses.
Seeing him surrounded by those proclaiming discourses on the ocean, announcing to sentient beings the oceans of the Buddha’s qualities,
he approached where the fisherman Vairo was.

Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of Vaira the fisherman, and having circumambulated Vaira the fisherman hundreds of thousands of times, he stood before Vaira the fisherman with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus: "Noble sir, I have generated the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor how one should practice it.
I have heard, however, that the Noble One gives instruction and advice to bodhisattvas.
"May the Noble One tell me this: how should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, and how should he practice?
He replied, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
Since you, having generated the mind set upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment, inquire about the cause for the arising of the attainment of great gnosis;
the cause for the arising of the manifestation of the various sufferings of saṃsāra; the cause for the arising of the journey to the support of the island of omniscience;

the cause for the arising of the indestructible Mahāyāna; and the cause for the arising of the practice of the path that eliminates the fear of falling into the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

You inquire about the cause for the arising of the path of knowledge that attains the turning toward the gateways of various peaceful samādhis; the cause for the arising of the path unimpeded by the wheel of the chariot of the vows and investigations of the bodhisattva’s conduct that leads everywhere;

the cause for the purity of the arising of the path of the method of the nature of the bodhisattva’s conduct, which is an array of waves of all splendors; the cause for the purity of the arising of the path that faces all directions of phenomena to their furthest limits;
and the cause for the purity of the arising of the path that enters the ocean of omniscience.
"Noble son, I dwell here in this great city of Mahāsāgaratīrakūṭāgāra, purifying the bodhisattva practice called the Banner of Great Compassion.
Noble son, having beheld the poor beings in Jambudvīpa, I undergo such austerities for their sake."
That is to say: "I shall fulfill their intentions;
I shall gather them through worldly gifts;
I shall satisfy them with the enjoyment of the Dharma; and I shall teach them the path of the accumulation of merit."
I shall generate the equipment of wisdom; I shall increase the power of the roots of virtue;
I shall give rise to the mind of awakening.
I shall purify the intention for enlightenment;
I shall strengthen the power of great compassion;
I shall pacify the suffering of saṃsāra.

I shall sustain the strength that endures the weariness of wandering through saṃsāra; I shall employ them in gathering the ocean of sentient beings; and I shall establish them in the gateway of practice toward the ocean of virtues.
I shall bestow upon them the light of knowledge from the ocean of Dharma; I shall cause the ocean of all Buddhas to turn toward them; and I shall cause them to enter the ocean of omniscience.
Engaged in such reflection and mental attention, noble son, I wander here in this city of the peaked palace on the shore of the ocean.
Engaged thus in the welfare and happiness of the world, noble son, I know all the jewel-islands of the great oceans;
I know all the mines of jewels, all the sources of jewels, and the root of all jewels.

I know all the abodes of the nāgas and all their disturbances; all the abodes of the yakṣas and all their disturbances; all the abodes of the rākṣasas and the pacification of all fear of rākṣasas; all the abodes of the bhūtas and the complete subsiding of all obstacles caused by bhūtas.
I know the avoidance of every whirlpool of rebirth, the evasion of the entry into great waves, and the variations in the color of the water.
I understand the revolutions of the moon, sun, luminaries, and the hosts of planets; I understand night and day, the moments (kṣaṇa), the instants (lava), and the hours (muhūrta).

I understand the distinctions between going and coming, safety and danger, the firmness of the construction of vessels and their mechanisms, the avoidance of vessels, the propulsion of vessels, the gathering of winds, the generation of winds, the turning back of vessels, the changing of vessels, the mooring of vessels, and the dispatching of vessels.

Thus, noble son, endowed with such knowledge, I am constantly engaged in activities for the benefit of sentient beings; like a merchant leader, I bring a multitude of people to the island of jewels by means of a sturdy vehicle— secure, auspicious, and free from fear— gladdening them according to their joy with Dharma-discourses that accord with their inclinations.
Having provided them with an abundance of all kinds of jewels, I bring them back again to Jambūdvīpa;
and, noble son, never before has any one of my vessels ever met with disaster.
Furthermore, noble son, for those beings who come within the range of my vision, I provide for their welfare.
And those beings who hear my teaching of the Dharma,
their fears of sinking into the ocean of all saṃsāra vanish,
and the knowledge of entering the ocean of omniscience becomes manifest before them.
They apply themselves to drying up the ocean of craving,
they attain the light of wisdom regarding the ocean of the three times,
and they exert themselves for the sake of exhausting the ocean of suffering of all sentient beings.
They apply themselves to clarifying the turbidity of the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings;
they exert vigor for the purification of the ocean of all buddha-fields;
and they do not turn back from pervading the ocean of all directions.
They penetrate the distinctions within the ocean of the faculties of all living beings;
they conform to the ocean of the conduct of all sentient beings; and they attain manifestations that appear according to the inclinations of the ocean of worlds.

Noble son, I have attained this bodhisattva liberation called "The Sound of the River's Flow: The Recollection of Dwelling Together with the Unfailing Sight and Hearing of the Banner of Great Compassion.

How could I possibly describe the bodhisattvas who roam the ocean of all saṃsāra, who are unsullied by the ocean of all afflictions, who are free from the fear of the crocodiles that seize one within the ocean of all views, and who roam through the waters of the intrinsic nature of the ocean of all phenomena?

the conduct of those who investigate the fundamental nature of the ocean of all worlds; who possess the nets that gather the articles for sustaining the ocean of all worlds; who dwell within the ocean of omniscience; who churn the ocean of all sentient beings' attachments; who abide in a state uninterrupted throughout the ocean of all times; who possess direct knowledge of the reality of the ripening of the ocean of all worlds; and who do not let the time for the discipline of the ocean of all worlds pass by.
To know or to speak of his virtues.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region there is a city named Nandihāra.
There dwells a merchant chief named Jayottama.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the fisherman Vaira, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at him again and again with a tearful face and weeping— insatiable in his longing to behold the spiritual friend—
he departed from the presence of the fisherman Vaira. 23.
(Gv 145) 26. Jayottama.

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, with a mind pervading the realm of sentient beings through the immeasurable state of great friendliness, and with his mental continuum saturated by the moisture of great compassion, [proceeded].

He has accumulated the magnificent array of the vast provisions of merit and wisdom; he is free from the dust, darkness, stains, and mire of all afflictions; he follows the equality of all phenomena; he has set out upon the path to omniscience which is devoid of highs and lows; he has been extracted from the gateways leading to immeasurable unwholesome states; he possesses the power, prowess, and strength of firm vigor that is indestructible against all unwholesome things;

he is established in the gateways of the vast pliancy of the inconceivable samādhis of the bodhisattvas; and he has dispelled the darkness of ignorance without remainder by means of the radiant splendor of the sun of wisdom.
Scattered with the flowers of wisdom stirred by the breezes of skillful means that are pleasant and cool, conforming to the method of knowledge that issues from the ocean of great vows,

possessing the knowledge that pervades the unobstructed realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and facing the entrance to the city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) without interruption, he— desiring the path of the bodhisattvas—
approached the city of Nandihāra and sought out and searched for the merchant leader Jayottama.
He saw him at the edge of the city of Nadihāra, in the Aśoka grove adorned with various banners, surrounded by many thousands of householders,
concluding various matters of state business and delivering a discourse on the Dharma for the purpose of illuminating the eradication of all egoism.
For the relinquishing of all sense of "mine," for the abandonment of all grasping, and for the renunciation of the appropriation of all things.
For the purpose of tearing asunder all dogmatic attachments, for cutting through the bonds of all craving,
and for shattering the door-panels of all views.

For the purpose of dispelling the darkness of all doubts, misgivings, and hesitations; for the removal of the turbidity of deceit and guile; and for the complete purification of the stains of envy and avarice.
For the purpose of clarifying the lake of the mind,
for establishing sentient beings in a state of untroubled mind,
and for the purpose of generating the power of untroubled faith and taking delight in beholding the Buddhas.

He was teaching the Dharma—namely, for the sake of delighting in the arousal of the thought of awakening—in order to receive the Buddha-dharmas by manifesting the power of the bodhisattvas; to generate the power of bodhisattva samādhis by indicating the bodhisattva practices; and to bring about the purification and transcendence of the power of bodhisattva mindfulness by demonstrating the power of bodhisattva wisdom.

Then, having waited for the conclusion of that discourse, the merchant’s son Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the merchant Jayottama, bowed down for a long time, and with an intention imbued with reverence for the Dharma, uttered these words: "I am Sudhana,
I am Sudhana, O Noble One!"
I am seeking the bodhisattva conduct;
may the Noble One instruct me so that I may train in the bodhisattva conduct,
and training therein, become oriented toward the bodies for the ripening and disciplining of all sentient beings.
May I never abandon the vision of all Buddhas;
may I hear the Dharma of all Buddhas;
may I uphold the clouds of Dharma of all Buddhas.
May I practice according to the systems of all the Buddha-dharmas;
may I engage in the conduct of a bodhisattva in all world-systems; and may I not become weary of the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout my dwelling in all kalpas.
May I comprehend the miraculous transformations of all Tathāgatas;
may I receive the empowerments of all Buddhas;
and may I obtain illumination within the powers of all Tathāgatas.
Then the merchant Jayottama said this to the merchant’s son Sudhana: "Excellent, excellent, noble son! It is well that you have resolved your mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Noble son, I purify the gateway to the bodhisattva practice that goes everywhere—that is to say, by the power of attaining non-activity while remaining non-abiding in existence."
Thus, standing here at the gateway of the purification of the bodhisattva conduct that leads everywhere, I [perceive] throughout the entire great trichiliocosm—
in all the worlds of the Thirty-three gods, in all the abodes of the Yāma gods, in all the Tuṣita heavens, in all the Nirmāṇarati heavens, and in all the Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens— (Gv 146)

In all the abodes of Māra, in all the realms of desire, within all the assemblies of gods, in all the palaces of the gods, in all the worlds of the nāgas, in all the abodes of the nāgas, in all the worlds of the yakṣas,
in all the abodes of the yakṣas, and in all the worlds of the rākṣasas, in all the abodes of the rākṣasas.
In all the worlds of the kumbhāṇḍas, in all the abodes of the kumbhāṇḍas;
in all the worlds of the pretas, in all the abodes of the pretas; in all the worlds of the gandharvas, in all the abodes of the gandharvas.
In all the worlds of the asuras, in all the abodes of the asuras; in all the worlds of the garuḍas, in all the abodes of the garuḍas;
in all the worlds of the kinnaras, in all the abodes of the kinnaras.
In all the worlds of the mahoragas, in all the abodes of the mahoragas;
in all the worlds of humans, in all the abodes of humans;
in all villages, cities, towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals—throughout everything contained within the realm of desire and in all the destinies of sentient beings—I teach the Dharma.
I renounce unrighteousness; I pacify disputes; I turn back strife.
I pacify quarrels;
I prevent war;
I settle strife.
I cause enmity to cease; I sever bonds; I break open prisons.
I turn back all fears;
I utterly sever the formative activities of unwholesome karma;
and I restrain sentient beings from the taking of life.
I restrain sentient beings from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
I turn sentient beings away from all unwholesome activities and cause them to engage in the performance of all wholesome dharmas.
I teach all sentient beings all the arts and crafts;
I illuminate and formulate all the treatises that bring benefit to the world.
I reveal and I manifest [this] for the sake of gladdening the world,
for the sake of maturing sentient beings, and to conform with all non-Buddhist sects.
In order to indicate the excellence of further knowledge, to turn back all forms of dogmatic views,
and to proclaim all the qualities of a Buddha, I teach the Dharma even as far as the Brahma-world, having surpassed all the gods of the realm of form;
and just as here in this trichiliocosm, so too elsewhere.

Likewise, in the ten directions, in world systems as numerous as the atoms in ten inexpressible hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields, I teach the Dharma; I teach the Buddha-dharmas;
I teach the dharmas of Bodhisattvas, the dharmas of Śrāvakas, and the dharmas of Pratyekabuddhas.
I teach the hells;
I teach the path leading to the hells;
I teach the causes for becoming a hell-being.
I teach the animal realm;
I teach the dissolution of the animal destiny, the path leading to the animal destiny, and the suffering of rebirth in the animal realm.
I teach the world of Yama.
I teach the path leading to the world of Yama and the suffering of the world of Yama;
I teach the heavenly realm, the path leading to the heavenly realm, and the enjoyment of the pleasures and refinements of the heavenly realm.
I teach the world of humans; I teach the path leading to the destiny of the human world, and I teach the variety of experiences of pleasure and pain in the world of humans.
Thus, noble son, I teach the worldly dharmas.

I also teach the arising of the world, the passing away of the world, the disadvantage of the world, and the escape from the world; that is to say, for the purpose of illuminating the path of the bodhisattvas, for the purpose of turning back from the faults of saṃsāra, for the purpose of demonstrating the qualities of omniscience, for the purpose of pacifying the suffering of delusion regarding the realms of existence, for the purpose of revealing the unobstructed nature of phenomena, and for the purpose of elucidating the activities of worldly progression.

I teach the Dharma for the purpose of indicating the pleasure and pain involved in the activities of all worlds; for the purpose of discerning the perceptions regarding the foundation of the entire universe; for the purpose of illuminating the Tathāgata’s dharmas which are without abode; for the purpose of turning back the wheel of all karma and afflictions; and for the purpose of indicating the turning of the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma.
Noble son, I know only this gateway to the purification of the bodhisattva conduct that goes everywhere, called the "Stainless Array of Non-conditioned Illumination."

What can be done by me [to describe those] bodhisattvas who possess all superknowledges; whose bodies of wisdom, having reached the illusory state, pervade the surface of all buddha-fields; who have attained the stage of the wisdom of the universal eye; who possess the supreme faculty of hearing regarding the communication of sounds through all paths of speech; who have attained mastery over the illumination of the gateways of Dharma that pervades the three times;

who are heroic beings possessing sovereignty over the wisdom of the convergence of all dharmas; and who, with their broad, beautiful, and slender tongues, emit a circle of unbroken voices that inconceivably and immeasurably communicate to sentient beings according to their inclinations?

To know the conduct or the qualities of those whose bodies are like illusions, equal to all bodhisattvas, possessing colors and forms pleasing to an ocean of sentient beings with diverse inclinations; who possess supreme atoms of bodies that are non-dual, non-conceptual, and inconceivable like all Tathāgatas; whose bodies of gnosis follow after all three times; and whose sphere of activity is as vast and immeasurable as the expanse of space.
To speak.
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region, in the country of Śroṇāparānta, there is a city named Kaliṅgavana.
There dwells a bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā.
Go to her and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the merchant Jayottama, circumambulated the merchant Jayottama hundreds of thousands of times, and, looking back at him again and again, departed from the presence of the merchant Jayottama. 24.
(Gv 148) 27. Siṃhavijṛmbhitā.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana proceeded by stages toward a city named Kaliṅgavana in the region of Śroṇāparānta.
He approached that place;
having arrived, while searching for the nun named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā and questioning every living being as he wandered here and there,
hundreds of young men and hundreds of young women gathered from the streets, crossroads, and junctions and followed him wherever he went.

And many hundreds of men and many hundreds of women expressed their desire, saying: "Noble son, this nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā dwells right here in the great garden called Sūryaprabha, bestowed by Jayaprabhānupradatta, within this city of Kaliṅgavana,
proclaiming the Dharma for the benefit of immeasurable beings."

Then, Sudhana the merchant’s son approached that great park, Sūryaprabha; walking about and looking all around, he saw in that great park trees named Candrodgata, covered with gabled pavilions, radiant with the color of flames and shining with the brilliance of flames, pervading the area for a league in every direction with their light.
He saw leaf-trees named Saṃpracchadana, shaped like parasols with foliage arranged in the form of canopies, shining like clouds of blue beryl;

and flower-trees named Kusumakośa, as beautiful and of various shapes as the Himalaya king of mountains, raining down inexhaustible floods of flowers of diverse colors, resembling the Pārijātaka and Kovidāra trees that adorn the city of the Thirty-three;
and fruit-trees named Sadāpakva, covered with incomparable, sweet fruits, shaped like the peaks of the golden Mount Meru, and always abundant in fruit.

And there were jewel-king trees named Vairocanakośa, having the form of incomparable king-jewels, which maintained a wealth of treasuries emitting divine garlands, wreaths, ornaments, and wish-fulfilling king-jewels, and which possessed the forms of countless colored precious gems;
and clothing trees named Prasādana, adorned with hanging displays from treasuries of divine jeweled garments of various colors;
and musical instrument trees named Pramodana, producing the exceedingly divine, delightful, and sweet sounds of instruments.

He saw fragrant trees named Samantaśubhavyūha, which gladden all directions with their delightful scents that are unimpeded in every form; and he saw springs, lakes, ponds, and lotus-pools built of bricks of the seven jewels, with jewel-staircases arranged in the four directions, surrounded by various jeweled railings smeared with black sandalwood paste from the Kālānusārin tree,
and having floors laid with the king of blue vaidūrya gems.
Their bottoms were strewn with sands of Jāmbūnada gold;
they were filled with delightful celestial water endowed with the eight qualities;
and their waters were covered with divine lotuses—blue, red, white, and yellow—possessing various colors, celestial fragrances, and exquisite textures.
They resounded with the sweet warbling of flocks of various birds of divine and exquisite beauty,
and were adorned by encircling rows of trees most splendid with diverse divine jewels.
At the foot of every one of those various jewel-trees, there were arranged lion-thrones of variegated and lovely form, featuring inconceivable arrays of many kinds of jewels.
They were furnished with various divine jewels and garments as offerings; they were perfumed by the incense of all kinds of celestial fragrances;
and they were covered by variegated jeweled canopies, from which hung jeweled ribbons surpassing those of the heavens.
He saw them covered with nets of Jambūnada gold variegated with various jewels,
emitting the delightful and sweet sounds of nets of jeweled bells,
and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of divine jewel thrones.
In one place, he saw a lion throne with a jewel-lotus interior prepared at the foot of a jewel-tree;
in another place, a lion throne with a lotus interior made of the king of fragrant jewels; and in another place, a lion throne with a lotus interior made of the king of naga-array jewels.
In some places there were lion thrones with lotus centers made of the king of jewels called Ratnasiṃha; in some places, lion thrones with lotus centers made of the king of jewels called Vairocana;
and in some places, lion thrones with lotus centers made of the king of jewels called Digvirocana.

In some places he saw lion thrones with lotus centers made of the finest indravajra jewels; in other places, lion thrones with lotus centers made of the finest jagadrocana jewels; and in others, at the foot of jewel-trees, lion thrones with lotus centers made of white-colored finest jewels were arranged.
And he saw that entire great garden, its surface strewn with various jewels like the great ocean filled with islands of gems;

its ground-portion possessed a soft touch like *kācilindika* cloth, inlaid with all kinds of jewels set within a bed of blue beryl, free from rising or sinking as the feet were placed down or lifted up; and its surface was covered with lotuses of delightful fragrance made of the finest *vajra-ratna*, providing a pleasant touch.
It resounded with the sweet cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, kuṇālas, kalaviṅkas, cuckoos, and jīvaṃjīvakas; it was adorned with magnificent arrays of divine sandalwood trees and jewel-trees;

it was showered by inexhaustible streams of rain from clouds of various jeweled flowers and precious blossoms; it surpassed the Miśrakāvana grove; it was graced by the constant incense of incomparable king-of-fragrances burning within exquisitely fashioned pavilions of various jewels; and its magnificent layout excelled even that of the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods.

Above, it was covered by a divine and extraordinary lattice of various jewels; its regions were adorned with clusters of hanging garlands of pearls, gems, and flowers; it was embellished on all sides by a radiant golden net inlaid with a variegated arrangement of jewel-bells; it resounded with the sweet and charming sounds produced by various musical trees, jeweled cymbals, and lattices of bells stirred by the wind; it possessed an exceedingly delightful resonance arising from the songs of the Apsarases led by the divine king Vaśavartin; and it was made magnificent by the raining down of clouds of celestial *kalpa*-cloth in diverse colors.

It was like the great ocean, with an infinite radiance of colors and a sight that never tires the beholder; it was adorned with hundreds of thousands of peaked pavilions arrayed with inconceivable and incalculable jewels;

it was as beautiful as the city of the Lord of the Thirty-three, adorned with various patterns of all kinds of gems; its appearance was auspicious on all sides due to the arrangement of well-fashioned parasols;
it was graced by wonderful peaks like the world of Mahendra; and it blazed with the light of the king of jewels that illuminates the world, emitting a constant, delightful, and great splendor.

Through the great power of inconceivable supernatural faculties bestowed by the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, he beheld that great garden, Sūryaprabha, which was as vast as the abode of Mahābrahmā, supported by incalculable world-systems, expansive as the treasury of space, and possessing immeasurable room.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana beheld these vast garden arrays, which were endowed with such immeasurable and inconceivable qualities;

which were perfected through the maturation of the karma of bodhisattvas; which were born from supramundane and expansive roots of virtue; which arose as the natural outflow of inconceivable offerings and services rendered to the Buddhas; which could not be overwhelmed by any remaining roots of virtue throughout all worlds; which were produced from the illusory nature of all phenomena; and which were brought forth as the ripening of pure, vast, and auspicious merit.

Surveying all around, he beheld the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, who— born from the empowerment of the natural outflow of her previously performed good deeds and virtuous conduct— possessed qualities uncommon even to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, unassailable by any heterodox teachers or opponents, and invisible to the activities of all Māras and paths of all foolish ordinary worldlings.

And upon all those great lion-thrones situated at the foot of various jewel-trees, the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā was seated, surrounded by a vast retinue; she possessed a serene physical presence, with a perfectly tranquil deportment, her senses calmed and her mind at peace;
she was well-guarded and had conquered her senses, being as thoroughly subdued as a noble elephant and as clear, untroubled, and translucent in heart as a lake.
Like the king of wish-fulfilling gems, she grants all desires; like a lotus, she is unsullied by worldly conditions;
like a lion, she is free from fear and the bristling of hair through the purity of her fearlessness;
and like the king of great mountain ranges, she is unshakable through the purity of her ethical discipline.
Like the Gandharva king Manohara, she gladdens the minds of the world; like snow and sandalwood, she pacifies the burning heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*);
like the Sudarśana king of medicines, she brings about the cessation of all suffering in the world; like the noose of Varuṇa, her sight is never in vain;

like the radiance of the Tathāgata, she generates the bliss of physical and mental pliancy (*prasrabdhi*); and like Mahābrahmā, she is free from the outbursts (*paryutthāna*) of passion, hatred, and delusion.
Like the king of water-purifying jewel-gems, it brings refreshing joy to the minds of sentient beings turbid with afflictions; like a fertile field, it causes the roots of virtue to increase.
And upon those thrones and their surrounding seats, he beheld a diverse assembly seated there.

In one place, in the assembly surrounding his seat, he taught the Dharma-door named "The Distinction of the Inexhaustible Liberation" to the goddess Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, who was seated among the sons of the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm, headed by the son of the gods Maheśvara.
In one place,

within the retinue of seats, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahma-realm, headed by Rucira-brahmā, as she was proclaiming the purity of the circle of sounds called Samantatalabheda.

In another place, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst a retinue of gods and goddesses, headed by the divine kings of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm and the Vaśavartin realm, as she was proclaiming the Dharma-door named "The Array of Mastery over the Purity of Bodhisattva Intent."

In another place, he saw the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst a retinue of Āsanaparivāra, together with the sons of the gods from the Nirmāṇarati heaven led by Sunirmitadevarāja, who were surrounded by divine maidens; she was proclaiming a gate of the Dharma called Sarvadharmaśubhavyūha.

In one place, within the surrounding assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst the sons of the gods belonging to the Tuṣita realm, headed by the divine king Saṃtuṣita, together with their retinues of celestial maidens, as she was proclaiming the entrance into the Dharma called *Svacittakośāvarta*. In another place, within the surrounding assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā [proclaiming] the [entrance into the Dharma] called *Anantavyūha* amidst the sons of the gods headed by the divine king Suyāma, together with their retinues of celestial maidens.
He saw her proclaiming a gateway to the Dharma.

In one place, within a circle of seats where the sons of the gods belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa realm— headed by Śakra, the king of the gods— and accompanied by their retinues of celestial maidens were seated, he saw the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā proclaiming a gateway to the Dharma called "The Face of Agitation."

In another place, within a surrounding assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst hundreds of nāga kings led by Sāgara, including Nanda, Upananda, Manasvin, Airāvata, Anavatapta, and others, together with their nāga maidens and retinues of nāga youths, as she was proclaiming the Dharma-door named "The Array of the Radiance of the Buddha’s Domain."

In one part of the assembly, he saw the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā teaching the dharma-gate named Jagatparitrāṇakośa to the lords of the yakṣas, headed by the great king Vaiśravaṇa, together with their retinues of yakṣa maidens and yakṣa youths,
as they sat there. In another part of the assembly, [he saw her] to the gandharvas, headed by the gandharva king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with their retinues of gandharva maidens and gandharva youths.

He saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated among those gathered there, proclaiming the Dharma-door named "Inexhaustible Delight. In another assembly of seats, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated among the lords of the asuras headed by Rāhu— the lord of asuras— along with their retinues of asura maidens and asura youths, proclaiming the Dharma-door named "Array of the Impetus of Wisdom in the Dharmadhātu."
In one place,

within a circle of seats, he saw the nun named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated at the head of the lords of the Garuḍas, led by the lord of Garuḍas who possesses great speed, together with their retinues of Garuḍa maidens and Garuḍa youths, as she was proclaiming a gateway to the Dharma.

In one place, within the surrounding assembly, he saw the Kinnara kings, headed by Drumakinnararāja, seated together with their retinues of Kinnara maidens and Kinnara youths, as they were proclaiming the gate of the Dharma called *Buddhacaryāvabhāsa* to the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā.
In another place, within the surrounding assembly, he saw the Mahoraga kings, headed by Bhṛkuṭīmukha-mahoragendra, together with their retinues of Mahoraga maidens and Mahoraga youths.

He saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated among those gathered, proclaiming the Dharma-door named *Buddhaprītisaṃbhava* (The Arising of Joy in the Buddha). In another assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst hundreds of thousands of men, women, boys, and girls, proclaiming the Dharma-door named *Jñānaviśeṣagamana* (Attaining Distinctive Wisdom).

In one part of the assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst a retinue of lordly rākṣasas headed by the rākṣasa king Nityaujohara-drumarāja, together with their retinues of rākṣasa maidens and rākṣasa youths, as she was proclaiming the Dharma-door named "The Source of Compassion. In another part of the assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated amidst beings who were devoted to the Śrāvaka vehicle, as she was proclaiming the Dharma-door named "The Radiance of the Distinction of Gnosis."

In one part of the assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, seated amidst a circle of beings who were devoted to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, proclaiming a gateway to the Dharma called "The Radiance of the Noble Qualities of the Buddha. In another part of the assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, seated amidst beings who were devoted to the Mahāyāna, proclaiming a gateway to the light of the knowledge of meditative concentration called "The Universal Gateway."

In one part of the assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated among bodhisattvas who had first resolved to attain awakening, as she was proclaiming the entrance into concentration called the Summit of All Buddhas’ Vows. In another part of the assembly, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated among bodhisattvas established in the second stage, as she was proclaiming the entrance into concentration called the Stainless Mandala.

In one part of the assembly of seats, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, seated amidst bodhisattvas established in the third stage, proclaiming the entrance into the meditative concentration named *Praśāntavyūha*. In another part of the assembly of seats, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, seated amidst bodhisattvas established in the fourth stage, proclaiming the entrance into the meditative concentration named *Sarvajñatāvegaviṣayasambhava*.

In one part of the surrounding assembly, he saw the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, seated among bodhisattvas established on the fifth stage, proclaiming the entrance into the meditative absorption named Cittalatākusumagarbha;

Thus, indeed, whatever designations of beings and destinations of beings there may be within the convergence of all places of rebirth, for those beings who were matured, ready to be trained, and had become fit vessels,

he gathered them together in that great grove; and as they sat each upon their own seat in attendance, having various inclinations, various resolute convictions, fixed intentions, and intense, flavorful faith, [he taught] the Lion’s Yawn.
He saw the bhikṣuṇī teaching the Dharma in such a manner that all became destined for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
For what reason? Because it was as follows:

the teachings of the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, headed by the "Universal Eye Equanimity," headed by the "Instruction on All Buddha-Dharmas," headed by the "Distinctions of the Foundation of the Dharma-Realm," headed by the "Dispelling of the Circle of All Obstructions," and headed by the "Arising of the Wholesome Mind in All Worlds."

He entered hundreds of thousands of incalculable gateways to the perfection of wisdom— beginning with the Array of Distinctions, the Matrix of the Method of Non-attachment, the Mandala of the Dharmadhātu, the Treasury of Mind, and the Matrix of the Simultaneous Manifestation of What is Appropriate—
and those bodhisattvas and other beings who entered that great garden, Sūryaprabha, in order to see the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā and hear the Dharma.
All of them were first established by the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā in the accumulation of the roots of virtue, and were rendered irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, having beheld such excellence of the park, excellence of the monastery, excellence of the walking-paths, excellence of the articles for enjoyment, excellence of the couches and seats, excellence of the circles of assemblies, excellence of sovereign power, excellence of miraculous transformations, and excellence of the array of eloquence belonging to the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, and having heard the inconceivable method of the Dharma, his mind was saturated by the vast cloud of Dharma.
Thinking, "I shall circumambulate hundreds of thousands of times, having offered this sublime gift of the perfection of pure intention before the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā," the entire great park,
along with the array of the circle of the assembly, was then suffused and illuminated by the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā with a magnificent radiance.
Having circumambulated her hundreds of thousands of times, he perceived this: while circumambulating, he saw the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā facing him from every side.
Standing before her with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus: "Noble Lady, I have set my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor how one should practice it.
I have heard, however, that the Noble Lady gives instruction and advice to bodhisattvas.
May the Noble Lady tell me this: how should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, and how should he practice?
She said, "Noble son, I am a possessor of the bodhisattva liberation called 'the eradication of all conceit'.
He asked, "Noble lady, what is the scope of this bodhisattva liberation called 'the eradication of all conceit'?
She replied, "Noble son, it is the light of gnosis whose intrinsic nature is the cognition, in a single moment of mind, of the array of all that pertains to the three times."
He asked: "Noble lady, what is the range of this light of knowledge?
She replied: "Son of good family, through the entry into and emergence from this gateway of the light of my knowledge, there arises a king of samādhis called 'Endowed with All Dharmas.
Upon the simultaneous attainment of this samādhi, by means of mind-made bodies, [I see] those who are bound to one more birth in all world-systems throughout the ten directions."

To each and every bodhisattva dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, I approach for the purpose of performing worship with bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields, and with varieties of offerings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields—
namely, with the hosts of lords of gods, and the hosts of lords of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.

They were encompassed by clouds of flowers, clouds of perfumes, clouds of incense, clouds of garlands, clouds of ointments, clouds of powders, clouds of garments, clouds of parasols, clouds of banners,
clouds of pennants, clouds of jewel ornaments, clouds of arrays of jewel nets, clouds of arrays of jewel canopies, and clouds of arrays of jewel lamps and jewel thrones.
I approach for the practice of worship;
indeed, I approach for the practice of worship just as I do for the Bodhisattvas who reside in the Tuṣita heaven and are bound to only one more birth.

Thus, for all the Tathāgatas— whether they are in the womb, being born, staying within the inner apartments, departing [from the city], approaching the seat of awakening, having reached the excellent seat of awakening, having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,

turning the wheel of all dharmas, or likewise having gone to the abodes of the gods, or to the abodes of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— [the same applies].

Until I have brought satisfaction to the mental inclinations of the entire world and entered final nirvana, I shall approach all the Tathāgatas while performing such worship with such mind-made bodies,
and [I shall approach those] sentient beings who understand this work of mine in honoring and serving the Buddha.
They all become destined for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And as for those beings who approach me,
to all of them I give this very instruction and admonition on the perfection of wisdom.
"Noble son, with the eye of wisdom I behold all sentient beings;
yet I do not give rise to the notion of a 'sentient being,' nor do I conceive of them as such.
I hear the mantra and mudrā of the entire world."
And I do not conceive [of them] because I am not attached to any path of speech;
nor do I conceive [of them] because of my thorough knowledge of the Dharma-body, whereby I see all the Tathāgatas.
I maintain all the wheels of Dharma of all the Tathāgatas, yet I do not conceive of them because I have awakened to the intrinsic nature of phenomena in every moment of mind.
I pervade the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), yet I do not conceive of it, because I have realized that the nature of phenomena is like an illusion.
Noble son, I know this bodhisattva liberation which has eradicated all conceit.
How could I possibly know the conduct or describe the virtues of those bodhisattvas who have entered the infinite and centerless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
who dwell without conceiving of any phenomena, and who pervade the entire realm of phenomena with a single cross-legged posture;
who manifest all buddha-fields within their own bodies?
And in a single moment, they approach all the Tathāgatas,
within whose own bodies all the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas proceed;
they who, with a single hair, shake many unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.

Those who, within the pores of their own skin, display the incalculably incalculable eons of the formation and dissolution of world-systems; those who, in a single instant, attain the equality of dwelling for incalculably incalculable eons;
and those who, in a single instant, undergo transmigration through incalculably incalculable eons.
Go, son of good family,
right here in the southern region, in the country of Durga, there is a city named Ratnavyūha.
There dwells a female devotee of the Blessed One named Vasumitrā.
Go to her and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, circumambulated her hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at her again and again, departed from the presence of the nun Siṃhavijṛmbhitā. 25.

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, had his mind illuminated by that great lightning-flash of wisdom.
Contemplating that light of the knowledge of the Omniscient One,
beholding that manifestation of the power of the intrinsic nature of reality (dharmatā-svabhāva),
and strengthening the method of dhāraṇīs, which is a treasury for understanding the sounds and communications of all sentient beings;
Expanding that method of dhāraṇīs which sustains the wheel of Dharma of all Tathāgatas; strengthening that power of great compassion which is the refuge for the entire world;
and contemplating that momentum toward omniscience which arises from the gateway of illumination into the methods of all phenomena.
Following that purity of the vow which pervades the mandala of the vast realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),

illuminating that light of wisdom which shines upon all directions of all phenomena, and bringing forth the power of supernormal knowledge that extends the array of all phenomena throughout the world-systems of the ten directions;

Fulfilling that vow to carry through with the undertaking, application, and recollection of all the deeds of the bodhisattvas, he proceeded by stages until he arrived at the city of Ratnavyūha in the district of Durga,
searching for the venerable Vasumitrā. There,
those men who were ignorant of the virtues of the venerable Vasumitrā and unacquainted with the methods of her sphere of knowledge—

This thought occurred to them: "How is it that he, whose senses are thus tranquil and subdued, who is thus clearly conscious, thus unconfused, thus undistracted in mind, who looks only a yoke’s length ahead, whose mind is not overwhelmed by sensations, who does not grasp at signs regarding any forms, whose eyes are cast down, and whose mind is thus unperturbed— how is it that he possesses such profound conduct and such handsome appearance?"
What need is there for Vasumitrā, the lady of the Blessed One, for one who is like the ocean, whose mind is unshakable and undaunted?
For such as these do not become addicted to passion,
nor do they have perverted minds.
In such as these, the perception of impurity does not arise;
such as these do not become slaves to desire; such as these do not fall under the power of women.
Such as these do not wander within the domain of Māra;
such as these do not frequent the realm of Māra;
such as these do not sink into the mire of sensual desire.
Such people are not bound by the snares of Māra,
nor do they become doers of what should not be done.
But those who recognize the specific qualities of the venerable Vasumitrā, or for whom she is directly perceived within the range of their knowledge—
They said this: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!
Well gained are your gains, you who consider Vasumitrā Bhāgavatī worthy of being questioned."
You certainly aspire to Buddhahood;
you certainly desire to make yourself a refuge for all sentient beings;
you certainly desire to extract the thorn of passion from all sentient beings.
"You certainly wish to transform this perception of beauty.
Noble son, this Vasumitrā, the wife of the Blessed One, resides in her own home to the north of the city crossroads."

Then, having heard these words, the merchant’s son Sudhana was satisfied, elated, uplifted, joyful, and filled with gladness and cheer. He approached the residence of the noble lady Vasumitrā and beheld her house— vast and expansive, surrounded by ten walls made of jewels, encircled by rows of ten palm trees made of jewels, and encompassed by ten moats filled with fragrant water whose surfaces were covered with divine, precious *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses.
It was completely encircled by ponds filled with water endowed with the eight qualities, their bottoms strewn with golden sand, their waters made fragrant by the wafting of enchanting scents,

and adorned with walls of many jewels; it possessed a magnificent splendor, radiant with various jewels, gems, and luminous banners, featuring well-arranged mansions, celestial palaces, gabled halls, turrets, gateways, arches, windows, lattices, crescent moons, lion-cages, and diverse star-like ornaments, all fashioned from every kind of precious substance.
It was adorned with countless walls made of various jewels; its floor was fashioned with strings of gems inlaid with beryl; it was graced by the application of all divine and beautiful perfumes;

it was fragrant, being incensed with the smoke of great black agallochum; it was attended by the application of all kinds of ointments; its walls were constructed with pedestals made of every kind of gem;
and its summit was covered with nets of Jāmbūnada gold set with various jewels.

It resounded with sweet and charming tones released by hundreds of thousands of networks of golden bells stirred by the wind; it was adorned with scattered jewels from clouds of flowers made of every kind of gem;
its gates were beautified by banners variegated with all kinds of jewels; its description was boundless due to the light and blazing radiance of various mani-jewels;

it possessed inexhaustible treasuries consisting of hundreds of thousands of accumulated hoards of mani-stones revealed as treasures beneath the branches of trees variegated with many gems and diamond slabs; and it was graced by ten great gardens.

There he saw Vasumitrā, a devotee of the Blessed One, who was beautiful, gracious, and lovely to behold; she was endowed with the highest excellence of pure complexion, possessed a golden-hued skin, and had deep-blue hair. Her major and minor limbs were well-proportioned and symmetrical, and her beauty of color, form, and shape surpassed that of all gods and humans in the realm of desire. Her voice exceeded even that of Brahmā, and she was skilled in the methods of the cries and mantras of all sentient beings; her lovely voice was endowed with the array of all vocal qualities.

She was endowed with skill in the liberation of the arrays of wheels and syllables; she had emerged from mastery in all arts and sciences; she was well-trained in the skill of the illusion of the knowledge of the Dharma;
she had attained all modes of the bodhisattva’s methods of skillful means; her body was adorned with various jewel ornaments; her form was pleasing to the mind;
her body was covered by a radiant net made of every kind of gem; and her resplendent body was embellished by an array of countless divine maṇi-jewel ornaments.
She wore a crown set with the great wish-fulfilling king of jewels;

her neck was adorned with a necklace of Vaiḍūrya gems whose center was beautified by a lion-shaped jewel variegated with diamond and precious stones. She shared the same roots of merit, conduct, and singular vow as those who were dear to her, and she possessed a vast retinue. She was a treasury containing the inexhaustible storehouse of merit and wisdom.
And by means of that [jewel], which issued from her own body and was full of affection, she caused that entire house—arrayed with all kinds of jeweled mansions and celestial palaces—to appear.
He saw that the world was illuminated by a magnificent radiance that produced physical refreshment and bliss, and brought joy and exhilaration to the mind.

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Vasumitrā, stood before her with palms joined in reverence, and said: "Noble Lady, I have set my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva."

How should I practice? I have heard, Noble Lady, that you give instruction and advice to the bodhisattvas; therefore, may the Noble Lady tell me: how should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
"How should one practice?
She replied, "Noble son, I have attained the bodhisattva liberation called 'Reaching the Limit of Detachment.

Noble son, through my exceedingly radiant and pure excellence of form, color, shape, height, and girth—which surpasses that of the celestial nymphs—I appear to those according to their inclinations and resolute beliefs."

In this way, O son of good family, I appear to the maidens of the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— appearing with forms, colors, shapes, heights, and proportions that are exceedingly radiant and pure, according to their inclinations and aspirations.
And for those beings who approach me with minds obsessed by passion,
I teach the Dharma to all of them for the sake of becoming free from passion.
Having heard that Dharma, they attain freedom from passion and acquire the bodhisattva samādhi called "the sphere of non-attachment.
Some, by the mere sight of me, attain freedom from passion.
They attain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Delight in Joy.
Some, by merely conversing with them, attain freedom from passion and attain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Unimpeded Treasury of Voice."
Some attain the state of passionlessness through the mere taking of hands and obtain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Going to and Abiding in All Buddha-fields.
Some attain the state of passionlessness through merely sharing a single dwelling.
They attain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Light of Disjunction.
Some, by a mere glance, attain freedom from passion and attain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Array of the Tranquil Aspect."
Some, by merely yawning, attain freedom from passion and acquire the bodhisattva samādhi called "Agitating the Opponents. Some, by merely closing their eyes, attain freedom from passion.
They attain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Illumination of the Buddha’s Domain.
Some, by mere embracing, attain freedom from passion and attain the bodhisattva samādhi called "The Embryo of Not Abandoning the Gathering of All Living Beings."
Some attain the state of detachment from passion merely through a kiss,
and they obtain the bodhisattva samādhi called "Touching the Treasury of Merit of All Worlds. Whatever sentient beings approach me, [they all attain these states].
I establish them all right here in this bodhisattva liberation that has reached the pinnacle of detachment and is oriented toward the stage of unattached omniscience.
He asked: "Noble lady, where did you plant the roots of merit, and what kind of karma did you accumulate, such that you possess this kind of prosperity?"
He said: "I remember, noble son,

that in the past there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Atyuccagāmin— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
Noble son, as that Tathāgata Atyuccagāmin entered the royal capital named Sumukhā out of compassion for sentient beings, and as he stepped upon the city’s threshold pillar (*indrakīla*),

that entire city trembled; it became vast and expansive, composed of many jewels, arrayed with the radiance of various gems, strewn with diverse jewel-flowers, and filled with the sounds of various celestial musical instruments.
And the sky became covered by clouds of vast and immeasurable hosts of devas.
At that time, noble son, I was the wife of a merchant named Sumati.

Then, stirred by the Buddha’s miraculous power, I ran together with my husband to the street where that Tathāgata had arrived, and having conceived a sublime faith, I offered a single precious kārṣāpaṇa coin.
It was thus established.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was the attendant of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Atyuccagāmin;
by him, I was inspired to generate the mind directed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Noble son, I know only this bodhisattva liberation that reaches the limit of detachment.

How could I possibly know the conduct or describe the qualities of those bodhisattvas who are established in skillful means and infinite wisdom, who possess vast and inexhaustible treasuries of merit, and whose domain of knowledge is invincible?
Go, son of good family;
right here in the southern region there is a city named Śubhapāraṃgama.
There, a householder named Veṣṭhila worships a Tathāgata shrine made of sandalwood.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?"

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Vasumitrā, circumambulated the venerable Vasumitrā hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at her again and again, departed from the presence of the venerable Vasumitrā. // 26 //
Veṣṭhila.
Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, went to the residence of the householder Veṣṭhila in the city of Śubhapāraṃgama.

Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the householder Veṣṭhila, he stood before him with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus: "Noble sir, I have resolved my mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor how one should practice."
"I have heard, noble one, that you give instruction and advice to the bodhisattvas.
Therefore, may the noble one tell me: how should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct, and how should they practice?"
He said: "Noble son, I am a possessor of the bodhisattva liberation that reaches the inexhaustible limit.

Noble son, from my spiritual lineage, a Tathāgata has not entered final nirvāṇa, does not enter final nirvāṇa, and will not enter final nirvāṇa in any world-system through ultimate final nirvāṇa, except as a matter of conforming to the needs of beings to be disciplined.
Therefore, noble son, I open the door of the Tathāgata’s shrine, the Sandalwood Pedestal."
And as I opened that gate of the shrine, I attained the bodhisattva-samādhi called "The Array of the Inexhaustible Lineage of Buddhas.
Noble son, I enter this samādhi in every single moment of thought;
in every moment of thought, I realize manifold specific distinctions of form.
He asked: "Noble one, what is the range of this samādhi?

He replied: "Son of good family, for me who has entered this samādhi, within this lineage of world-systems, there is the succession of Buddhas beginning with Kāśyapa; all the Tathāgatas, headed by Kanakamuni, Krakucchanda, Viśvabhū, Śikhin, Vipaśyin, Tiṣya, Puṣya, Yaśottara, Padmottara, and so forth."

All the Tathāgatas become manifest before me. In the continuous succession of beholding the Buddhas, through the uninterrupted lineage of Buddhas, in every single moment of mind I see a hundred Buddhas;
immediately thereafter, with the next moment of mind, I enter into a thousand Buddhas.
Immediately following that thought, I enter into the presence of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;

likewise, I enter into ten million Buddhas, a hundred million Buddhas, a billion Buddhas, ten billion Buddhas, a hundred billion Buddhas, a trillion Buddhas, ten trillion Buddhas, a quadrillion Buddhas, and even up to an inexpressible number of successions of the arising of Buddhas, all by means of that immediate thought.
With the immediately succeeding thought, I penetrate as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa;
with the immediately succeeding thought, I penetrate as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
And I penetrate the succession of the accumulations from the first production of the thought of enlightenment of those Tathāgatas.
I enter into the miraculous manifestation of attaining the first production of the thought of enlightenment; I enter into the purity of accomplishing the various levels of vows;
I enter into the purity of conduct; I enter into the fulfillment of the perfections.
I enter into the realization of all the bodhisattva stages; I enter into the purity of attaining patient acceptance;
I enter into the lion’s roar that scatters the strife of Māra.
I enter into the array of the miraculous manifestations of perfect enlightenment; I enter into the diversity of the purification of Buddha-fields;
I enter into the diversity of the maturation of sentient beings.
I enter into the diversity of the assemblies gathered; I enter into the diversity of the circles of light;
I enter into the bull-like prowess in turning the wheel of Dharma.
I enter into the miraculous display of the Buddha's transformations; I remember, and I uphold, their well-distinguished and comprehensive teachings of the Dharma.
I grasp it with mindfulness; I discern it with understanding; I analyze it with devotion.
I follow after them with my intellect; I illuminate them with my wisdom;
and I enter into the succession of future Buddhas, headed by Maitreya.
In a single moment of mind, I enter into the presence of a hundred Buddhas; with the next moment of mind, I enter into the presence of a thousand Buddhas;
with the subsequent moment of mind, I enter into the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

And I enter into the succession of the accumulations from the first production of the thought of enlightenment of those Tathāgatas; I remember and maintain their well-distinguished and unconfused teaching of the Dharma.
I grasp with mindfulness; I investigate with understanding; I analyze with intelligence.
I follow with my intellect;
I illuminate with my wisdom;
and just as I behold here, within this lineage of world-systems, the succession of Buddhas included within the past and the future limits, so do I see.
I enter;

likewise, I enter the succession of all Tathāgatas throughout the lineages of world-systems in the past and future, in the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
And I enter the succession of the accumulations for the first production of the thought of enlightenment of those Tathāgatas.

And I enter that unbroken succession of the lineage of Buddhas, reaching its ultimate consummation— an incomparable state to be approached through faith, accessible through the resolute effort of a bodhisattva’s vigor, increasing the momentum of a bodhisattva’s vigor,
and unshakeable by any worldling, by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and even by those bodhisattvas who have not yet entered their domain, regarding those of the present.
And in all world-systems throughout the ten directions, I enter into the succession of Tathāgatas beginning with Vairocana.
In a single moment of thought, I see and enter into a hundred Buddhas;
by the subsequent thought-moment, I enter into a thousand Buddhas.
Immediately following that thought, I enter into as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
and whichever Tathāgata I desire to see, him I see at that very moment.
And whatever has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— all that I hear;
and having heard it, I take it up.
I sustain it with mindfulness; I investigate it with understanding; I analyze it with intelligence.
I follow it with my intellect;
I illuminate it with my wisdom.
Noble son, this is the bodhisattva liberation that reaches the limit of non-extinction which I know.

What is possible for me [to know] regarding those bodhisattvas who have attained the knowledge of the three times in a single moment; who dwell in the array of meditative absorptions throughout ten million moments; who have entered the day of the Tathāgata; who have realized the equality of all conceptual constructions of kalpas; who are bound to the samādhi of the equality of all Buddhas; who dwell in the non-duality of self, sentient beings, and Buddhas;
whose mandalas are arrays of phenomena naturally luminous; who pervade the net of the world with the machinery of gnosis; and who dwell without disturbing the Dharma-seals of all Tathāgatas?

To know the conduct, or to speak of the qualities, of those whose sphere of activity is the knowledge that makes known the entire realm of phenomena, and whose sphere of activity is the knowledge that makes known the Dharma-teachings of all Tathāgatas.
Go, noble son;
right here in the southern region is a mountain named Potalaka.
There dwells a bodhisattva named Avalokiteśvara.
Go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva train in the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How should one practice?
At that moment, he spoke these verses:

For, Sudhana, in the midst of the ocean of Śrī, on the auspicious peak of the king of mountains, Potalaka, in its heroic region, there is a supreme tree made of jewels, strewn with flowers, and provided with gardens, lotus ponds, and springs. (1)
And on that supreme mountain dwells the steadfast, wise Avalokiteśvara for the benefit of the world.
Go to him, Sudhana, and ask about the qualities of the Leaders; he will teach you the vast and magnificent entry into the method. // 2 //

Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the householder Veṣṭhila, circumambulated the householder Veṣṭhila hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at him again and again, departed from the presence of the householder Veṣṭhila. // 27 //
(Gv 159) 30. Avalokiteśvara.
Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, reflecting upon the instruction of the householder Veṣṭhila, [proceeded].
Bringing to completion that treasury of bodhisattva resolve,
recollecting the power of that mindfulness of the bodhisattvas, and sustaining the power of that succession of the Buddhas' eyes,
Following that continuity of the succession of Buddhas,
recollecting that hearing of the names of the Buddhas, and conforming to that method of the Buddhas' teaching of the Dharma,
Entering into that array of the complete attainment of the Buddha-dharma,
placing his faith in that roar of the Buddhas' perfect enlightenment,
and bringing before him that inconceivable activity of the Tathāgatas, he gradually approached Mount Potalaka.
Having ascended Mount Potalaka and searching everywhere for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,

he beheld the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara seated cross-legged upon a diamond-jewel stone in a great forest glade, on the slope of a mountain in the western direction, which was adorned with springs, lakes, and cascades, and possessed a ground of soft, lush green grass as tender as young curls of hair.

Having seen him seated there, surrounded by an immeasurable host of bodhisattvas resting upon a floor of various precious gems, teaching the Dharma and proclaiming the Dharma-discourse named *The Illumination of the Gateway of Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion*, which is the sphere for gathering all living beings; and having seen this, he was again satisfied, uplifted, joyful, delighted, filled with gladness and cheer, his eyes wide open with joy and unblinking.
With palms joined in reverence, his mind undistracted by the force of his inspired faith in the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), he perceived the spiritual friends as the vision of all Buddhas;
he perceived them as receiving the clouds of all dharmas originating from the spiritual friends; he perceived the realization of all virtues as dependent upon the spiritual friends;
he perceived the encounter with spiritual friends as difficult to find; and he perceived the acquisition of the jewels of the knowledge of the Ten Powers as arising from the spiritual friends.
Perceiving the spiritual friend as the source of the light of inexhaustible wisdom, perceiving the sprout of merit as nurtured by reliance upon the spiritual friend,
perceiving the gateway to omniscience as revealed by the spiritual friend, perceiving the entry into the great ocean of great gnosis as pointed out by the spiritual friend,
and perceiving the accumulation of the provisions for omniscience as generated by the spiritual friend, he went toward where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, seeing the merchant’s son Sudhana approaching from afar, addressed him:

"Come! Welcome to you, O one who has set out in the peerless, noble, and inconceivable Mahāyāna; whose intention is to protect the entire world that is afflicted by various root sufferings and is without refuge;
who has transcended all worlds; who is peerless and immeasurable; who desires direct realization of all the Buddha-dharmas; and who is possessed by the force of great compassion."

O you whose mind is directed toward the vision and conduct of Samantabhadra for the sake of protecting all the world; O you whose mind purifies the mandala of great vows; O you who, through the accumulation of roots of goodness desired for upholding the clouds of all Buddha-dharmas, possess an insatiable intention; O you who have correctly engaged in the instructions of spiritual friends; O you who are born from the ocean of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom; O you who are a lotus-pool of virtues; O you who are facing the attainment of the empowerment of the Buddhas; O you who have obtained the momentum of the light of samādhi; O you whose mind desires to uphold the clouds of all Buddha-dharmas.

O you whose mind is thrilled by the surge of joy and serene faith from beholding the Buddha; whose heart is moistened by the surge of inconceivable and immeasurable well-performed conduct; whose treasury of merit and wisdom is purified by the surge of the practice of virtues; whose intention is to manifest to others the mere surge of the omniscient knowledge through the gateway of your own direct realization; and whose resolve is rooted in the surge of the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom brought forth by the force of great compassion—O you of steadfast mind!
Then, Sudhana the merchant’s son approached the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,

bowed his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, circumambulated the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara hundreds of thousands of times, and standing before him with palms joined, spoke thus: "Noble One, by me..."
I have generated the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor how one should practice it.
"I have heard, noble one, that you give instruction and admonition to the bodhisattvas.
Therefore, may the noble one tell me: how should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct, and how should he practice?"

Then the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara extended his right arm— which was the color of Jāmbūnada gold and emitted clouds of arrays of various, immeasurable nets of light— and placing his hand, which was like a cluster of blossoms with its mass of radiating rays that produce a vivid, stainless, and boundless joy in body and mind through the diffusion of the primary and secondary marks,
upon the head of the merchant’s son Sudhana, he said: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!"
Since you have resolved your mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, noble son, I know this bodhisattva practice gateway called "The Uninterrupted Entrance of Great Compassion.
