May you not find pleasure in sexual misconduct, nor may your mind today be given over to falsehood. 13.
Let not your mind be intent on the alienation of friends; do not speak words that pierce the vital organs.
Let there be no covetousness toward the wealth of others, nor a mind of malice even toward living beings. 14.

Do not stand upon the path of the wilderness of false views; do not have a mind hardened by the lineage of karma; do not be deceitful or follow the power of guile; do not afflict the world with such wickedness. (15)
Do you maintain affection and respect for your mother, father, kinsmen, friends, and teachers?
And do you have a mind inclined toward giving in order to gather those who have become impoverished? (16)
Those who address you with love as a virtuous friend, or who speak to you at the proper time according to the Dharma, properly produce in you the fitness and pliancy of both body and mind. (17)
Do you have reverence for the Buddhas, or even intense love for the sons of the Buddha? Do you understand that supreme dharma from which the offspring of the Sugatas are born? (18)

I hope you remain established in the lineage of Dharma and that your mind has no inclination to practice unrighteousness; and toward you, who possess infinite renown and are an ocean of virtues, do they maintain supreme love and reverence? (19)
Is your mind full of loving-kindness toward those who are helpless and without a guide?
And do you feel intense compassion for those who are deeply afflicted as they engage in actions leading to the lower realms? (20)
Upon seeing the supreme prosperity of others, do you indeed attain the highest satisfaction?
And toward people who are not independent due to their afflictions, do you generate equanimity through the power of wisdom? (21)
Beholding the people asleep in ignorance, do you aspire for the firm, supreme enlightenment?
As you practice the conduct throughout infinite eons, is there no weariness in you because of that aspiration? (22)

Then Sudarśanā, the chief courtesan and mother of the girl Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī, said this to Prince Tejodhipati: "O Prince, this daughter of mine was born spontaneously, having arisen from the heart of a lotus; she has never before departed from the house.
And at that moment, she spoke these verses:
Listen, O prince, as I speak to you regarding that girl who questions you;
I shall relate to you in due order, gentle youth, how this girl was born and how she was raised. (23)
At the very place where you were born at the end of the night, this daughter of mine was born;
she appeared spontaneously within the heart of a stainless lotus, with all her limbs complete and her eyes wide and beautiful. (24)
In the springtime, the most excellent of seasons, when the crops and medicinal herbs have fully grown,
I went out for a long time into my own preeminent garden, Sālaprabha.

In this forest, where the trees have the color of thick clouds, their branches spread wide with variegated buds and they are in full bloom; where the groves resound with the songs of various birds—I dwell here, free from sorrow and filled with joy.
I was accompanied by eight hundred maidens who were well-adorned and exceedingly beautiful;
they wore garments of various jewels and were highly trained in song and instrumental music. (27)
I was seated on the bank of a pond adorned with lotuses and various fragrant banners, upon a patch of ground strewn with flowers and filled with a well-trained company of women. // 28 //

Then, in the midst of the water, there suddenly appeared a thousand-petaled lotus made of the finest jewels, with a stalk of beryl, petals of the king of gems, and a pericarp of pure Jāmbūnada gold. (29)

Rich with fragrant, red, and excellent filaments, and emitting a great radiance born from the banner of Jambudvīpa, the multitudes of people were then filled with doubt, wondering: "Has the sun risen in the night? (30)
The radiance released from this sun, the great lord of lotuses, as it awakens at the end of the night,
and the sweet sound produced thereby, are the precursors of her birth.
Indeed, this jewel of a woman has appeared in the world of men through the purity of her supreme conduct;
for there is no destruction of a deed that has been performed—this is the ripening of what was well-practiced in the past. (32)
With dark-blue hair and eyes as blue as a lotus, possessing a voice like that of Brahmā and a complexion as pure as gold;
adorned with garlands and ornaments, elegantly attired, she was like the goddess Śrī born from a lotus, radiant and stainless. (33)
With pure limbs and a symmetrical body, her form complete and her frame well-proportioned, she shines forth, illuminating all directions like a golden image polished with jewels. (34)
Born of noble lineage, the fragrance of the king of sandalwood wafts from her, pervading all directions;
and as she utters a divine and sweet voice, a scent like that of a blue lotus blows from her mouth.
Whenever she utters a divine smile, the sound of celestial music resounds;
for this jewel among women shall never fall under the power of ordinary beings in this world. (36)
Indeed, there exists no other husband for her in the world of men besides you—one whose beautiful form is adorned with excellent marks; therefore, accept this maiden. (37)
She is neither too short nor too tall, neither too stout nor excessively thin; with a waist like a bow and full breasts, O lady of faultless limbs, she is a perfect match for you.
She possesses mastery in the principles of numerical notation and scripts, as well as in the application of mudrās and the systems of the treatises;
she has reached the further shore of all the arts that exist throughout the entire world. (39)
Supreme in her knowledge of archery and weapons, skilled in ritual procedures, and perfectly certain in her application toward sentient beings;
she has reached the highest perfection in every respect, whether in attracting others or in gladdening the minds of enemies. (40)

Adorned with a halo of radiance released from her entire body, which is composed of the finest pure jewels, this well-adorned attendant is a fitting companion for you, owing to the merits you have previously cultivated. (41)

Those who know the methods for the origin of whatever diseases exist in the world of the living, and who possess the excellence of correctly discerning the medicinal treatments for their complete pacification; 42.

Whatever various distinctions of mantra and etymology exist among all people in Jambudvīpa, and wherever there is a multitude of worldly conventions, this [teaching] has entered everywhere and reached the supreme goal. (43)
They have entered into the principles governing the production of vocal tones and their various distinctions;
they are also supreme experts in the rules regarding all the songs and dances that exist in the world.

She has mastered the movement of musical instruments and cymbals, the application of pleasure, laughter, and dance; she is skilled in dealing with men who are passionate as well as those who are dispassionate, whether they are conciliated or filled with resentment. (45)

He understands all the cries of women here in this world, especially in their various particulars; and as for the immeasurable faults of womankind, he does not find them to exist in their entirety. (46)

Whether gazing directly or glancing from the corner of your eye, whether offering a limb or revealing your body, you have reached perfection in all the arts; you are the fulfiller of all desires. (47)

Free from envy and free from jealousy, neither lustful for sensual pleasures nor greedy for drink, she is secure, upright, gentle, and courageous; she is without anger, not harsh, and easy to understand. (48)
Diligent in rising, speaking no disagreeable words, always obedient to her elders, full of reverence, and seeking what is beneficial—she is worthy of following your conduct. (49)
Toward those who are decrepit, aged, afflicted by disease, fallen into poverty, and deeply suffering;
toward those deprived of sight and without any refuge—he constantly generates a cloud of compassion. (50)
Always delighting in the contemplation of the welfare of others, she does not even think of her own benefit;
desiring the welfare of the entire world, she is well-adorned with the noble qualities of the mind. (51)

Always vigilant, established in mindfulness and clear comprehension—whether sitting, lying down, walking, or even speaking in silence—she is always mindful and is thus ever esteemed by the world. (52)
On every side, she shines forth as one possessed of merit and is ever beloved by people; gazing upon her, one never reaches satiety, yet she has no attachment anywhere in the world. (53)
She is full of reverence for spiritual friends and is ever eager to behold you;
she possesses far-sighted vision, her conduct is unblemished, and her pure mind is as stable as Mount Sumeru. (54)
Always adorned by her own merits, there is no enemy found anywhere for her; nor is there any woman equal to her in wisdom. O Prince, she is a worthy match for you. (55)

Then, having entered the Gandhāṅkuraśikharaprabhamegha park, Prince Tejodhipati spoke thus to the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī in the presence of her mother, the preeminent courtesan Sudarśanā: "Daughter, I have indeed set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Therefore, by me, the immeasurable accumulations for omniscience must be gathered;

while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout eons that have no middle or end, all the perfections must be purified; and throughout eons reaching to the furthest limit of the future, the Tathāgatas must be honored.
All the teachings of the Buddhas must be upheld;
all the Buddha-fields must be purified;
and the lineages of all the Tathāgatas must not be interrupted.
The lineages of all sentient beings must be brought to maturity;
the sufferings of saṃsāra for all sentient beings must be averted;
and sentient beings must be established in ultimate happiness.
The eye of wisdom of all sentient beings must be purified;
one must apply oneself to the realization of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
and one must abide in the equanimity of all Bodhisattvas.
All the stages of a bodhisattva must be accomplished;
the realm of all sentient beings must be purified by relinquishing all one's own possessions in order to eliminate the poverty of all sentient beings.
Practicing the perfection of generosity for as many eons as reach the furthest limit of time, one must satisfy sentient beings with gifts of food and drink.
By relinquishing all articles of utility, the entire assembly of supplicants must be fully satisfied.
As I am thus practicing the renunciation of all possessions, there is no internal or external thing whatsoever that should not be given away.
Therefore, I must give away my sons, daughters, and wife.
The eyes, head, hands, feet, and all the major and minor limbs must be relinquished.
If you, at that time, act toward others [with attachment], you will create an obstacle to my giving;
you will be displeased when your beloved sons are being given away.
"You will experience much physical and mental suffering.

When my mind is intent upon the renunciation of all my possessions, you will give rise to a mind of stinginess. As I cut off my limbs and members to bestow them upon supplicants, you will become distressed and dejected."
And there will come a time when, having abandoned you, I shall go forth into the teaching of the Tathāgata;
at that time, you will be displeased.
Then, at that time, the prince Tejodhipati addressed the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī in verses:

“I must fulfill the immeasurable great oceans of the provisions for perfect enlightenment; for it is out of compassion for all living beings that I have set out upon the path to awakening after a very long time. (56)
One's vow should be purified by oceans of virtues that are perfectly endowed, without end or middle, and as immeasurable as space;
likewise, one must perform the preparatory cultivation for the stages of departure of the Tathāgatas throughout infinite eons. (57)
I have trained in the paths of the perfections under the Jinas dwelling in the three times; the excellent path to awakening must be purified by means of the great system of unsurpassed gnosis. (58)

All fields in every direction, however defiled, must be purified by me in their entirety; indeed, all unfavorable conditions and miserable rebirths throughout the entire world must be turned away. (59)
All sentient beings without exception, shrouded by afflictions and blinded by the darkness of delusion, must be purified;
having ripened them through various means, they should be established on the path leading to omniscience. (60)

I must purify the stages [of the path] which are free from attachment, and I must worship the Victors throughout oceans of eons; and having generated loving-kindness toward the entire world, I shall give all kinds of gifts to the world. (61)

Seeing supplicants gathered before me, who am always delighted in giving everything away, may you not then become dejected, miserable, or wretched, nor develop a mind that is contrary to this [generosity]. (62)

"Seeing my purpose, which seeks the head, and knowing that you were then devoted to noble conduct, you will become intensely tormented by grief; having heard this matter, therefore, remain steadfast. (63)

"You will experience mental anguish; you will even have to cut off my hands and feet for the sake of beggars. You, being weak and distressed, will speak harsh words—consider these matters well upon hearing this. (64)
"I shall give even my beloved possessions, as well as my sons and you yourself, to whoever asks;
if, having heard this matter, you do not falter, then let everything be exactly as you desire. (65)
When this had been said, the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī spoke thus to the prince Tejodhipati: "It shall be so, O Prince, just as you say.
I am to be done with by you according to your desire; I am to be enjoyed by you according to your wish; I am to go wherever you please, following you everywhere without end."
I shall be constantly devoted, eager for all tasks, acting in accordance with [their] intentions, possessing right exertion, and employing practices of application that are free from unevenness.
Then the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī addressed the prince Tejodhipati with these verses:
"Even if this body of mine were to go to destruction, being scorched by the fires of hell, I would still venture across oceans of births to serve as your attendant, sharing in your conduct. (66)
Even if, throughout infinite births, my body were to be excessively mangled time and again, I would still strive with a firm and steady mind: "O you of noble form, become my husband! (67)
Even if for infinite eons the Cakravāla mountains were to crush my head to pieces, I would endure it with an untiring mind; O inconceivable one, become my master! (68)
Having severed even immeasurable other births, give your own limbs to others;
having established mastery over the mind within me, firmly establish me in my own duty.
O son of a god among men, I shall surrender this body of yours forever; while practicing the conduct throughout oceans of eons, grant me joyfully to those who seek me as their object.

Having set out for the most excellent and supreme enlightenment, having generated infinite compassion for sentient beings, and in order to gather the ocean of all beings without exception, please accept me as well out of compassion. (71)
Not for the sake of enjoyments, nor for the sake of wealth, nor for the purpose of indulging in the pleasures of sensual desires,
do I desire you, O Lord, the Supreme Being, but rather so that we may practice a life in common. (72)
O you with pure, deep-blue eyes, since you look upon the entire world with a mind of loving-kindness, yet with a heart colored by compassion, you will undoubtedly become a Lord of Sages. (73)

Since this stainless earth stands before you, shining with jewels as you walk step by step, you will undoubtedly become a universal monarch (cakravartin) adorned with the excellent marks in the world of men. (74)

In a dream during the night, I saw the Sugata seated at the foot of the king of trees upon the seat of enlightenment, which shone like a cloud of the Sudharma heaven, surrounded by many sons of the Buddha. (75)

That Lord of Jinas, the most excellent among those with bodies as radiant as the sun, resembling a great mountain of refined Jāmbūnada gold, placed his hand upon my head within a dream; having awakened from it, I am therefore filled with joy. (76)
The deity named Ratiprabhā, who was my kinswoman in former lives and possesses a pure body, has informed me: "This Tathāgata is moving about here in this sublime seat of enlightenment. (77)
"Indeed, this was my former thought: 'I would behold the Prince Tejodhipati.
And now, a deity announced to me: 'Today, within the night, you shall see the Prince. (78)
"Today in a dream I beheld the Sugata, and you as well, O pure being; having attained my heart's desire together with you, I shall today worship that Lord of Sages. (79)

Then, having heard the name of the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara, Prince Tejodhipati obtained the opportunity to behold the Buddha; overcome by a surge of great joy and serene faith, he scattered five hundred precious jewels over the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī and gave her a crest-jewel named Śrīgarbhaprabhāsa.
And he covered her with a precious garment variegated with great jewels and gems, brilliant as fire.

Thus honored, she was neither elated nor exultant, nor did she act with negligence; rather, with palms joined in reverence and unblinking eyes, she remained standing, gazing at the face of Prince Tejodhipati.
Then Sudarśanā, the chief courtesan, addressed Prince Tejodhipati with these verses:
"I have indeed long desired, 'May I give this maiden to you';
now she has been given to you—she of beautiful form, well-adorned, and endowed with the qualities of merit. (80)

In the world of men, no maiden is found anywhere who is her equal, nor one superior to her in virtue, intelligence, or other such qualities; indeed, she is the most excellent among women in the entire world. (81)
Born from a lotus, she is indeed not subject to the corruption of arguments regarding birth;
for her mind is unstained by any defects, and her conduct became entirely consistent with yours. (82)
Her limbs bring about the most excellent pleasure of touch and are exceedingly soft;
by the mere contact with them, those afflicted by disease attain health at that very moment. (83)
For that pure fragrance of her body wafts forth, surpassing all other excellent scents;
and by smelling that fragrance, all people become established in pure morality. (84)
For her body, shining like gold and possessing the luster of the interior of a stainless lotus, glows brilliantly;
indeed, upon beholding her, all sentient beings without exception become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness. (85)
Her speech is affectionate, sweet, charming, lovely, and a delight to the ears of people;
merely by hearing it, that which destroys the darkness of faults causes them not to desire to perform unwholesome deeds. (86)
With pure intentions and a stainless mind, there is indeed no deceit in her anywhere; for whatever she speaks in her heart is exactly so, since she gladdens the world with her voice. (87)
She does not delude sentient beings with deceit, nor does she entice them for the sake of profit;
possessed of modesty and a restrained mind, she is always respectful toward both elders and juniors. (88)
Neither by birth nor by lineage, nor intoxicated by beauty, should she likewise be understood as being intoxicated by her retinue;
free from pride and arrogance, she is ever humble and bowed before the Victors. (89)

Then the prince Tejodhipati, together with his retinue— the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī and her twenty thousand maidens— departed from that garden, Gandhāṅkuraśikharaprabhamegha, and proceeded toward the seat of awakening where Dharmodgataprabhāsa was, and toward the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara.
He approached in order to see, pay homage to, worship, and attend upon the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would permit, he alighted from the carriage and proceeded on foot toward the presence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara.
There, the prince Tejodhipati beheld the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara.

From afar, he saw the Tathāgata, the Great One, the Perfectly Awakened One—gracious, beautiful to behold, with senses calmed, mind at peace, and faculties guarded; like a well-tamed elephant, like a lake that is clear, undisturbed, and serene.
Upon seeing him, his heart became filled with faith.

With a serene mind, he increased the surge of great joy and faith from beholding the Buddha. With a heart suffused by the intensity of great joy, faith, and rapture, he circumambulated the Blessed One hundreds of thousands of times. Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, together with the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī and her companions, he [proceeded].
Together with his entire retinue, he covered that Blessed One with five hundred thousand great jewel-lotuses made of precious gems.
He also had five hundred monasteries constructed for that Blessed One, made entirely of fragrant jewel-gems and variegated with all kinds of sovereign jewels.
And each individual monastery he adorned with five hundred thousand sovereign great jewel-kings.
Then, noble son, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara, having understood the high resolve of the prince Tejodhipati, proclaimed the sūtra called *Samantanetradvārapradīpa*.
Having heard it, he attained ten oceans of gateways to meditative concentration regarding the principles of all dharmas.

That is to say: he attained the entrance into concentration named "The Radiance Arising from the Ocean of Vows of All Tathāgatas," and he attained the entrance into concentration named "The Matrix of the Radiance of the Three Times."

He attained the entrance to concentration called "Departure Facing All Buddha-mandalas," the entrance to concentration called "Entry into the Supreme Illumination of All Sentient Beings," and the entrance to concentration called "Engaged in the Illumination of the Knowledge of the Arising of All Worlds."

He attained the gateway to concentration called Illuminating Lamp for the Ocean of the Faculties of All Sentient Beings; he attained the gateway to concentration called Cloud of Knowledge for the Protection of the Entire World;
and he attained the gateway to concentration called Lamp Facing the Ripening and Disciplining of the World of All Sentient Beings.

He attained the entrance into concentration called "Proclaiming the Resonance of the Dharma-Wheel of All Tathāgatas," and he attained the entrance into concentration called "Cloud of Vows for the Purification of the Maṇḍala of Samantabhadra’s Conduct.
With these ten entrances into concentration as the foremost, he attained oceans of ten entrances into concentration regarding all methods of the Dharma.
And the girl Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī attained the mental realization called Duryodhanajñānasāgaragarbha,
and she became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Then the prince Tejodhipati, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Sūryagātrapravara, the Tathāgata, circumambulated that Blessed One many thousands of times and, together with the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī and his entire retinue, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
He went to where the royal capital Drumameruśrī was, and to where his father, King Dhanapati, was;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of his father, King Dhanapati, and announced this matter: "Indeed, [that which...]"

"O Deva, you should know: a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sūryagātrapravara has appeared in the world—one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwells right here in your own realm, at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) called Dharmameghodgataprabhāsa, having recently attained perfect enlightenment."
Then King Dhanapati said this to Prince Tejodhipati: "Prince, by whom was this matter announced to you—by a god or by a human?
He replied: "By the maiden Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī."
Then King Dhanapati, upon hearing of the appearance of a Buddha, conceived the notion that he had obtained a great treasure; the notion that he had acquired the exceedingly rare jewel of a Buddha;

the notion that in the sight of the Tathāgata there was the turning back of all fear of falling into the precipices of the miserable destinies; the notion that he had obtained the Great King of Physicians who pacifies the disease of all afflictions; the notion that [the Buddha] was the liberator from all the sufferings of saṃsāra; the notion that he was the establisher in ultimate security; and the notion that he was the one who reveals the light of knowledge free from darkness.
Perceiving the appearance of a great torch that destroys the darkness of ignorance; perceiving the attainment of a guide in the method of Dharma for a world that was leaderless;

perceiving the arising of a guide to omniscience for those who had no guide; having heard of the birth of a Buddha, they attained great joy, serene confidence, and gladness—namely, the kṣatriyas, brahmins, merchants, country folk, ministers, domestic priests, princes, and vassal kings.
Having assembled the gatekeepers and courtiers who were proclaiming the joyful news of the Buddha’s appearance, he bestowed the kingdom of Tejodhipati Kumāra upon Dharmākṣāda.
Having consecrated that prince in the kingship, he approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara, together with ten thousand living beings.

Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One, circumambulated that Blessed One hundreds of thousands of times, and sat down before that Blessed One together with his own retinue.

Then, noble son, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara, having looked upon King Dhanapati and the entire circle of the assembly, at that moment emitted from the circle of hair between his brows a ray of light named "Lamp Illuminating the Minds of All Beings.
It illuminated all world-systems in the ten directions and established all the lords of the worlds face-to-face with inconceivable Buddha-transformations.
Having revealed himself to those beings who were to be disciplined by a Buddha and having purified their inclinations, at that moment, through the inconceivable sovereign power of a Buddha,
with a Buddha-body risen above all worlds, and with a Buddha-voice endowed with an ocean of all vocal qualities,

he proclaimed the entrance to the dhāraṇī called *Sarvadharma-vitimirārtha-pradīpa* (The Lamp of Meaning that Dispels the Darkness of All Dharmas), accompanied by a retinue of entrances to dhāraṇīs as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field.
Then, having heard this entrance to the dhāraṇī from King Dhanapati, a great illumination of the Dharma regarding all phenomena appeared.

And in that assembly, as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa attained the dhāraṇī called "The Lamp that Illuminates the Meaning of All Phenomena Free from Obscurity. Furthermore, the minds of sixty million living beings were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
The dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified for ten thousand living beings;
and for immeasurable beings, the thought of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—which had never arisen before—was produced.
Through the manifestation of inconceivable Buddha-transformations in the ten directions, the infinite and boundless realm of sentient beings was brought to discipline by means of the three vehicles.

And to King Dhanapati, who had attained the great illumination of the Dharma, this thought occurred: "It is not possible for one dwelling in the midst of a household to resolve upon such dharmas as these, nor to bring forth such knowledge as this.
What if I were to go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One?"
Then King Dhanapati said this to the Blessed One: "May I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk in the presence of the Blessed One.
He replied: "Now is the time for that, Great King; do as you deem fit."
Then, indeed, King Dhanapati went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara, together with ten thousand living beings.
Not long after he had gone forth, he accomplished and cultivated the dhāraṇī-gateway called *Sarvadharmavitimirārthapradīpa* along with its retinue,
and he attained an equal number of gateways to meditative concentration (*samādhimukha*).
He attained the ten supernormal knowledges of a bodhisattva and entered the ocean of the methods of analytical knowledge, which is without end or center. Furthermore,
he attained the purity of body called "the unimpeded range," by means of which he approaches the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
He received and upheld the Wheel of Dharma of that Blessed One, acted as a master of discourse,
and served as a great preacher of the Dharma.
He undertook the protection of the teaching;

and by the power of attaining the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), having pervaded the entire world-system, he manifested his body according to the inclinations of sentient beings, thereby manifesting this appearance of a Buddha and illuminating that reality (*dharmatā*) which is the source of all Tathāgatas.
Manifesting that perfection of his former practices and extolling the power of that Buddha’s miraculous transformations,
he undertook the protection of the teaching.
And on that very day, during the full moon of the *pūrṇamāsī*, Prince Tejodhipati obtained the seven jewels.

While he was situated upon the terrace of his upper palace, surrounded by a host of women, there appeared before him a divine wheel made of Jāmbūnada gold, possessing a hundred thousand spokes, adorned with every kind of jewel, named Apratihata-vega (Unobstructed Speed), radiant in all directions, and endowed with the excellence of every form.
The great precious wheel appeared;
the great precious elephant named Vajraratnagiritejas appeared;
and the precious horse named Nīlagiryanilavega appeared.
A great maṇi-jewel named Ādityagarbhaprabhamegharāja appeared;
and that maiden named Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī appeared as a jewel among women;
and a householder-jewel named Prabhūtaghanaskandha appeared.
And the seventh precious counselor, named Vimalanetra, appeared.

Endowed with these seven treasures, he became a universal monarch (cakravartin), a ruler of the four continents, righteous, a king of Dharma, victorious, and one who had attained power and valor over the lands.
Furthermore, he had a full thousand sons who were brave, heroic, possessed of excellent forms, and capable of crushing enemy armies.

Having conquered this entire great earth, bounded by the oceans and mountains, making it free from thorns, free from injustice, free from calamities, prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and teeming with many people and inhabitants, he dwelt there, ruling by means of the Dharma.

In that Jambudvīpa, within eighty-four thousand royal capitals, he had five hundred monasteries constructed in each capital, endowed with every excellent form and complete with all means of enjoyment, utility, and service; they were adorned with rows of groves, gardens, palaces, walkways, and pleasure-groves for delightful recreation.
And in each monastery, he had a Tathāgata-caitya built—vast in height, exceedingly arrayed with many kinds of jewels, and variegated with the finest of all precious gems.
In all those royal capitals, he invited the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara, together with his retinue, to enter the cities.
In every capital, while honoring the Tathāgata with every form of inconceivable worship due to a Tathāgata, he caused him to enter.
Through that miraculous display of entering the Buddha-city, he generated roots of merit in immeasurable sentient beings.
Therein, sentient beings with unpurified minds attained clarity; those with purified minds increased the force of their joy upon seeing the Buddha;
and those whose force of joy had increased attained the purification of their resolve for awakening.
Beings whose intentions for awakening were purified gave rise to the volition of great compassion;
beings committed to the welfare of sentient beings became devoted to seeking all the qualities of a Buddha;
and beings who knew the methods and procedures of the Buddha’s teachings directed their minds toward the thorough realization of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

Beings who had entered into the equality of phenomena directed their minds toward entering into the equality of the three times. Beings who had attained the illumination of the knowledge of the three times entered the light of knowledge for the sake of perceiving the succession of all Buddhas. Beings who had entered into the diverse manifestations of the Tathāgatas directed their minds toward the gathering of all living beings.

Beings engaged in gathering all the world generated the vow for the purification of the bodhisattva path. Beings who had entered into the equality of the path generated the light of wisdom for the manifestation of the wheel of Dharma of all Tathāgatas. Beings oriented toward the discipline of the ocean of Dharma directed their minds toward pervading the entire network of fields with their own bodies.
Having entered into the equality of all fields, beings made a vow for the sake of fully knowing the ocean of the faculties of all beings.
Beings who were engaged in investigating the inclinations of the faculties of the entire world purified their resolute intention for the attainment of omniscience.
Having thus caused these beings to enter into this very accomplishment of purpose, King Tejodhipati, in all [directions]...

He caused that Tathāgata, the most excellent Sūryagātra, to enter the royal capitals, manifesting inconceivable miraculous displays of the Buddha’s transformations in order to bring those sentient beings to maturity and discipline.
What do you think, noble son—was that prince named Tejodhipati at that time and on that occasion someone else?
Indeed, you should not view it in this way.
This very Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, was at that time and on that occasion the prince named Tejodhipati.
By him that sovereignty of a universal monarch was obtained, and he propitiated the Tathāgata named Sūryagātrapravara.
What do you think, noble son— was the king named Dhanapati, the father of Prince Tejodhipati, someone else at that time and on that occasion?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, at that very moment, the Tathāgata named Ratnakusumaprabha was the king named Dhanapati;
he is the one who, at present, in the world-system to the east, [presides over] world-system oceans as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of world-systems.

Beyond that, in the ocean of world-systems named Clouds Manifesting the Sky of the Dharmadhātu, within the lineage of world-systems centered on the family of the jewel-kings manifesting the three times,

in the world-system called Lamp of the Splendor of the Buddha’s Halo of Light, upon the seat of awakening marked by the banner reflecting the body of the Good Moon, he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, and is teaching the Dharma.

And by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnakusumaprabha, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, the ocean of world-systems known as the Cloud of Reflections in the Sky of the Entire Dharmadhātu was purified;

and all those Tathāgatas who have arisen, are arising, and will arise within that ocean of world-systems were all brought to maturity for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnakusumaprabha, while he was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva.
"What do you think, noble son? Was that queen named Padmaśrīgarbhasambhavā, the mother of Prince Tejodhipati and the wife of the king at that time and on that occasion, someone else?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
Noble son, she was Queen Māyā, the mother of the Blessed One, the mother who gave birth to the Bodhisattva, established in the liberation of universal radiance and non-obstruction."

At that time and at that moment, she was the chief queen of King Dhanatara, named Padmaśrīgarbhasambhavā; she had directly perceived the arrival of oceans of all the incalculable Tathāgatas and knew the methods for manifesting the births of all bodhisattvas.
What do you think, noble son—was that chief courtesan named Sudarśanā at that time and at that moment someone other than her?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
This very woman named Sunetrā, the wife of the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi and my mother, was at that time, on that occasion, the chief courtesan named Sudarśanā.
What do you think, noble son—was she someone else at that time, on that occasion, who was the courtesan’s daughter named Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, I was that courtesan’s daughter, Sucalitaratiprabhāsaśrī.
What do you think, noble son—was the retinue of King Tejodhipati at that time and on that occasion anyone else?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.

All these bodhisattvas have been established by the Blessed One in the fulfillment of the vows and conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra; they are seated here in this very circle of the assembly, having attained the manifestation of all world-systems.
With a body that is inseparable from the dwelling in all bodhisattva samādhis; with a mind that is informed by the direct presence and speech of all Tathāgatas;
with an eye that is informed by the thundering resonance of the clouds of melodic tones of the sky of all Tathāgatas;
with an ear that is informed by the sound of the breath-inhalation and exhalation that has mastery over the dwelling in all dharmas; and with a voice that does not stir from any buddha-field.

They were endowed with the manifestation of a body that never ceases its approach to the circles of assemblies of all Tathāgatas; a body that faces the inclinations of Bodhisattvas according to their aspirations;
a body produced in accordance with the ripening and disciplining [of beings]; a body extended throughout the net of all directions without exception; a body uninterrupted through all future eons;
and they were possessed of the attainment and fulfillment of the vows and conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. Of the Blessed One...
They were seated within the circle of the assembly.

Indeed, noble son, that Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara was attended by me, by the universal monarch Tejodhipati, and by others for as long as he lived, with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Furthermore, noble son, immediately after that Tathāgata Sūryagātrapravara had passed into parinirvāṇa, in that very world-system there appeared a Tathāgata named Prasannagātra.
He also appeared;
he too was pleased by us, and we honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped him.
Immediately after him, a Tathāgata named Sarvagātrajñānapratibhāsa-candra appeared in the world.
He too was pleased by us when we had become lords of the gods.
Immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Jāmbūnadatejorāja was pleased;
immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Lakṣaṇabhūṣitagātra was pleased.

Immediately after that, he propitiated the Tathāgata named Vicitraraśmijvalanacandra; immediately after that, he propitiated the Tathāgata named Suvilokitajñānaketu; immediately after that, he propitiated the Tathāgata named Vipulamahājñānaraśmirāja.
Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Nārāyaṇavajravīrya was propitiated;
immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Aparājitajñānasthāma was propitiated;
and immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Samantavilokitajñāna was propitiated.
Immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Vimalaśrīmegha was propitiated; immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Siṃhavijṛmbhitaprabha was propitiated;
immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Jñānaraśmijvalanacūḍa was propitiated.
Immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Guṇaraśmidhvaja was propitiated;
immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Jñānabhāskaratejas was propitiated; immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Ratnapadmapraphullitagātra was propitiated.
Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Puṇyapradīpadhvaja was propitiated;
immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Jñānaraśmimeghaprabha was propitiated;
and immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Samantavairocanacandra was propitiated.

Immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Ābharaṇacchatranirghoṣa. Immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Samantajñānālokavikramasiṃha. Immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Dharmadhātuviṣayamaticandra.
Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Sattvagaganacittapratibhāsabimba was propitiated. Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Praśamagandhasunābha was propitiated.
Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Samantānuravitashāntanirghoṣa was propitiated.
Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Sudṛḍhajñānaraśmijālabimbaskandha was propitiated.
Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Amṛtaparvataprabhātejas was propitiated. Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Dharmasāgaranigarjitaghoṣa was propitiated.
Immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Buddhagaganaprabhāsacūḍa was propitiated; immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Raśmicandra was propitiated;
immediately after that, the Tathāgata named Raśmicandrorṇamegha was propitiated.
Immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Suparipūrṇajñānamukhākṣa; immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Suviśuddhajñānakusumāvabhāsa;
and immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Ratnārciḥparvataśrītejorāja.

Immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Vipulaguṇajyotiḥprabha. Immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Samādhimervabhyudgatajñāna. Immediately after that, he pleased the Tathāgata named Ratnacandradhvaja.
Immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Arcirmaṇḍalagātra was propitiated; immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Ratnāgraprabhatejas was propitiated;
and immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Samantajñānacaryāvilamba was propitiated.
Immediately after that, he propitiated the Tathāgata named Arciḥsamudramukhavegapradīpa. Immediately after that, he propitiated the Tathāgata named Dharmavimānanirghoṣarāja.
Immediately after that, he propitiated the Tathāgata named Asadṛśaguṇakīrtidhvaja.
Immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Pralambabāhu was propitiated; immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Pūrvapraṇidhinirmāṇacandra was propitiated;
and immediately after him, Ākāśajñānārthapradīpa.
The Tathāgata named [Nāma] was pleased;
immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Dharmodgatanabheśvara was pleased;
immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Vairocanaśrīgarbharāja was pleased.

Immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Dharmanārāyaṇaketu was pleased; immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Jñānaketu was pleased; immediately after him, the Tathāgata named Dharmasāgarapadma was pleased.
In this way, noble son, with these Tathāgatas as the foremost, six hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Buddhas appeared in that world-system,
whom we have pleased, honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
"O son of good family, among those six million billion nayutas of Buddhas, the very last Tathāgata to appear was named Vipuladharmādhimuktisaṃbhavatejas.

When that Blessed One entered the city, I, being his queen together with my husband, performed worship of the Tathāgata by engaging in every mode of offering; and [therein] I heard the Dharma-discourse of the Tathāgata named *Sarvatathāgatotpattisaṃbhavapradīpa*."
I have heard this from the presence of the Blessed One,
and upon hearing it, the eye of wisdom was attained by me;
and this bodhisattva liberation, which is the sphere of observing the ocean of methods of all bodhisattva samādhis, has been attained.
Indeed, noble son, while cultivating this liberation, I have passed through eons equal to the atoms in a hundred Buddha-fields, practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva together with a bodhisattva.

And during those eons, which were as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field, I have propitiated Tathāgatas who were infinite and without middle. In some eons, I propitiated even a single Tathāgata throughout the entire duration of that eon.
In some eons, two Tathāgatas were propitiated;
in some eons, as many as ineffable numbers of Tathāgatas were propitiated;
and in some eons, Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field were propitiated.
Furthermore, I never knew the body of that bodhisattva—its dimensions, its shape, or its color.

I did not know his physical actions, nor his vocal actions, nor his mental actions; I did not know his vision of knowledge, nor the range of his knowledge, nor the domain of his meditative concentration of knowledge.

Moreover, noble son, those beings who, having seen the bodhisattva practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, conceived a heart of affection toward him, [were all born in the presence of the Tathāgata].
Through various conventions and various modes of living together, they generated faith;
all of them were gathered by the Bodhisattva through various worldly and transcendent means and became the Bodhisattva’s retinue.
While the Bodhisattva was practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, they remained in his retinue and were irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

"Son of good family, as soon as I beheld the Tathāgata Vipuladharmādhimuktisaṃbhavatejas, I attained this bodhisattva liberation called 'The Sphere of Contemplating the Ocean of All Bodhisattva Samādhis.
Since then, I have come along with a bodhisattva for as many eons as there are atoms in a hundred Buddha-fields, cultivating this liberation."
And as for those Tathāgatas who appeared during those eons, which were as numerous as the atoms in those Buddha-fields, I have pleased, honored, and attended upon them all;
and I have heard the Dharma teachings of all those Tathāgatas.

Having heard it, I have taken it up and retained it; and from the presence of all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, I have attained this liberation through various methods, through the sounds of various sūtra-methods, through various bodies of liberation, through various doors of liberation, through various investigations of liberation, and through entries into various banners.

Through entries into oceans of various buddha-fields; through perceptions of oceans of visions of various buddhas; through entries into the various circles of assemblies of Tathāgatas; through the paths of the methods of oceans of various bodhisattva vows; through the expansions of various bodhisattva practices; through the accomplishments of various bodhisattva practices; and through the various manifestations of bodhisattvas.
And yet, I do not enter the method of the Samantabhadra liberation of the Bodhisattva.
Why is that?

Noble son, for the methods of liberation of the Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas are immeasurable, like the entry into the expanse of space; they are immeasurable, like the expanse of all the mental conceptions of sentient beings; they are immeasurable, like the depths of the ocean of the revolutions of the three times.

“Noble son, the methods of liberation of the Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas are immeasurable as the surface of the oceans of directions; they are immeasurable as the depths of the oceans of the principles of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); for their modes of liberation possess bodies equal to the domain of the Tathāgatas.”
O son of good family, for as many eons as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, I have gazed upon the body of a bodhisattva without ever being satiated by the sight.

It is just as, O son of good family, when a man and a woman who are exclusively driven by passion meet together after having made an appointment, there arise immeasurable mental states produced by improper mental attention, born from the delusion of perceptions and discursive thoughts regarding the beautiful.

In the same way, noble son, as I behold the body of me, the Bodhisattva, from each and every pore there issue forth successions of world-systems that are infinite, without middle, and immeasurable in their description; they have various foundations, various arrangements of joints, various shapes, various arrays of mountains, various descriptions of the arrays of the earth’s surface, various ornaments covered by clouds in the sky, and various descriptions of the names and numbers of their eons.

Arising from the lineages of various Tathāgatas born from the appearance of various Buddhas; adorned with various bodhimaṇḍas; displaying various miraculous transformations in turning the wheel of the Dharma of various Tathāgatas;

arrayed with various circles of assemblies of various Tathāgatas; resounding with the proclamations of the explanations of the methods of various sūtras; originating from the accomplishment of the methods of various vehicles;
and illuminating with the light of various pure radiances—such signs, never seen before, come into the range of vision at every moment of thought.
From each and every pore, oceans of Buddhas without end or middle appear before the eyes;

adorned with various *bodhimaṇḍas*, performing various miracles of turning the wheel of Dharma, and manifesting various miracles of the resonance of the *sūtrāntas*, they appear before the eyes at every moment of thought through an uninterrupted yoga.
From each and every pore, oceans of sentient beings without end or middle—dwelling in various abodes, groves, mountains, celestial palaces, rivers, and seas—also appear.
Bodies of various forms, with various objects of enjoyment, with various modes of conduct, yoga, and practice, and with various faculties, perfections, and configurations,
appear to the eye at every moment of thought;
from each and every pore of the skin, there appear infinite and boundless oceans of the three times through the method of entry.
The oceans of the bodhisattvas' vows, without end or middle, become purified;

the oceans of the various stages and practices of the bodhisattvas, without end or middle, come into view; and the purifications of the oceans of the methods of the bodhisattva perfections, without end or middle, come into manifestation.
Oceans of the former spiritual practices of bodhisattvas, without end or middle, come into view; oceans of methods for purifying buddha-fields, without end or middle, come into view;

and oceans of methods of the great loving-kindness of bodhisattvas, oceans of methods of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and oceans of the application of valorous effort in maturing and disciplining all sentient beings, enter [into my perception].
Oceans of methods for the clouds of the great compassion of bodhisattvas, without end or middle, arise;

oceans of the surges of great joy of bodhisattvas, without end or middle, increase; and in every moment of thought, oceans of applications for gathering all sentient beings, without end or middle, are perfected.

O noble son, throughout those eons equal in number to the atoms in a hundred Buddha-fields, as I have entered into oceans of methods of the Dharma— each infinite and without center— from every single pore of the Bodhisattva at every moment of thought, I do not reach their limit; nor do I enter now what I have not entered before.

I do not attain what was never attained before; for even when the noble son Sarvārthasiddha was in the midst of his inner apartments, surrounded by a host of women, I—through the entry into oceans of methods of various liberations from each and every pore—entered infinite and boundless oceans of methods of the three times, by means of entering oceans of methods for entering the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Noble son, I know and enter into this bodhisattva liberation called "The Sphere of Surveying the Ocean of All Bodhisattva Samādhis.

But what can I possibly say of the bodhisattvas who have set out upon an ocean of infinite and limitless methods and principles; who manifest bodily communications appearing in forms and postures identical to all sentient beings; and who display conduct that accords with the inclinations of the entire world?

They emit from every pore clouds of manifested forms of infinite and centerless colors; they are naturally pure by the very nature of the reality of all bodies; they are free from conceptual construction through their realization of the world’s nature as having the characteristic of space; they are supreme in their mastery of the Tathāgata’s equal miraculous transformations through the certainty of an intelligence that pervades everywhere; they have emerged from the miraculous displays within the domain of infinite and centerless liberations; they possess sovereign power over the entry and dwelling in the arousal of the mind toward the vast realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and they sport with the ocean of liberations of all stages and all dharmas through universal gates.
To know his conduct, or to speak of his virtues,
or to fully demonstrate him as a treasury of all virtues.

Go, noble son, right here at the feet of the Blessed One Vairocana, where the goddess named Māyā—the mother of Bodhisattvas—is seated upon a lion throne with a core of lotuses made of a great king of jewels arrayed with various gems.
Approach her and ask: "How do Bodhisattvas, while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, remain unstained by the impurities of all worldly phenomena?"
They become unflagging in their applications of worship to the Tathāgatas;
they become irreversible from all the activities of a bodhisattva;
and they become free from all obscurations in their entry into the liberations of a bodhisattva.
They become independent of others in all the dwellings of the bodhisattvas;
they come into the direct presence of all the Tathāgatas;
and they do not turn back from their applications for the gathering of all sentient beings.
They do not turn back from dwelling in all the bodhisattva practices throughout kalpas reaching to the furthest limit of the future; they do not retreat from their vow for the Mahāyāna;
and they do not sink into despondency because of their sustaining and increasing the roots of virtue of the world.

Then, indeed, Gopā, the Śākya maiden, demonstrating this very method of the gate of liberation, through the empowerment of the Buddha, at that time spoke these verses: “Those beings who behold the Supreme Being truly engaged in the practice of the conduct for perfect enlightenment—whether their minds are full of faith or full of hostility—all of them go to his gathering. (90)
I remember as many eons here as there are atoms in a hundred fields;
after that, the world-system Meruprabhābhuva arose in the eon named Vyūha.
In that [eon], there were twenty-six million times ten thousand thousands of sages;
among them, the last of those lords of sages was named Dharmadhvaja, a lamp for the world.

At that time, when that lord of sages had passed into final nirvana, a king named Śrīteja became the supreme sovereign in this Jambudhvaja; he had destroyed the circle of his enemies, and his commands were unimpeded.
He had five hundred sons who were brave, heroic, and handsome; their bodies were complete in all limbs and perfectly pure, adorned with unsurpassed splendor. (94)
The king, together with his son, was filled with serene faith toward the Sugata and performed extensive worship of the Jina;
and he, being devoted to the Dharma, became constantly engaged in upholding the True Dharma and remained unshakable. (95)
And this prince of that king, named Suraśmi, was of pure being;
he was handsome to behold and of pleasing form, his limbs adorned with the thirty excellent marks. // 96 //
Having renounced his kingdom, he then went forth as a monk, surrounded by fifty million men;
having gone forth, endowed with firm vigor, he upheld the Dharma of the Jina. (97)
There was a city named Drumāvatī, surrounded by thousands of millions of excellent cities;
there stood a forest of manifold branches, with a tranquil resonance and unsurpassed splendor.
Since Suraśmi, confident, pure in wisdom and eloquence, was sporting there, he illuminated the Dharma of the Jina for the sake of purifying the multitude of afflicted beings. (99)

For alms, the wise one entered the city with a pleasing deportment and a tranquil appearance; his eyes were not cast about, he was mindful and self-possessed, his movements were deep, and his gait was steady and firm. (100)
In former times, there was a preeminent merchant in the cities named Nandīdhvaja, whose fame was widely proclaimed;
at that time, I was his beloved daughter, named Bhānuprabhā, possessed of a most beautiful form. (101)
Then,
at the gate of that northern palace, I saw Surashmi together with his retinue;
he was gracious, his limbs adorned with the primary marks, and there arose within me a very great faith.
When he arrived at the door of my house, I gave him a jewel for his alms-bowl;
having set aside all my ornaments, I, guided by a mind of loving-kindness, then gave it to him. (103)
Having performed worship with a mind still possessed of passion to Surasriketu, the son of the Sugata,
he certainly never fell into the lower realms for two hundred and fifty eons during that supreme kalpa.
Born among the gods in the families of the lords of gods, and as the daughter of a lord of men among humans,
I have been endowed everywhere with infinite beauty and stature from the very moment I was seen.
When two hundred and fifty kalpas had passed, I was born as Saṃcālitā, the daughter of Sudarśanā, the most excellent of courtesans, among those who bring fearlessness. (106)
Then, having seen the youth Tejodhipati, I joyfully offered him worship;
having dedicated myself to him alone, I have indeed become his submissive wife. (107)
Honored by him together with me, that great seer, Sūryagātrapravara, was filled with joy;
and upon beholding the Buddha with a serene mind, the supreme thought of enlightenment was generated within me.
In that very same eon, sixty billion Jinas indeed arose; among them, the final of those Jinas was then the Buddha Adhimuktitejas. (109)

Within that, my pure Dharma-eye was purified and the intrinsic nature of phenomena was realized by me; having attained illumination, I then became one for whom baseless conceptualization had utterly ceased. (110)
From that very moment, I have beheld the stage of meditative concentration of the Sons of the Conquerors;
in a single mental instant, I perceive oceans of buddha-fields beyond thought, extending in all directions.
I behold in all directions various pure realms, immeasurable and wondrous;
having seen them, my mind does not cling to them, nor is it repelled by those that are afflicted. (112)
In all those very fields, and at every seat of enlightenment without exception, I behold all the Buddhas; with a single thought, I survey their oceans of radiance and their infinite forms. // 113 //
In that very same way, I enter their oceans of assemblies without attachment in a single moment of thought;
I know all their meditative absorptions without exception, as well as their immeasurable liberations.
I uphold their vast conduct and enter all the stages without exception;
moment by moment, I enter infinite oceans of incalculable vows.
Beholding the body of this True Being and his conduct throughout infinite eons, I never reach the end of the miraculous transformations from even a single one of his pores. (116)

I behold even oceans of fields beyond all calculation within a single pore, as well as world-systems consisting of masses of wind, great floods of water, filled with fire, and having earth for their body. (117)

[They see] forms consisting of various conceptualizations of abodes, entering into diverse systems of arrangement; [they see] beings of various kinds through the distinctions of elements and bodies, with physical forms whose limits and middles are infinite. // 118 //
In immeasurable world-systems, I behold various inexpressible elements;
I see the Victors engaged therein, training the multitude through the designations of phenomena.
I have not perceived his physical action, nor his speech, nor his mind, nor the actions of those two;
there is no supernatural power, nor any distinct miraculous transformations as he practices vast and excellent conduct throughout the eons.
Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, bowed his head at the feet of Gopā, the Śākya maiden;
he circumambulated Gopā, the Śākya maiden, hundreds of thousands of times, and looking back at her again and again, he departed from the presence of Gopā, the Śākya maiden. // 41 //
(Gv 339) 44. Māyā:
Then, as the merchant’s son Sudhana was about to go into the presence of Queen Māyā, he had set out upon the wisdom that investigates the range of the Buddhas.

This thought occurred to him: "By what means can I [approach] those spiritual friends who have transcended the six sense-bases of all worlds, who are non-abiding, whose bodies have completely surpassed all attachments, who have set out upon the path leading to the state of non-attachment, whose dharma-bodies are utterly pure, whose physical actions consist of bodies well-manifested through illusion, and who investigate the world through the illusory nature of their gnosis?"

Of those whose bodies are the form of their vows; whose bodies are mind-made through the empowerment of the Buddhas; whose bodies are neither born nor ceased; whose bodies are neither true nor false; whose bodies neither transmigrate nor perish; whose bodies neither arise nor dissolve;
whose bodies have the single characteristic of being characterless; and whose bodies are liberated from duality and attachment.

Of those whose bodies have no abode yet abide nowhere; whose bodies are unimpaired; whose bodies are non-conceptual like reflections; whose bodies are as if examined in a dream; whose bodies are pervaded by forms resembling the surface of a mirror; whose bodies are established in tranquility equal to all directions; and whose emanation-bodies pervade all directions.

To behold, encounter, meet with, and grasp the signs of the spiritual friends whose bodies are undifferentiated by the three times, whose bodies are non-conceptual as they are without body or mind, whose bodies have completely transcended the range of vision of all the world, whose bodies for conversion are to be known through the expansion of the eye of Samantabhadra, and whose sphere of activity is the unattached sky.
or to understand the circle of sounds, or to comprehend the applications of mantras, or to grasp the instruction.

While Sudhana was thus engaged in such reflection and mental attention, a city goddess named Ratnanetrā, surrounded by a host of sky-deities, appeared in the expanse of the sky. Her body was adorned with various ornaments, and she held baskets of divine flowers of many forms and colors. As she scattered them before him, she addressed the merchant’s son Sudhana: "By one who is intent on protecting the city of the mind..."
Noble son, you should be one who does not dwell in delight within the spheres of all saṃsāra.
Noble son, you should be intent upon adorning the city of the mind by taking the ten powers of the Tathāgata as the object of meditative concentration.
Noble son, you should be intent upon purifying the city of the mind by removing envy, stinginess, and deceit.
Noble son, you must be intent upon pacifying the heat within the city of the mind through the thorough investigation of all phenomena.
Noble son, you must be intent upon expanding the city of the mind by increasing the force of great vigor for the accumulation of the requisites for omniscience.

Noble son, you must be engaged in protecting the array of the palace-treasury within the city of the mind by exercising mastery over all meditative concentrations, attainments, dhyānas, liberations, and the vast dwellings of the Dharma-discipline.

Noble son, you should apply yourself to illuminating the city of the mind by receiving and attaining the perfection of wisdom that encompasses the entire ground and the assembly of the maṇḍalas of all Tathāgatas.
Noble son, you should apply yourself to supporting the city of the mind by converging the path of skillful means through which all Tathāgatas arise within the city of one’s own mind.

Noble son, you should apply yourself to constructing the firm ramparts of the city of the mind for the sake of purifying the mind through the accomplishment of the vows and conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

Noble son, you should apply yourself to accomplishing the invincibility and impregnability of the city of the mind, so as not to be crushed by any afflictions, the hosts of Māra, evil friends, or the wheel of Māra.
Noble son, you should apply yourself to illuminating the city of the mind, by proceeding toward the illumination of the Tathāgata’s wisdom for all sentient beings.
Noble son, you should apply yourself to causing the city of the mind to overflow, by receiving the rain-clouds of the Dharma from all the Tathāgatas.
Noble son, you should be intent upon supporting the city of the mind by receiving the ocean of merit of all Tathāgatas within the intention of your own mind.
Noble son, you should be intent upon expanding the city of the mind by pervading the entire world with great loving-kindness.
Noble son, you should be intent upon roofing over the city of the mind by accomplishing the vast parasol of Dharma as an antidote to all unwholesome phenomena.

"Noble son, you must be devoted to the stabilization of the city of the mind by means of vast great compassion and sympathy for all living beings. Noble son, you must be devoted to opening the gates of the city of the mind by means of bringing all internal and external things to all living beings.
Noble son, you must be devoted to purifying the city of the mind by means of turning your back on all delight in the realms of saṃsāra."
Noble son, you must apply yourself to establishing the firm foundation of the city of the mind by ensuring that no unwholesome states arise within your own mental continuum.
Noble son, you must apply yourself to the vigor of the city of the mind by accomplishing the vigor that gathers the provisions for omniscience.
Noble son, you must apply yourself to illuminating the city of the mind by illuminating the recollection of the mandalas of the Tathāgatas of all three times.

Noble son, you must become one who knows the method for investigating the city of the mind, by virtue of having heard and mastered the various methods for investigating the diverse doors of the Dharma within the sūtras of the wheel of Dharma of all Tathāgatas.
Noble son, you must become one who knows the method for regulating the city of the mind, by virtue of manifesting the various paths to the gateway of omniscience that faces all worlds.
Noble son, you must become one who knows the method for sustaining the city of the mind, for the sake of purifying the accomplishment of the vows of all Tathāgatas throughout the three times.

Noble son, you must be one who knows the method for increasing the power of the provisions for the city of the mind, by means of increasing the vast provisions of merit and wisdom throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Noble son, you must be one who knows the method for emitting the universal radiance of the city of the mind, by means of the knowledge and supernormal powers regarding the intentions, faculties, and inclinations of all sentient beings, as well as their affliction and purification.
Noble son, you must be one who knows the method for exercising mastery over the city of the mind, by means of the convergence upon the principles of the entire realm of phenomena.
Noble son, you should be devoted to the luminosity of the city of the mind by means of the illumination of the mindfulness of all Tathāgatas.
Noble son, you should be devoted to the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature of the city of the mind by means of penetrating the principle that all phenomena are bodiless.
Noble son, you should be devoted to the contemplation of the city of the mind as being like an illusion by means of proceeding to the city of the dharma of omniscience.
In this way, noble son, it is possible for that bodhisattva who is devoted to the purification of the city of the mind to attain the accumulation of all roots of virtue.
Why is that?
Because for a bodhisattva whose city of the mind is thus purified, no obscurations stand before him.

Whether it be an obstruction to seeing the Buddha, an obstruction to hearing the Dharma, an obstruction to honoring and attending upon the Tathāgata, an obstruction to the practice of gathering in sentient beings, or an obstruction to the purification of the buddha-field—
by means of a mental disposition free from all such obstructions, noble son, spiritual friends appear with little difficulty to a bodhisattva who is devoted to seeking out spiritual friends.
And, noble son, the omniscience of bodhisattvas is dependent upon spiritual friends.

There, the body-attendant goddess Dharmapadmaśrīkuśalā, whose splendor was like a cluster of the glory of modesty (*hrīśrīmañjariprabhāvā*), surrounded by an immeasurable host of goddesses, emerged from the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) while extolling the virtues of Queen Māyā; she stood in the expanse of the sky facing the merchant’s son Sudhana, emitting from her respective bodies many nets of light rays in various jewel-hues and the pure, radiant colors of various fragrant incenses.

He emitted nets of light rays whose colors gladdened the disposition and intentions of the mind, whose colors increased the surge of joy in the mind, whose colors cooled the burning of the body, and whose colors manifested the purity of the body; these rays had as their domain the arising of unimpeded physical prowess.
Having illuminated vast realms, they followed Sudhana the merchant’s son everywhere and were directed toward him from all sides.
Having manifested the bodies of all the Tathāgatas and circumambulated the entire world, they descended upon the crown of the head of the merchant’s son Sudhana;
entering through his crown, they permeated all his pores.
As soon as the merchant's son Sudhana was touched by those rays of light from the goddesses,
he immediately obtained the eye called Viraja-prabhāsa (Stainless Radiance),
which does not coexist with any darkness or gloom.
He obtained the eye named Vitimira,
by which he penetrates the intrinsic nature of sentient beings;
and he obtained the eye named Virajaḥpati.
And by means of that, he beheld the mandala of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
he obtained the eye called "Pure Course," by which he beholds the fundamental nature of all fields.
He obtained the eye named Vairocanaprabha, by which he beholds the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata;
and he obtained the eye named Viśuddhagati.
By means of which he beholds the inconceivable perfection of the Tathāgata’s form-body;
and he obtained the eye named Samantaprabha, by means of which he beholds the inconceivable manifestation of the Tathāgata’s form-body.
He obtained the eye named Unattached Radiance,
by which he beholds the distinct manifestations of the arising of world-systems throughout the expanse of the oceans of all fields;
and he obtained the eye named Universal Illumination.
By means of which he surveys the direction of the accomplishment of the methods of the sūtras within all the teachings of the Tathāgatas;

and he obtained the eye named "Universal Domain," by which he surveys the empowerment for the training of sentient beings through the infinite and centerless miraculous transformations of the Buddhas.
And he obtained the eye named Samantadarśa, by which he beholds the arising of Buddhas as they extend throughout the manifestation of all realms.
Then, indeed, the lord of rākṣasas named Sunetra, who was the gatekeeper of the Bodhisattvasaṃgīti palace and the leader of ten thousand rākṣasas,

together with his wife, his sons, and his circle of kinsmen and attendants, scattered flowers of various colors and pleasing fragrances over the merchant’s son Sudhana and spoke thus: "Noble son, a bodhisattva endowed with ten qualities..."
He comes close to all spiritual friends.
By which ten?
Namely, by means of a perfectly pure intention that is free from deceit and guile.
By means of great compassion that is undifferentiated in its embrace of the entire world;
by means of discernment that realizes the nature of all beings as being without a self-nature of a sentient being;
and by the power of resolute intention that is irreversible in its arrival at omniscience.
By the power of resolute conviction directed toward the maṇḍala of the Tathāgata,
by the eye that is stainless and pure regarding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
and by great loving-kindness that is undifferentiated toward the entire circle of sentient beings;
By the light of knowledge that scatters all obscurations;
by the great cloud of Dharma that serves as a parasol against all the sufferings of saṃsāra;
and by the eye of knowledge that extends everywhere throughout the entire realm of phenomena and is directed toward approaching spiritual friends.
Noble son, a bodhisattva endowed with these ten qualities draws near to all spiritual friends.
Furthermore, by observing through ten gateways of meditative concentration and discernment, a bodhisattva attains the direct presence of all spiritual friends.
What are these ten?

Namely: by means of the gateway of meditative realization through the sphere of the stainless movement in the sky of phenomena; by means of the gateway of meditative realization through the eye facing the oceans of all directions;
and by means of the gateway of meditative realization through the non-conceptualization and non-discursiveness regarding all objects of focus.

And by the entrance of the meditative absorption called "Arising from Clouds of Tathāgatas in All Directions," and by the entrance of the meditative absorption called "Womb for Accumulating the Ocean of Merit and the Wisdom of Omniscience," and by the entrance of the meditative absorption called "Proximity to the Arising of Spiritual Friends Never Separated from the Production of the Thought of Enlightenment."

And by the gateway of meditative concentration and contemplation known as the "Arising of Happiness through the Virtuous Friends who possess all the qualities of the Tathāgatas," and by the gateway of meditative concentration and contemplation known as the "Never Being Separated from Any Virtuous Friend," and by the gateway of meditative concentration and contemplation known as the "Application of Constant and Universal Approach to the Equality of All Virtuous Friends."
And through tireless application in the skillful means and conduct of all spiritual friends, by means of the gateway of the contemplation of meditative concentration—
noble son, a bodhisattva endowed with these ten gateways of the contemplation of meditative concentration attains the direct presence of all spiritual friends.
And he attains the samādhi-liberation named Sarvatathāgatadharmacakrakalyāṇamitramukhanirghoṣa, by practicing which a bodhisattva enters into the undifferentiated equality of all Buddhas.
And he obtains spiritual friends who are undifferentiated and pervasive everywhere.
When the lord of the rākṣasas, Sunetra, had spoken thus, Sudhana, the merchant’s son, looked toward the expanse of the sky and said: "Excellent, excellent, noble one!
You are compassionate toward us, intent on bestowing favor, and a revealer of spiritual friends.
Therefore, it would be well if you would correctly instruct us in the gateway of skillful means; how shall we proceed?"
Toward which direction shall I hasten?
Upon what basis shall I search?
What object of focus shall I contemplate in order to see the spiritual friend?

He said: "Therefore, noble son, you should approach the presence of the spiritual friend with a body prostrated toward all directions, with an intention focused on all objects and bound by mindfulness of the spiritual friend, with a universal speed through the pursuit of samādhi, with a mental speed like a dream, and with an investigation and movement of the mind-body like a reflection."

Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, proceeding according to the instructions given by Sunetra, the lord of the rākṣasas, saw before him, rising from the surface of the earth, a great jewel-lotus with a stem made of the bodies of all vajras, a core of the king of jewels of the ocean of all worlds, petals arranged in rows of every king of jewels, a pericarp of the king of vairocana-jewels, filaments of the king of jewels of every precious color and fragrance, and covered by an incalculable net of jewels.

And upon that great king of precious lotus-stalks, he saw a gabled pavilion named Dharmadhātu-dik-samavasaraṇagarbha (Womb of the Convergence of the Directions of the Dharma-realm), variegated and beautiful to behold, resting upon a ground of diamond-Vairocana, adorned with a thousand pillars made entirely of the finest jewels,
its interior inlaid with every kind of gem, draped with divine bands of pure Jāmbūnada gold, and hung with countless nets of various pearl necklaces.

It was adorned with various arrangements of the king of jewel-gems, surrounded on all sides by a display of jambū-dhvaja jewel-gems, encircled by countless jeweled railings, and beautifully provided with stairways made of the king of jewels facing every direction.

In the center of that gabled hall, he saw a throne with a lotus-womb made of the king of wish-fulfilling jewel-gems, established upon images of jewel-forms representing the forms of all the lords of the world.
It had the color and form of every kind of precious gem, its shape was like the brilliance of Indra’s banner, and it was established upon a ground-surface of diamond-jewel wheels;

it was arrayed with rows of various king-like jewels, surrounded by railings of many gems, beautifully adorned with the king of light-bearing jewels, graced by a manifold display of various jewels, excellently draped in garments of king-like jewels surpassing those of the heavens, and well-finished with robes of variegated colors and diverse jewel-stuffs.
