for the sake of liberating all suffering sentient beings, for the sake of drying up all miserable rebirths, for the sake of turning back from all unfavorable conditions, for the sake of diverting all treacherous paths, for the sake of dispelling the blinding darkness of all ignorance, and for the sake of completely crossing over the wilderness of all saṃsāra.

For the sake of turning back from the wheel of all destinies; for the sake of completely transcending the realm of all Māras; for the sake of rising up from all places of attachment; for the sake of shaking off all dwellings and abodes; for the sake of pulling oneself out from the mire of desire; for the sake of abandoning delight and passion; for the sake of removing the fetters of views;
for the sake of turning back the clinging to the view of a self-identity; and for the sake of utterly severing the snare of conceptualization.

For the purpose of turning back from the path of perversion; for the purpose of extracting the thorns of latent tendencies; for the purpose of breaking open the doors of the hindrances; for the purpose of shattering the mountain of obstructions; for the purpose of uprooting the net of craving; for the purpose of loosening the fetters of ignorance;

for the purpose of illuminating existence; for the purpose of abandoning deceit and guile; for the purpose of clarifying the turbidity of the mind; and for the purpose of completely eradicating doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation.
He has set out for the sake of crossing over the great flood of ignorance and for the sake of revulsion toward all the defects of saṃsāra.

For this son of good family, noble beings, desiring to provide for sentient beings the crossing over the four floods by means of the great gift— the great ship of Dharma— desiring to establish a great bridge of Dharma for those submerged in the mire of false views,

desiring to produce the light of wisdom for those fallen into the darkness of delusion, desiring to show the Noble Path to those lost in the wilderness of saṃsāra, [and] for those tormented by the disease of the great afflictions...

Desiring to bestow the medicine of the Dharma upon those afflicted by birth, old age, and death; desiring to grant the realm of the Deathless (*amṛtadhātu*); desiring to refresh with the waters of tranquility (*śamatha*) those burning with the three fires; desiring to grant great relief to those tormented by sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; desiring to grant the abandonment through knowledge to those imprisoned in the jail of existence; and desiring to release those bound by the fetters of false views.
Desiring to bring forth the weapon of wisdom; desiring to show the gate of liberation to those confined within the city of the three realms;

desiring to show the door of release to those imprisoned in the city of the three realms; desiring to point out the direction of safety to those facing the direction of insecurity; and desiring to grant great relief to those afflicted by the formative forces of the afflictions and those terrified by the fear of falling into the miserable destinies.

Desirous of giving a hand to those struck down by the executioners that are the aggregates; desirous of pointing out the city of Nirvana to those surrounded by the serpents that are the elements; desirous of declaring the means of escape for those dwelling in the empty village of the sense-bases;
desirous of leading those who have entered upon false paths onto the true path; [desirous of rescuing] those who have fallen into the hands of enemies...
Desiring to reveal true spiritual friends, desiring to establish those who delight in the domain of the dharmas of fools within the noble dharmas,
and desiring to uproot those who delight in the city of saṃsāra and lead them into the city of omniscience;

O sons of good family, this true person, thus never ceasing his efforts to protect sentient beings and seeking the purification of the arousal of the thought of awakening, is untiring in the undertaking of the Mahāyāna and remains insatiable with the vehicles that are clouds of all dharmas.
He is ever-diligent in fulfilling all the provisions;
he does not cast off his burden in order to bring to completion the gateways of all dharmas;
and his vigor is independent in order to achieve the conduct of all bodhisattvas.
His application is irreversible for the sake of accomplishing all his vows;
he is insatiable in beholding all spiritual friends,
and his body never tires of attending upon all spiritual friends.
He accepts with reverence all the instructions and exhortations of all spiritual friends.
Those beings in all the worlds, O son of good family, who set their aspiration upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment are rare;
therefore, those beings are even rarer still.
Those who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment gather the qualities of a Buddha through such an application of the exertion of vigor,
and they seek the path of a bodhisattva with such intense aspiration.
With such a sense of purpose, they purify the conduct of a bodhisattva;
with such diligence, they attend upon spiritual friends;
and with such a sense of urgency as if their hair or clothing were on fire, they do not contradict the wisdom of the spiritual friends.
By such a practice of firm resolute intention, they act upon the instructions of spiritual friends;
by such a state of receptive compliance, they cultivate all the factors of enlightenment;
and by such a lack of desire for gain, honor, and praise, they perform the action of not disturbing the element of a bodhisattva’s resolute intention.

Through such a state of renunciation—disregarding all things, including the pleasures of domestic life, desires, and delight, as well as their parents and kinsmen—they seek the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattvas.
Through such disregard for body and life, they aspire to omniscience.

Indeed, noble son, other bodhisattvas dwelling in the awakening of a Buddha will not attain the fulfillment of the vows and conduct of a bodhisattva even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
Whether it be for the purification of the buddha-field,
or for the ripening and disciplining of sentient beings,
or for entering the knowledge of the dharma-realm;
Whether in the full accomplishment of the perfections,
or in the extensive unfolding of the web of conduct,
or in the fulfillment of the realization of vows;
Whether it be in the transcending of the deeds of Māra, or in pleasing the spiritual friends,
or in the complete accomplishment and purification of all the bodhisattva practices;
Or they will attain the perfection of the power for accomplishing the conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, which he shall realize in this single acquisition of a birth.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, having praised the true qualities and virtues of the merchant’s son Sudhana, and having strengthened the resolve for the factors of enlightenment in hundreds of thousands of living beings by means of that occasion, said this to the merchant’s son Sudhana:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son!"

Since you have generated the mind for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the entire world, for the protection of the realm of all sentient beings, and for the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha—
well-gained, noble son, are your gains, and welcome is your attainment of human birth.
Well-lived is your life among the worlds of living beings; you have propitiated the appearance of a Buddha,
and you have clearly beheld Mañjuśrī, the spiritual friend.
Your mental continuum is that of a worthy vessel;
it has been well-saturated by roots of virtue and firmly supported by pure qualities.
Your noble inclination and virtuous resolute intention have been thoroughly purified;
you are attended by all the Buddhas,
and you, son of good family, are well-sustained by spiritual friends.
Because of that resolute intention with which you have generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—
for what reason is this? For,
noble son, the thought of enlightenment is the seed of all the qualities of a Buddha.
It is like a field, because it causes the white dharmas of the entire world to grow; it is like the earth, because it is the refuge for all the world;
it is like water, because it washes away the stains of all afflictions.
He is like the wind, because he has no fixed abode in any world;
he is like fire, because he burns away the dry grass of all views and grasping;
he is like the sun, because he illuminates the dwellings of all sentient beings.
It is like the moon, by virtue of fulfilling the mandala of pure dharmas; it is like a lamp, by virtue of producing the light of the Dharma;
it is like an eye, by virtue of discerning the level and the uneven.
It is like a path, by virtue of leading to the entry into the city of omniscience; it is like a ford, by virtue of avoiding false paths;
it is like a vehicle, by virtue of being mounted upon by all bodhisattvas.

It is like a gateway, because it provides entry into all the gateways of the conduct of bodhisattvas; it is like a celestial palace, because it is the seat for the cultivation of meditative concentrations;
it is like a pleasure garden, because it experiences the delight in the Dharma.
It is a dwelling place because it protects the entire world; it is a refuge because it carries out the welfare of all people;
it is a support because it is the practice of all bodhisattvas.
It is like a father because it protects all bodhisattvas; it is like a mother because it gives birth to all sentient beings; it is like a nurse because it nurtures and sustains them in every way.
It is like a king, because it overcomes all the minds of those in training, those beyond training, and pratyekabuddhas; it is like a sovereign, because it is superior to all vows;
it is like the great ocean, because it is the gathering place for the jewels of all virtues.
He is like Mount Meru because of his equanimity toward all sentient beings;
he is like the Cakravāla mountain range because he is a refuge for the entire world;
he is like the Himavat mountains because he increases the medicinal herbs of wisdom.
It is like Mount Gandhamādana, being the locus for the fragrance of all virtues;
it is like the sky, being vast with great qualities;
it is like a lotus, being unsullied by any worldly phenomena.
He is like a dragon through his state of being tamed and noble;
he is like a thoroughbred horse through his freedom from all stubbornness;
he is like a charioteer through his leading the way for the attainment of the Great Vehicle.
It is like medicine, because it cures the disease of the afflictions;
it is like the underworld, because it brings about the complete purification of all unwholesome dharmas.
It is like a diamond because it penetrates all phenomena;
it is like a casket of fragrance because it produces the fragrance of virtuous qualities;
it is like a great flower because its appearance is pleasing to all the world.
He is like Himalayan sandalwood because he refreshes the heat of passion;
he is like a peacock’s tail-feather because he pervades the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
he is like the great medicinal king Sudarśana because he eradicates the disease of all afflictions (kleśa).
It is like a medicine for the removal [of suffering], because it completely extracts the thorns of all latent tendencies;
it is like Indra, because it possesses sovereignty over all the sense faculties;
it is like Vaiśravaṇa, because it utterly destroys all poverty.
It is the glorious being, by virtue of being adorned with all excellent qualities;
it is the ornament, by virtue of gracing all bodhisattvas;
it is the fire that consumes the eon, by virtue of incinerating all misdeeds.
It is like a great medicinal king with an inexhaustible root, because it causes all the qualities of a Buddha to increase;
it is like a naga-jewel, because it dispels the poison of all afflictions; it is like a water-clearing gem, because it removes all turbidity.
It is like a king of wish-fulfilling gems because it accomplishes all aims; it is like an auspicious vase because it fulfills all intentions;
it is like a wish-granting tree because it rains down the ornaments of all virtuous qualities.
It is like a garment marked with swans because it is unsullied by any of the defects of saṃsāra;
it is like cotton thread because its nature is luminous;
it is like a plow because it purifies the field of the dispositions of sentient beings.
It is like a barbed arrow because it strikes down the phenomena of the view of a self-existent body; it is like a shaft because it pierces the target of suffering;
it is like a spear for the sake of conquering the enemy of the afflictions.
It is like armor because it shields against improper mental attention; it is like a sword because it strikes off the heads of the afflictions;
it is like a blade-leaf because it cuts through the armor of pride, intoxication, and arrogance.
It is like a razor for its ability to pierce through the nature of latent tendencies; it is like a hero’s banner for its ability to topple the banner of pride;
it is like a weapon for its ability to fell the tree of ignorance.
It is like an axe, by way of cutting down the tree of suffering; it is like a weapon, by way of protecting against all calamities;
it is like a hand, by way of preserving the body of the perfections.
It is like a foot, because it is the foundation for all virtues and gnosis;
it is like a probe, because it thoroughly cleanses the cataracts of the sheath of ignorance; it is like a healing ointment, because it draws out the thorn of the view of a self-existent body.

It is like a probe, by way of extracting the thorns of latent tendencies; it is like a friend, by way of liberating one from the bonds of saṃsāra; it is like a treasure, by way of warding off all misfortunes.
It is like a teacher, because it possesses mastery over the path of departure for all bodhisattva practices; it is like a treasure store, because its merit is inexhaustible;
it is like a fountainhead, because its wisdom is inexhaustible.
It is like a circular mirror because it displays the reflections of all gateways to the Dharma; it is like a white lotus because it is unstained;
it is like a great river because it flows with the current of the perfections and the articles of attraction.
It is like a great lord of serpents by virtue of raining down the clouds of Dharma; it is like the life-faculty by virtue of sustaining the great compassion of all bodhisattvas;
it is like nectar by virtue of leading to the attainment of the immortal realm.

It is like a universal net of snares, by way of gathering in and attracting all sentient beings who are to be trained; it is like a casket of perfumes, by way of containing the fragrance of all virtuous qualities;
it is like an elixir, by way of producing ultimate health.
It is like an antidote, by virtue of neutralizing the poison of sensual pleasure; it is like a mantra-dhāraṇī, by virtue of exhausting all poisons of improper mental attention;
it is like a whirlwind, by virtue of dispersing all hindrances and obstructions.

It is like an island of jewels because it is a mine of all the jewels of the factors conducive to enlightenment; it is like a lineage because it brings about the accumulation of all pure dharmas; it is like a source because it is the gateway for the entry of all virtuous qualities.
It is like a marketplace because it is frequented by all bodhisattva-merchants;
it is like an element of flavor because it thoroughly purifies all karmic and afflictive obscurations;
it is like honey because it fulfills the equipment for omniscience.
It is like a path, because it leads to the city of omniscience for all bodhisattvas; it is like a vessel, because it sustains all pure dharmas;
it is like rain, because it settles the dust of the afflictions.
It is like a foundation, because it provides the basis for the establishment and teaching of all bodhisattvas; it is like a magnet, because it does not adhere to the liberation of the śrāvakas;
it is like lapis lazuli, because its intrinsic nature is stainless.
It has become like a sapphire because it surpasses and exhausts all the knowledge of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all the world;
it has become like a drum at the end of the watch because it awakens beings who are asleep due to the afflictions;
it has become like clear water because it is free from turbidity.

It is like an ornament of Jāmbūnada gold, because it eclipses the accumulation of all roots of merit belonging to the realm of conditioned phenomena; it is like the king of great mountain ranges, because it is unshakable by the entire triple world;
it is a refuge, because it never abandons those who have come for shelter.
It is the true wealth by way of providing for the needs of others; it is the true mind by way of bringing satisfaction to the heart;
it is the true sacrificial implement by way of satisfying the entire world.
It has become the intellect because it is the most senior and most excellent among the minds of all living beings; it has become a treasury because it upholds all the qualities of a Buddha;
it has become a summary because it encompasses all the practices and vows of Bodhisattvas.
It is like a protector by virtue of guarding all worlds; it is like a guardian by virtue of turning back all evils;
it is like a magical net by virtue of drawing in the asuras of the afflictions.
He is like the noose of Varuṇa by virtue of drawing in those to be trained;
he is like Indra and Agni by virtue of burning away all latent tendencies, underlying propensities, and afflictions;
and he is like a shrine for the world of gods, humans, and asuras.
Thus, noble son, a bodhisattva is endowed with these and other immeasurable special qualities.

In brief, noble son, as many as there are all Buddha-dharmas and all Buddha-qualities, so many are the qualities of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and so many are the benefits of the qualities of the thought of awakening to be understood.
For what reason?
From this arises the entire mandala of the conduct of all bodhisattvas;
from this emerge all the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present.

Therefore, noble son, one who has generated the mind directed toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment becomes endowed with immeasurable qualities, because they are well-sustained by the resolute intention of the mind set on omniscience.
For example, noble son,
there is a medicinal herb called Abhayā;
by means of it, the five fears do not arise.
Namely: one is not burned by fire,
one is not overcome by poison,
and one is not wounded by a weapon.
He is not carried away by water and does not die from smoke.
In the same way, noble son, a bodhisattva who is sustained by the medicinal herb of the mind of omniscience is not burned by the fire of passion.
He is not assailed by the treachery of sense objects, he is not wounded by the weapon of the afflictions, and he is not swept away by the flood of existence.
One does not die from the smoke of conceptual construction.
Son of good family, it is just as there is a medicinal herb called "Unreleased";
when it is held, all fears of harm from others do not arise.
In the very same way, for a bodhisattva who is sustained by the medicine of the wisdom of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), all fears of the onset of *saṃsāra* do not exist.
For example, noble son,
there is a medicinal herb named *maghī*.
When that [medicine] is taken, all venomous serpents flee by its mere scent;
in the very same way, all the venomous serpents of the afflictions (*kleśa*) flee by the mere scent of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Noble son, it is just as a man who has taken the "Invincible" medicine (*aparājita-bhaiṣajya*) becomes unconquerable by any circle of enemies.
In the same way, a bodhisattva who has taken up the invincible medicine of the mind of omniscience becomes unassailable by the entire host of Māras and adversaries.
For example, noble son, there is a medicine called "Removal";
by it, all arrows fall away.
In the same way, for a bodhisattva who is sustained by the medicine that is the absence of the thought of awakening, all the thorns of passion, hatred, delusion, and wrong views fall away.
Son of good family, it is just as there is a great king of medicines named Sudarśana;
when taken, it eradicates all diseases.
In the same way, a bodhisattva who has taken up the great medicinal king known as the Sudarśana of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) eradicates all diseases of afflictions and ignorance.
For example, noble son, there is a great medicinal tree named Saṃtāna;
its bark, when applied, heals all wounds.
Just as its bark grows back once it has been peeled away,
even so the tree of the continuum of omniscience, produced from the seed of a bodhisattva, heals the wounds of karma and afflictions for faithful sons of noble family at the mere sight of it;
and that tree of omniscience remains unhurt and unimpaired by the entire world.
For example, noble son, there is a species of great medicinal herb called Unfailing Root,
by whose power all the trees throughout Jambudvīpa flourish and grow.

In the same way, by the power of the great medicinal root produced from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), all the trees of the Dharma belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas flourish.
For example, noble son, there is a medicinal herb called "Attainment of Delight" (*ratilambhā*); whoever has it within their body, [they become invulnerable].
Wholesomeness of body and mind arises for him.
In the same way, the medicinal herb of attaining the joy of generating the mind of omniscience produces wholesomeness of body and mind for all bodhisattvas.
For example, noble son, there is a medicinal herb named "Attainment of Mindfulness."
By means of that, mindfulness of the mind is purified.

In the same way, the medicinal herb of obtaining the mindfulness of the resolve for omniscience leads to the purification of unobstructed mindfulness regarding all the qualities of a Buddha for bodhisattvas.
For example, noble son, there is a medicinal herb named Mahāpadmā.
By that, the measure of one's lifespan becomes an eon.
In the very same way, a bodhisattva who is devoted to the great medicinal herb of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) attains mastery over a lifespan of incalculable eons.
For example, noble son, there is a medicinal herb named "Invisible."
When that [medicine] is taken, one is not seen by any humans or non-humans.

In the same way, a bodhisattva who has taken the great medicinal herb of the invisible thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is not seen within the entire domain of Māra, even while dwelling amidst worldly distractions.
Noble son, it is just as there exists in the great ocean a sovereign of great jewels named "The Collection of All Jewels" (*sarvamaṇiratnasamuccaya*).

It is impossible and there is no occasion for the fire that burns at the end of all eons to dry up even as much as a palm tree’s height of the great ocean, provided it has not moved to another world-system.

In the same way, it is impossible and there is no occasion for even a single wholesome root dedicated toward omniscience to perish for those bodhisattvas whose mental continuums are sustained by the resolute intention of the great king of jewels that gathers together all the jewels of the mind set on omniscience.
This is impossible.
Furthermore, once the production of the mind set on omniscience has been abandoned, all roots of virtue wither away.
It is, for example, like the great maṇi-jewel named Sarvaprabhāsasamuccaya.
By that [jewel] fastened around his neck, all ornaments of gems and jewels are eclipsed;

in the same way, a bodhisattva who has bound upon himself the great gem-jewel ornament of the resolve that gathers all the radiance of a bodhisattva surpasses all the jewel ornaments of the production of the thought of enlightenment belonging to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, just so, son of good family.
There is a great jewel called "water-clearer";
when it is cast into water, it clarifies all the turbidity of mud.
In the very same way, the great jewel that clarifies the water of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) clarifies all the turbidity of the mud of the afflictions (kleśa).
Just as, noble son, a fisherman who wears a water-dwelling *maṇi* jewel does not die in the water,
even so a bodhisattva who holds the water-dwelling *maṇi* jewel of the mind of omniscience does not die in the ocean of all saṃsāra.
Just as, noble son, there exists a great jewel called the *nāga-maṇi* armor.
Just as fishermen and others who live by the water, when accompanied by that [jewel], become unassailable by all *nāgas* and serpents upon entering all *nāga* abodes,

even so the Bodhisattva who maintains the jewel of the Dharma— the knowledge arising from the production of the mind of omniscience— is not harmed when entering all the abodes of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Noble son, it is just as Śakra, the king of the gods, when adorned with the *Śakrābhilagna* precious jewel, surpasses all the hosts of gods.

In the same way, a bodhisattva who has bound upon his crown the great wish-granting jewel-king that clings to Śakra— the great jewel of the mind of omniscience— overcomes the entire triple world. Just as, noble son, a man who holds the great wish-granting jewel-king does not fear any poverty,
even so a bodhisattva who holds the great wish-granting jewel-king of the arousal of the mind of omniscience does not fear any lack of requisites or threats to his livelihood.
Noble son, it is just as the sun-gem (*sūryakānta-maṇiratna*) releases fire when exposed to the sun;

in the same way, the sun-gem of the resolve for omniscience (*sarvajñatā-cittotpāda*), when touched by the rays of the jewel of wisdom (*prajñā-ratna*), releases the fire of primordial cognition (*jñāna*).
Noble son, it is just as the great precious gem called the moon-gem (*candrakānta*), when touched by the light of the moon, releases a stream of water.

In the same way, the great jewel of the moonstone of the arousal of the thought of enlightenment, when touched by the moonlight of the dedication of roots of goodness, releases streams of water consisting of all roots of goodness and vows. Just as, noble son, for the great dragon kings who wear crowns bound with the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, there is no fear of harm from others;

In the same way, for those who have bound upon their heads the crown-jewel of the king of thoughts— the great compassion of the mind of awakening— there is no fear of descending into the miserable states or the lower realms. Just as, noble son, the great jewel called *jagadvyūhagarbha* never comes to exhaustion because it fulfills the intentions of all sentient beings,

even so, the great jewel of the mind of awakening of a bodhisattva, which contains within it the array of the entire world, never comes to exhaustion because it fulfills the aspirations for awakening and the intentions of all sentient beings.
Just as, noble son, the great jewel of a universal monarch dispels darkness and illuminates even when situated within the inner apartments,
even so the great jewel of the universal monarch that is the production of the mind of omniscience dispels all the darkness of ignorance as it moves among the realms of sentient beings.
And while abiding in the desire realm,
he emits the light of great primordial wisdom.
For example, noble son, those who are touched by the radiance of the great sapphire jewel, [are transformed].
All of them take on the color of the great sapphire jewel;

in the same way, wherever the great sapphire jewel of the production of the mind of omniscience is examined or sent forth, and whatever roots of virtue are dedicated by means of that production of the mind of omniscience, [they all take on its color].

All of them take on the color of the great jewel of omniscience. For example, noble son, just as a lapis lazuli jewel, even if it remains in the midst of impurities for a hundred thousand years, does not coexist with any foul odor, in the same way, the jewel of the mind of omniscience— possessing a radiance that is utterly stainless and pure— surpasses the mines of jewels that are the qualities of all ordinary beings, those in training, those beyond training, and pratyekabuddhas.
For example, noble son, just as a great jewel called "Agni" (Fire) dispels all darkness and gloom,

even so does the great fire-jewel of the single production of the mind set on omniscience, when conjoined with insight and applied through appropriate mental attention, dispel the entire darkness and gloom of ignorance. For example, noble son, just as a priceless jewel placed upon a ship in the great ocean, held in the hand of a merchant, surpasses hundreds of thousands of glass jewels found in cities by its color and [value].

In the very same way, even when it has entered the great ocean of saṃsāra, the priceless great maṇi-jewel of the resolve for omniscience— having been placed upon the ship of the vow and residing within the mental continuum of the high resolve of a bodhisattva who has first generated that mind— surpasses all the glass trinkets of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even though it has not yet reached the city of omniscience or entered the city of liberation.

For example, there is a precious jewel called the Sovereign King (Vaśirāja), which, even when located in Jambudvīpa, displays the reflected arrays of the palaces and celestial mansions of the sun and moon discs situated forty thousand yojanas away.
In the very same way, the Sovereign King jewel of the resolve for omniscience, purified by all virtues, even while remaining within saṃsāra,
displays the reflected arrays of the entire mandala of the buddha-sphere of the great sun and moon of the Tathāgatas’ wisdom, whose domain is the sky of the dharma-realm.
For example, noble son, as far as the orbs of the sun and moon illuminate with their radiance,
whatever wealth, grain, jewels, gold, silver, flowers, perfumes, garlands, garments, or articles of enjoyment there may be within that range—
all of these are not equal in value to the sovereign king of jewels.

In the same way, as long as the omniscient wisdom illuminates the realm of the *dharmadhātu* throughout the three times, all the various wholesome qualities of gods, humans, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas— whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—
are not worth even a fraction of the price of the great jewel-king, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
For example, noble son, there is a great jewel called the "Womb of the Oceanic Array" which displays all the arrays of the great ocean;
in the same way, the great jewel called the "Womb of the Oceanic Array of the Arousing of the Mind of Enlightenment" displays the oceanic array of the sphere of the knowledge of omniscience.
For example, noble son, with the exception of the wish-fulfilling king of jewels, there is nothing more distinguished than divine Jāmbūnada gold.

In the same way, with the exception of the great cintāmaṇi jewel of the wisdom of the omniscient one, there is nothing more distinguished than the divine Jāmbūnada gold of the production of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Just as, noble son, a snake-charmer who has attained mastery over the circle of *nāgas* brings all *nāgas* and serpents under his control, so it is with the production of the thought of awakening.

In the same way, the bodhisattva snake-charmer, accomplished in the mandala of the nāga that is the practice of generating the mind of omniscience, brings under his control all the nāgas and serpents that are the afflictions.
Noble son, just as a hero who has taken up weapons becomes invincible to the host of enemies,
even so the bodhisattva who has taken up the weapon of generating the mind of omniscience becomes invincible to the host of enemies that are the afflictions.
For example, noble son, a single grain of powder from celestial uragasāra sandalwood pervades a thousandfold world system with its fragrance;
a measure of it, the size of a *karṣa*, cannot be matched in value by filling the entire three-thousandfold world system with jewels.

In the same way, a single element of resolute intention from the celestial uragasāra sandalwood of the production of the mind of omniscience pervades the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) with the fragrance of its qualities.
It also surpasses all the minds of those in training, those beyond training, and pratyekabuddhas.
For example, noble son, just as the great sandalwood jewel called Himavat-candana pacifies all burning heat and makes its entire substrate cool;
In the same way, the Himalayan sandalwood jewel of the resolve for omniscience pacifies the burning heat of all afflictions, conceptual constructions, passion, hatred, and delusion,
and refreshes the basis of wisdom.
Just as, noble son, those who approach Sumeru, the king of mountains, [find relief...]
They all become of one color, namely, the color of gold;
in the same way, those bodhisattvas who approach others who have generated the mind set on omniscience all become of one color, namely, the color of omniscience.

For example, noble son, the fragrance that wafts from the bark of the Pāriyātraka Kovidāra tree cannot be found among any of the varieties of flowers in all of Jambudvīpa, such as the vārṣika, jātī, or sumana; in the same way, the fragrance that wafts from the bark of the tree of the bodhisattva’s vow— the seed for the arising of the mind of omniscience— consisting of its qualities and gnosis, [cannot be matched by anything else].

It does not exist among all inferior roots of goodness, nor among the annual *vārṣika* and *jātisumanā* flowers of all *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, nor among their untainted (*anāsrava*) morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
rather, noble son, it should be understood that when the *pāriyātraka* or *kovidāra* tree has formed its buds, it will become the gateway for the emergence of many hundreds of thousands of flowers.

In the same way, it should be understood that when the sprout of the roots of goodness of the *pāriyātra* tree of the resolve for omniscience has emerged, it will become a gateway for the flowers of the enlightenment— both with-outflows and without-outflows— for incalculable gods and humans. Son of good family, it is just as when the fragrance of a cloth or oil perfumed with *pāriyātra* flowers for a single day wafts abroad.
It does not equal the scent of the oil of *campaka*, *vārṣikā*, or *sumanā* flowers that has been infused for a thousand days.

In the same way, the fragrance of the qualities and wisdom of a bodhisattva’s mental continuum—which has been cultivated through a single lifetime—pervades the presence of all Buddhas in the ten directions;

it cannot be matched by the fragrance of the knowledge of untainted wholesome dharmas belonging to the minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even if those have been cultivated for hundreds of thousands of eons.
For example, noble son, there is a species of tree called the coconut palm that grows in the Udyataka ocean;
from its roots up to its flowers and fruits, it is at all times a source of sustenance for all sentient beings, never failing to provide support.

In the very same way, the Bodhisattva’s first production of the mind set on omniscience—which is born from the root of the vow of great compassion—is at all times a source of sustenance for the world including the gods, until the final disappearance of the True Dharma.
It is so, noble son. For example, there is a type of elixir called *hāṭakaprabhāsa*;
a single *pala* of it turns a thousand *palas* of iron into gold.

And that single *pala* of mercury cannot be exhausted by those thousand *palas* of iron, nor can it be turned into iron. In the very same way, the single element of the essence of the resolve for omniscience (*sarvajñatā-cittotpāda*), when embraced by the knowledge of the dedication of roots of goodness, exhausts all the iron of the obscurations of karma and afflictions, and transforms all phenomena into the color of omniscience.
Furthermore, the elixir-element of the arousal of the mind of omniscience cannot be defiled or exhausted by the metals of all karma and afflictions.
Noble son, just as even a very small fire emits flames to the extent that it finds fuel,
even so, even a very small fire of the arousal of the mind of omniscience emits its radiance to the extent that it finds the fuel of the accumulations through its engagement with objects.
To that extent, the flame of knowledge increases by way of its radiance.

Just as, noble son, from a single lamp many hundreds of thousands of millions of lamps are lit, yet that original lamp remains inexhaustible and undiminished by all those lamps that have issued forth; even so, from the single lamp of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience, [the light of] the past, future, and present...
That single lamp of the arousal of the mind of omniscience of all the Tathāgatas shines forth unceasingly and inexhaustibly through its issues from the lamp of the arousal of the mind of omniscience.
It is just as if, noble son, a single lamp were brought into a house or a window.
Just as a lamp, upon being brought inside, dispels even the darkness of gloom accumulated over a thousand years and brings forth illumination,

even so, the single lamp of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience, when it is introduced into the deep cavern of a sentient being’s mental disposition— a place shrouded in the darkness of the gloom of ignorance— dispels, upon its entry, the darkness of the veil of afflictions accumulated even over hundreds of thousands of inexpressible eons.
And he generates the light of wisdom.
Just as, noble son, a lamp produces illumination according to the nature of its wick, and burns for as long as there is a store of oil; so too does it proceed.
In the same way, whatever specific excellence of the wick of the vow a bodhisattva possesses,
such is the illumination of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) produced by the lamp of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience;
and for as long as there is an accumulation of the oil of the practice of great compassion, [the light continues].
To that extent, there occurs the purification of the field for training sentient beings and the manifestation of the Buddha-activity.

Just as, noble son, the divine ornament of Jāmbūnada gold bound upon the head of the celestial king Vaśavartin cannot be taken away by any of the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*),
even so, the divine ornament of Jāmbūnada gold— the arousal of the mind set on omniscience— is established through the quality of practice.

For Bodhisattvas who are irreversible, this great vow is bound to their crowns and becomes unshakeable by all ordinary worldlings, learners, non-learners, and Pratyekabuddhas. Just as, noble son, by the roar of the lion, the king of beasts, newborn lion cubs are nourished;
Just as all deer go to their destruction,

even so, when the lion’s roar of the Tathāgata— the lion among men— uttering the praise of the thought of awakening and the cry of omniscience is applied, all the young lion-cubs that are beginner bodhisattvas flourish through the qualities of a Buddha, while all sentient beings who rely upon apprehension go to their destruction.

Just as, noble son, by the sound of the strings of a lute made from lion sinew all other lute strings are severed, even so, by the sound of the qualities and praises of the stringed instrument of the bodhicitta-sinew of the Tathāgata-lion— the body of the perfections— all the lute strings of delight in the qualities of sensual pleasures are severed, and all discourses on the qualities of the conduct of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are completely suppressed.

Just as, noble son, when a single drop of lion’s milk is cast into a great ocean filled with the milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats, all that milk is expelled and does not coalesce, even so, the great ocean of the milk of karma and afflictions accumulated over hundreds of thousands of eons is entirely and without remainder expelled by the casting of a single drop of the milk of the resolve for omniscience from the Great Man Lion, the Tathāgata.
They go to exhaustion;
the liberations of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not remain, nor do they coexist with it.

Just as, noble son, the excellence of the power of the cry of a young *kalaviṅka* bird that has not yet emerged from its eggshell is not matched by all the flocks of birds dwelling in the Himalayas, even those endowed with every strength and speed—just so, the excellence of the power of the cry of the great compassion and the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) of the young *kalaviṅka* bodhisattva who is still within the eggshell of saṃsāra is not matched by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Just as, noble son, the power and prowess of the wind from the wings, and the quality of the purity of the eyes, of a recently born young king of the great garuḍas [is unsurpassed]... (Gv 403)

That which does not exist in all other birds that have grown to full body size is likewise found in the Bodhisattva, the great garuḍa prince, who has arisen from the family and lineage of the Tathāgata, the great garuḍa king, at the moment of his first production of the thought of awakening; it is his power and prowess in producing the mind of omniscience, as well as the quality of the purification of the eye of the resolute intention of great compassion.
This does not exist among all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have emerged over hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

Son of good family, just as an iron arrow held in the hand of a great man pierces even the most solid armor, in the very same way, the iron arrow of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience held in the hand of a bodhisattva of firm vigor pierces the armor of all views and latent tendencies.
For example, noble son,
as long as a boil remains on the forehead of a great wrestler possessed by anger,
he is unassailable by all the people of Jambudvīpa.

In the same way, for the great athlete-like Bodhisattva who is permeated by great loving-kindness and great compassion, as long as the basket of the arousal of the mind of omniscience remains within his resolute intention, he remains unassailable by all Māras and all karmas included within all world-systems.

Son of good family, it is just like the specific power of skillful application and mastery in the arts possessed by a student of archery who has been trained and has practiced extensively in the knowledge of archery.
That which does not exist for a master of archery who has completed all his training,
even so, the specific excellence of the power of aspiration, gnosis, resolute conviction, and conduct belonging to a noble Bodhisattva— a beginner who has practiced on the stage of omniscience—
does not exist for any of those in training or those beyond training, nor for Pratyekabuddhas, who have not yet generated the mind of enlightenment.
Just as, noble son, for one training in archery, the initial practice of mastering footwork is the precursor to all knowledge of weaponry,

even so, for a bodhisattva training in the stage of omniscience, the initial setting forth of the resolute intention toward the mind of omniscience is the precursor to the realization of all the qualities of a buddha.

Just as, noble son, for a magician who displays the range of magical illusions, the accomplishment of all his actions occurs simply by focusing his mind on the initial production of the success of the mantra-words; even so, for a bodhisattva who displays the miraculous transformations within the range of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, it is the very production of the vow of the first arousal of the thought of enlightenment that serves as the instigator of the entire range of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Just as, noble son, all the spells and mantras of illusion— though formless and invisible— manifest all the forms produced by illusion through the mere arising of a thought,

even so the arising of the mind of omniscience, though formless and invisible, establishes the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through the mere mastery of the arising of that thought, by means of the arrays of the ornaments of all virtues.
Just as, noble son, at the mere sight and movement of a cat, all mice go to their destruction;
In the same way, by the mere investigation of the application of the resolute intention arising from the thought of omniscience, all karmas and afflictions of a bodhisattva come to dissolution.

Just as, noble son, an ornament of Jāmbūnada gold, when fastened, eclipses all other ornaments, even so a bodhisattva who has fastened the ornament of the resolute intention of the Jāmbūnada gold of the thought of awakening surpasses and eclipses all the ornaments of the qualities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Just as, noble son, even a very small particle of the king of magnetite shatters all firm iron bonds,
even so, even a very small element of the resolve for omniscience generated through high resolve shatters all bonds of ignorance and craving created by [wrong] views.
For example, noble son, wherever the magnetite element is applied, there all other pieces of iron flee;
they do not remain, nor do they adhere.
In the very same way, wherever the element of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience is examined— whether among karmas, afflictions, or the liberations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—
from that very place the karmas and afflictions, as well as all the liberations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, flee; they do not remain and they do not persist.

Just as, noble son, a fisherman who has boarded a vessel pierced by a makara is free from all fear of aquatic creatures and remains unhurt even when entering the mouth of a makara, in the very same way, a bodhisattva who relies on the vessel pierced by the *bodhicitta* of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is freed from all fear of the karma and afflictions of saṃsāra; he cannot be harmed by reaching the intermediate stages of realization of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because he does not fall into the path of the destruction of the direct realization of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Just as, noble son, a person who has drunk the nectar of immortality does not die from any assault by others,

even so a bodhisattva who has drunk the nectar of the production of the mind of omniscience does not die within any of the stages of the śrāvakas, nor does he cease from his vow of great compassion for bodhisattvas.
Just as, noble son, a person who has attained the power of an ointment wanders through all human dwellings yet is not seen by any humans,
even so a bodhisattva supported by the generation of the thought of awakening, wisdom, and aspiration wanders through all the domains of Māra,
yet is not seen by any Māras.

Just as, noble son, a man who relies upon a great king does not fear any ordinary person, even so a bodhisattva who relies upon the Great Dharma King— the arousal of the mind set on omniscience— does not fear any obscurations, hindrances, or miserable rebirths. Just as, noble son, in mountain dwellings there is no fear of fire because of the fear that water pervades all the ground;

In the same way, for a bodhisattva whose mental continuum is moistened by the roots of merit of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), there is no fear of the fire of the knowledge of liberation belonging to the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
Noble son, just as a man who relies on a hero does not fear any enemies,
even so a bodhisattva who relies on the hero that is the generation of the mind of omniscience does not fear any enemies that are misdeeds.

Just as, noble son, Śakra, the lord of the gods, having taken up his vajra weapon, crushes the entire host of asuras, even so the bodhisattva, having taken up the vajra weapon of the firm resolute intention that is the production of the mind of omniscience, crushes the entire host of Māras, adversaries, and asuras. Just as, noble son, a man who has employed an elixir preserves a long life and does not become weak...
In the same way, a bodhisattva who applies himself to the accumulation of the elixir of the resolve for omniscience does not grow weary while wandering through saṃsāra for incalculable eons,
nor is he defiled by the faults of saṃsāra.
Just as, noble son, water is the primary ingredient in all medicinal compounding of juices and is never corrupted, so it is with this resolve.
In the very same way, among all the applications of the equipment for the vows and conduct of a bodhisattva, the arousal of the mind set on omniscience is the precursor;
it does not fail in any respect.
Just as, noble son, for a person the life-faculty is the precursor in all activities, so it is here.

In the same way, for a bodhisattva, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is the precursor in the undertaking of all the qualities of a Buddha. Just as, noble son, a man who is deprived of the life-faculty becomes incapable of supporting his parents and circle of kinsmen because he is unable to perform any work,

even so, a bodhisattva who is separated from the production of the mind of omniscience becomes incapable of supporting the qualities of omniscience for all sentient beings, because he is unable to cause them to attain the wisdom of a Buddha.

Just as, noble son, the great ocean cannot be defiled by any poisons, even so the great ocean of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience cannot be defiled by the poisons of all karma, afflictions, or the arousal of the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Just as, noble son, the orb of the sun is beyond limit in its illumination compared to the light of all the stars, [so too is the bodhicitta].

In the same way, the solar disk of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience is not included within [the realms of] ordinary existence, and it outshines all the stainless qualities of the stars that are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Just as, noble son, a prince newly born outshines all the elder ministers who have reached the pinnacle of their careers by virtue of his noble lineage and sovereign authority; so too does this solar disk of the mind of omniscience outshine all the stainless qualities of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

In the same way, a beginner bodhisattva who has recently generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and has been born into the family of the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, surpasses even senior *śrāvakas* who have long practiced the holy life through the sovereign power of the thought of awakening and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Noble son, it is just as a minister, however old he may be, must prostrate before a prince, however young;
yet the prince need not show deference to the aged minister.
In the same way, even those who are very advanced and have long practiced the holy life—whether Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—should bow down before a beginner Bodhisattva;
yet a Bodhisattva should not fail to show respect toward Pratyekabuddhas. It is just so, noble son (Gv 405).

Just as a prince, though not yet despised by anyone, is not equal even to the king’s ministers who have attained the highest rank because he is not yet separated from the marks of royalty due to his status as the lord of the lineage;

even so, a beginner bodhisattva, though still somewhat despised due to his karma, afflictions, and grasping, is not equal even to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have attained the highest rank, because he is not separated from the mark of the production of the mind set on omniscience due to his sovereignty over the Buddha-lineage.
For example, noble son, just as a perfectly pure jewel appears to be impure due to the defect of cataracts in the eye,

even so, sentient beings perceive the jewel of the production of the mind of omniscience— which is by nature perfectly pure— as being impure because of the defect of the cataracts of ignorance and the lack of faith in their eyes.
For example, noble son, just as a personified medicine that contains a collection of all spells and herbs pacifies the diseases of sentient beings through being seen, touched, or lived with;

In the very same way, the body of the bodhisattva’s vow and gnosis— comprised of the medicinal elixir of wisdom and skillful means that accumulates all roots of virtue, and conjoined with the thought of awakening— pacifies the diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings through the application of hearing, seeing, dwelling together, and recollection.

Just as, noble son, a cloth marked with the sign of a swan is not defiled by the stains of any mud, even so the cloth marked with the sign of the arousal of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is not defiled by the stains of the mud of the afflictions (kleśa) of saṃsāra.
Just as, noble son, a wooden figure held together by a pin in its head does not fall apart, [so too is the bodhisattva].
And it experiences all activities;

in the very same way, the body of the wisdom of the vow for omniscience, when held by the arrow-head of the vow for the arousal of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), becomes capable of the activities of a bodhisattva,
and yet it is not scattered because it is the body of the vow for omniscience.
Just as, noble son, a mechanical device from which the pin has been removed becomes incapable of performing its function, even though it consists of those very same wooden parts;
in the same way, a bodhisattva who is separated from the high resolve of generating the mind set on omniscience becomes incapable of perfecting the qualities of a Buddha,
and so too are those accumulations of the factors of enlightenment.
For example, noble son, there is a black aloe-wood jewel called "Elephant-Womb" belonging to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
As soon as it is burned together with [the army], the entire fourfold army of the king stands suspended in the air.

In the very same way, the roots of merit of a bodhisattva, when perfumed by the aloe-wood of the resolve for omniscience, transcend the entire triple world and culminate in the sphere of the sky-like wisdom of all Tathāgatas, which is unconditioned.
Just as, noble son, a diamond does not arise from any other source of jewels, but only from a diamond mine or a gold mine,
even so is the diamond-like production of the mind set on omniscience.

It does not arise from any other source of the jewel-mine of the roots of goodness within the dispositions of beings, but only from the diamond mine of great compassion that protects beings, or from the great gold mine of the objective support for the wisdom of omniscience.

For example, noble son, there is a species of tree called "rootless. Its foundation as a root is not to be found, yet it is seen to be like a network among the trees, fully blossomed with all its branches, leaves, and foliage.
In the very same way, the foundation as a root for the production of the thought of omniscience is not to be found.

And he, blossomed with all merit, knowledge, and supernormal powers, is seen as a great web of vows manifested in all births throughout the worlds. Just as, noble son, a diamond does not shine when placed in an inferior vessel, nor can it be held by a vessel that is cracked or porous, except by a flawless vessel; so too is this Bodhisattva.

In the same way, the diamond of the resolve for omniscience cannot be sustained by any vessel of beings whose resolute intention is inferior—those who are miserly, immoral, malicious, lazy, forgetful, or of poor wisdom—nor by any vessel whose mind is unstable due to a corrupted superior intention; it can be sustained only by the precious vessel of a bodhisattva’s superior intention.
Son of good family, it is just as a diamond pierces through all other jewels.
In the same way, the diamond of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience pierces through all the jewels of phenomena.
Just as a diamond splits all mountains,
so too does the diamond of the arousal of the mind toward omniscience split all the mountains of dogmatic views.
Just as, noble son, even a broken diamond jewel surpasses all other jewels and outshines ornaments of gold,
even so, the diamond jewel of the resolve for omniscience, though broken by a failure of intention, outshines the golden ornaments of all the qualities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Just as, noble son, even a broken diamond jewel dispels all poverty, [so too does this jewel].
In the same way, even when broken, the diamond-jewel of the arousal of the mind of omniscience dispels all the poverty of saṃsāra.

Just as, noble son, however small a diamond-mine may be, it has the characteristic of splitting all gems and stones; in the same way, however slight an object of focus the diamond-mine of the arousal of the mind of omniscience may extend toward, it has the characteristic of splitting all ignorance.
Just as, noble son, a diamond jewel does not come into the hands of ordinary people,
even so the diamond jewel of the arousal of the mind of omniscience does not come into the hands of gods or humans who possess ordinary intentions and meager roots of virtue.

For example, noble son, just as a man unskilled in examining jewels, not knowing the qualities of a diamond-jewel (*vajramaṇiratna*), does not experience its specific excellence, even so a person of poor wisdom, being ignorant of the qualities of the diamond-jewel of the great wisdom of the bodhisattva-mind, does not experience its specific excellence. For example, noble son, just as a diamond cannot be worn out, [so too is this mind].

In the same way, the diamond of the arousal of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), which is the cause of omniscience, cannot be worn down. Just as, noble son, the diamond great weapon cannot be wielded even by a great athlete except by the power and force of Mahānārāyaṇa,
even so the great diamond weapon of the arousal of the mind for omniscience cannot be wielded even by all the great athletes among the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

It cannot be sustained by anyone other than great bodhisattvas who have attained a great radiance, who are supported by the power of the causes for omniscience, and who possess the distinguished might of Mahānārāyaṇa through their immeasurable roots of virtue.
Noble son, it is just as when no weapons can prevail, yet the thunderbolt prevails there and is not repelled.

In the same way, where the weapons of the aspirational knowledge of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not prevail— whether in the ripening and disciplining of sentient beings, or in dwelling amidst the sufferings of conduct throughout the kalpas of the three times—
there the bodhisattva, grasping the great vajra weapon of the arousal of the mind set on omniscience, prevails with an untiring mind and is not struck down.
Just as, noble son, it is impossible for any part of the earth to support a vajra except for a vajra-base, even so,

it is impossible for all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to support the vajra of the bodhisattva’s equipment for the vow of departure, except by the firm ground of the vajra of the resolve for awakening born of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Just as, noble son, because it is a vessel with no cracks due to its base of solid vajra, the water in the great ocean does not leak away;

In the same way, the roots of merit of a bodhisattva— firmly established through a dedication that is as solid and without fissures as a diamond— do not perish throughout all births in existence. Noble son, just as the great earth, being supported by a diamond base, neither splits nor sinks, even so the vows of a bodhisattva, firmly established on the diamond-like base of the arousal of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), do not split nor sink within the entire triple world.
Just as, noble son, a diamond is not moistened by water,
even so the diamond of the production of the thought of awakening is neither moistened nor scorched by the water of all karmic afflictions or by cohabitation with all karmas.
Just as, noble son, a diamond is not burned or consumed by the heat of any fire, [so too is the diamond of the thought of awakening].
In the same way, the diamond of the arousal of the mind of omniscience is not burned by the scorching fires of all the sufferings of saṃsāra,
nor is it tormented by the heat of the fires of all afflictions.
Son of good family, it is just as, for example, at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

For those who sit down, who fight against Māra, and who aspire to the realization of omniscience, no other spot of earth is capable of supporting their seat, except for the surface of the foundation of the great trichiliocosm which has a vajra-navel;

even so it is for Bodhisattvas who direct their resolve toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment, who practice the conduct, who fulfill the perfections, who enter into patience, who attain the stages, and who dedicate their roots of merit.

For those who receive their prophecy, who support the equipment for the path of all bodhisattvas, and who uphold the great clouds of Dharma of all Tathāgatas, the force of the empowerment of their great roots of virtue cannot be sustained by any other state of mind,
except by the arousal of the thought of omniscience, which has the adamantine, firm hub of the knowledge of all vows.
Thus, noble son, the production of the mind set on omniscience is endowed with these and other immeasurable qualities, even unto those that are ineffable and beyond description.
Those beings who have produced the minds set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment have likewise been, and will be, endowed with such qualities of dharma.
Therefore, noble son, you have gained a great gain, in that having resolved upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment, you seek the conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of attaining these qualities.
Moreover, noble son, as for what you have asked— how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice and how one should apply oneself— go, noble son.
Enter the interior of this great peaked pavilion, the Vairocana-vyūhālaṃkāra-garbha, and look within;
there you will know how one should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, and what kind of perfection of qualities arises for one who is so training.
Then the merchant’s son Sudhana, having circumambulated the Bodhisattva Maitreya, spoke thus: "Noble One, open the door of this peaked pavilion;
I shall enter.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Maitreya approached the base of the door of the peaked pavilion named Vairocana-vyūhālaṃkāragarbha and, with his right hand, made a snapping sound.
Its door opened of its own accord.
He said, "Enter this gabled hall, noble son.
Then Sudhana, the merchant’s son, overcome with supreme wonder, entered that gabled hall.
As soon as he had entered, that door closed behind him.
He beheld that peaked pavilion, vast and expansive, extending for many hundreds of thousands of yojanas,
immeasurable like the expanse of the sky, as wide as the realm of space in every direction, adorned with countless parasols, banners, and flags, and embellished with innumerable jewels.

It was adorned with countless hanging pearl necklaces, adorned with countless hanging jewel necklaces, adorned with countless hanging red pearl necklaces, adorned with countless hanging lion-pearl necklaces, adorned with countless lion-banner ornaments, adorned with countless moon and crescent-moon ornaments,
adorned with countless hanging garlands of various colored silk ribbons, and adorned with countless diverse silk pendants.
It was adorned with an incalculable network of jewel-lattices, adorned with an incalculable network of gold, adorned with an incalculable array of jeweled bands,
adorned with an incalculable array of inlaid precious golden threads, adorned with an incalculable resonance of sweet-sounding bells,
adorned with an incalculable network of jeweled tinkling-bells producing delightful sounds, and adorned by an incalculable rain of showers of celestial flowers.
It was adorned with countless hanging garlands of divine flowers; adorned with the service of incense burning from countless censers;

adorned by the raining down of countless showers of golden powder; adorned with countless networks of pavilions; adorned with countless windows; adorned with countless arched gateways; adorned with countless turrets; adorned with countless circular mirrors; and adorned with countless bricks made of precious gems.
It was adorned with countless jewel walls, adorned with countless pillars, adorned with clouds of countless jewel garments,
adorned with countless jewel trees, adorned with countless jewel railings, adorned with countless jewel pathways,
adorned with the arrays of all kinds of canopies made of countless jewels, and adorned with the various arrays of countless levels of ground upon which it rested.
It was adorned with palaces piled high with incalculable jewels; adorned with thrones made of incalculable jewels; adorned with incalculable maṇi-maidens;
adorned with walkways strewn with incalculable jeweled cloths; adorned with well-arranged pillars of Jāmbūnada gold-colored plantain trees in incalculable numbers;

adorned with incalculable figures made of every kind of jewel; adorned with the bodies of incalculable bodhisattvas; and adorned with the resonant cries of flocks of various beautiful birds in incalculable numbers.

It was adorned with incalculable jewel lotuses; it was adorned with the support of incalculable jewel pillars; it was adorned with incalculable lotus ponds; it was adorned with incalculable white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*);
it was adorned with incalculable jewel staircases; it was adorned with the arrangement of incalculable jewel railings; it was adorned with ground surfaces heaped with incalculable various jewels.

It was adorned with the radiance of incalculable great maṇi-jewels, adorned with incalculable arrays of all kinds of jewels, and adorned with the emergence of incalculable qualities and praises. Within that great peaked pavilion, he saw hundreds of thousands of other peaked pavilions likewise adorned with such arrays,
featuring incalculable adornments of jewel parasols, banners, and flags, up to and including incalculable adornments consisting of the emergence of qualities and praises.
He saw those gabled palaces, vast and expansive, becoming like an immeasurable treasury of space, beautifully arranged on all sides.

And these arrays of his gabled palaces—unmixed with one another, characterized by mutual friendliness toward one another, and not intermingled—appeared as reflections upon a single focal point through the power of manifestation. And just as they appeared upon that single focal point, so too...
Likewise with all remaining objects of focus.

Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Sudhana, having seen such an inconceivable manifestation of the miraculous power within the scope of this great peaked palace, the Vairocana-vyūhālaṃkāra-garbha, his body and mind drenched with great joy and rapture increased by an incomparable surge of delight, his mind shaken free from all states of conceptualization, his mind turned away from all obscurations, and all delusion departed.
With divine eyes free from forgetfulness, with ears possessing mindfulness and cognition unattached to all sounds, and being devoid of distraction regarding all mental attentions;

with an intellect that follows the eye of unobstructed liberation; with a tranquility of body directed toward the currents of all directions; and with eyes sent forth without obstruction toward all objects of perception;
he prostrated with his entire body through the power of accomplishment that pervades everywhere.
As soon as the merchant’s son Sudhana had prostrated himself, through the power of the Bodhisattva Maitreya’s empowerment, he perceived himself as having entered within all those gabled chambers.
And in all those gabled chambers, he beheld inconceivable miraculous displays of various and diverse natures within their respective domains.

In a certain gabled hall, where the Bodhisattva Maitreya first generated the mind of aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— by what name and clan he was born, by what root of merit, by what instigation, by what exhortation of a spiritual friend,
at what measure of lifespan, in what named eon, in the presence of which Tathāgata, in what kind of array, and in what kind of assembly, and by what [means]...
Through the accomplishment of the excellence of his vows,
he saw all of that, perceived it, and followed after it.
And for as long as the lifespan of those beings and of that Tathāgata was at that time,
for that entire duration he perceived himself as having gone to the feet of that Tathāgata;
and he saw all those activities.

In one place he saw the peaked pavilion where the Bodhisattva Maitreya first attained the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrasamādhi*), from which time forth his name "Maitreya" arose; and in another place he saw where his various spiritual practices (*caryā*) were performed.
In some places where the perfections were fulfilled;
in some places where patience was entered; and in some places where the stages were traversed.
In some places, where the arrays of Buddha-fields were embraced; in some places, where the teaching of the Tathāgata was maintained;
and in some places, where receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena was attained.

In some places, he saw where [the Buddha] had been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—how he was prophesied, by whom he was prophesied, and after how long he was prophesied; he saw all of that.
In another place, he saw the Bodhisattva Maitreya in a gabled palace, having become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), establishing sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action.

In some places he appeared as a world-protector, bestowing benefit and happiness upon all beings; in some places he appeared as Śakra, turning beings away from delight in the qualities of sensual desire; in some places he appeared as Brahmā, praising for beings the delight in the meditative absorptions and the immeasurables.
In some places he appeared as the sovereign lord of the Suyāma gods, extolling the immeasurable virtues of sentient beings;
in some places he appeared as the lord of the Tuṣita gods, proclaiming the qualities of Bodhisattvas bound to one more birth;
in some places he appeared as the king of the Sunirmita gods, displaying within the assembly of gods the array of all the emanations of Bodhisattvas.
In some places he appeared as the divine king Vaśavartin, manifesting the sovereignty over all phenomena; in other places he assumed the state of Māra,
teaching the gods the impermanence of all prosperity.

In some places, he saw [the Buddha] born in the palaces of the lords of the asuras, teaching the Dharma to the assembly of asuras for the sake of abandoning all pride, intoxication, and arrogance, for the sake of plunging into the great ocean of wisdom, for the sake of plunging into the ocean of knowledge of the Dharma, and for the sake of attaining the illusory nature of the knowledge of the Dharma;
in other places, he saw him in a gabled hall in the world of Yama.
There he saw the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having illuminated the great hells with his radiance, pacifying all the sufferings of the hell-beings born therein.
In another place, he saw a palatial mansion belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts;
there he saw the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having brought forth abundant food and drink for the beings born in the realm of hungry ghosts, pacifying their hunger and thirst.
In one gabled hall, he saw him disciplining beings born in the animal realm by means of the various distinctions of their places of rebirth;
in another gabled hall, he saw him teaching the Dharma to the world-protectors in the assembly of the gods of the Four Great Kings;
in some, to the assembly of Śakra, king of the gods; in others, to the assembly of Suyāma, king of the gods; and in others, to the assembly of Saṃtuṣita, king of the gods.

In some places he saw him in the assembly of the god-king Sunirmita, in some places in the assembly of the god-king Vaśavartin, and in some places in a gabled hall within the assembly of Brahmā and Indra, where the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having become a Great Brahmā, was teaching the Dharma.
In some places he saw him in the assembly of nāgas and mahoragas, in some places in the assembly of yakṣas and rākṣasas, and in some places in the assembly of gandharvas and kinnaras.

In some places, in the assemblies of the lords of asuras and dānavas; in some places, in the assemblies of the lords of mahoragas; in some places, in the assemblies of the lords of humans; and in some places, in gabled palaces within assemblies of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—he saw the Bodhisattva Maitreya teaching the Dharma.

In some places he saw him teaching the Dharma to an assembly of śrāvakas, in some places to an assembly of pratyekabuddhas, in some places to an assembly of bodhisattvas, and in some places within a gabled hall to bodhisattvas who were beginners having first resolved their minds toward enlightenment; in all these places, he saw him teaching the Dharma to the bodhisattva Maitreya.

In some places he saw [the Lord] extolling the excellence of the stages of the bodhisattvas— those engaged in conduct, those who have attained forbearance and are irreversible, those bound to only one more birth, those who have received the consecration, and those bodhisattvas established on the first stage within a peaked pavilion;
and in other places he saw him singing together with bodhisattvas established on all ten stages, including the bodhisattva Maitreya, about the excellence of all the stages.

In some places, the immeasurability of the complete fulfillment of all the perfections; in some places, the equality of entering into the manifestation of all the trainings; in some places, the vastness of entering the gateways of meditative concentration; in some places, the profundity of the methods of liberation; in some places, the pervasion of the domain of peaceful dhyāna, meditative absorption, attainment, and supernormal knowledge;
in some places, the entry into the gateways of the bodhisattva’s conduct, discipline, and skillful means; and in some places, the vastness of the accomplishment of vows.

In one place, he saw the Bodhisattva Maitreya in a gabled hall, engaged in walking meditation together with Bodhisattvas of similar conduct, chanting in unison for the sake of performing deeds that benefit the world— specific treatises on various arts and sciences that are conducive to establishing the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
In one place, he saw him singing together with bodhisattvas bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) upon the gateway of the consecration into the wisdom of all buddhas;
in another peaked pavilion, he saw the bodhisattva Maitreya engaged in walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), never laying down his burden for hundreds of thousands of years;

in some places, he was engaged in recitation and study (*uddeśasvādhyāya*); in others, engaged in the contemplation of gateways to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*); and in others, engaged in the communal chanting of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃgāyana*).

In some places he saw the Bodhisattva Maitreya engaged in writing down the Dharma; in some places, absorbed in the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); in some places, absorbed in all the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); in some places, absorbed in the liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); and in some places, within a gabled pavilion, absorbed in the concentration of the application for accomplishing the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva.
In some gabled chambers, he saw bodhisattvas who had entered the bodhisattva-samādhi called Nirmāṇavatī;
and he saw from every pore of their bodies clouds of all manner of emanations streaming forth.
He saw that from the pores of some, clouds of divine hosts were issuing forth;
from others, clouds of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, world-protectors, and universal monarchs;
from others, clouds of regional kings; from others, clouds of princes; and from others, clouds of guild-masters, ministers, and householders.

He saw some [bodhisattvas] emitting clouds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; some emitting clouds of the bodies of tathāgatas; and some emitting from every pore of their bodies immeasurable clouds of emanations of all sentient beings.
From the pores of some, he heard various gateways of the Dharma emerging, namely:

The gateways that extol the qualities of the bodhisattvas; the gateways of the perfection of generosity; and the gateways of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and primordial awareness.

He heard sounds emerging from the entry into all such dharma-gates as the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the attainments of meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the sciences (*vidyā*), the mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*), eloquence (*pratibhāna*), the truths (*satya*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), the doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the reliances (*pratiśaraṇa*), the summaries of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), discourses on the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*), discourses on the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), discourses on the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), the stages (*bhūmi*), the practice of patient acceptance (*kṣānticaryā*), and the gates of aspiration (*praṇidhānamukha*).
In some peaked pavilions, he saw the assemblies of the circles of the Tathāgatas' retinues gathered together;

and he beheld the various diversities of those Tathāgatas— their diversity of birth and family, the diversity of the immeasurable arrays of their bodies, the diversity of their lifespans, the diversity of their buddha-fields, the diversity of their eons, the diversity of their teaching of the Dharma, the diversity of the gateways of their emanations, and the diversity of the duration of their True Dharma.
He beheld the diversity of the entire circle of the assembly in all its aspects, without exception.

And in the center of that great peaked palace, the Vairocana-vyūhālaṃkāragarbha, he saw another peaked palace— more magnificent and more vast than all others, adorned with an array of ornaments that surpassed every other arrangement without exception.
